teile.einleitung: A main group is a vertical column in the periodic table of the elements. All the elements in a main group have the same number of outer electrons and therefore behave similarly in chemistry. In the classic arrangement there are eight main groups.
wichtigste: Main groups are vertical columns in the periodic table.
Classically there are 8 main groups.
Elements of the same main group have the same number of valence electrons.
Main group 3 is called the boron group after its first element; aluminium is also in it.
Main group 4 is called the carbon group; below carbon is silicon.
Main group 6, with oxygen and sulphur, is called the chalcogens.
Many main groups have their own names, such as alkali metals, halogens and noble gases.

abschnitte.text: In the **periodic table**, all the chemical elements are arranged in rows and columns. The rows are called periods, and the vertical columns are called **groups**. The eight groups on the left and right edges are called main groups. Between them are the **transition groups** with metals such as iron, copper and gold. In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev was the first to arrange the elements so that similar elements are placed one below another.

Every atom has electrons arranged in shells around the nucleus. The electrons in the outermost shell are called **valence electrons**. They determine how an element reacts with others. For the main groups, the group number equals the number of valence electrons: sodium in main group 1 has one, chlorine in main group 7 has seven. That is why elements in a group react in a similar way, like brothers and sisters with the same characteristics.

Main group 1 is called the **alkali metals**; it includes lithium, sodium and potassium. Main group 2 are the alkaline earth metals such as magnesium and calcium. Group 3 is the **boron group** with boron and aluminium, group 4 the carbon group with carbon, silicon and tin. Group 5 is called the nitrogen group, group 6 the **chalcogens** with oxygen and sulphur. Main group 7 are the halogens such as fluorine and chlorine, group 8 the noble gases such as helium, neon and argon.

Alkali metals are so reactive that they react violently with water. Halogens form salts with metals; table salt, for example, consists of sodium and chlorine. **Noble gases** hardly react at all, because their outer shell is full. That is why light bulbs are filled with argon and neon signs with neon. Within a group, the atoms get larger from top to bottom, and the properties often change step by step too.

Today the international chemistry organisation **IUPAC** recommends numbering all 18 columns in order. The main groups then have the numbers 1, 2 and 13 to 18. So the boron group is group 13, and the noble gases are group 18. In many school books, including in Switzerland, the classic numbering from 1 to 8 is still used, however. Both systems describe the same columns.

begriffe.erklaerung: A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.
The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
Main group 6 with oxygen and sulphur.
Main group 7; the name means “salt formers”.
Main group 8, gases that hardly ever react.

gewusst: Silicon is directly below carbon and is the most important material in computer chips.
Helium is among the noble gases even though it has only two outer electrons.
The name halogens means “salt formers”.

teile.einleitung: Electrochemistry studies how chemical reactions and electric current are connected. On the one hand, reactions can produce electricity, as in a battery. On the other hand, electricity can force chemical reactions to happen, as in electrolysis.
wichtigste: Electrochemistry links chemistry and electricity.
In a galvanic cell, a chemical reaction produces electric current.
Oxidation takes place at the anode.
A Daniell cell supplies 1.10 volts under standard conditions.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a standard potential of 0 volts.
In the electrolysis of water, hydrogen forms at the negative pole.
The Faraday constant is about 96,485 C/mol.
From 1888, aluminium was produced by molten salt electrolysis in Neuhausen am Rheinfall.

abschnitte.text: Around 1780 the Italian Luigi Galvani noticed that frogs' legs twitch when they touch two different metals. Alessandro **Volta** realised that the current comes from the metals. In 1800 he built the **voltaic pile**, the first battery, from discs of zinc and copper with card soaked in salt water between them. The unit volt is named after him.

In a **galvanic cell**, a metal gives up electrons; it is oxidised, and this happens at the **anode**. The electrons flow through a wire to the **cathode**, where a reduction takes place. In the Daniell cell of 1836, zinc and copper stand in solutions of their salts; it supplies 1.10 volts under standard conditions. The voltage of different metals is compared with the standard hydrogen electrode, which is fixed at 0 volts.

In **electrolysis**, electricity is used to force a reaction that would not happen by itself. In the electrolysis of water, hydrogen forms at the negative pole and oxygen at the positive pole. In the 1830s Michael Faraday found the laws for how much substance is produced. The **Faraday constant** of about 96,485 C/mol gives the charge of one mole of electrons. One mole of electrons deposits, for example, about 31.8 grams of copper, because each copper ion needs two electrons.

Aluminium can be obtained from its ore only with a lot of electricity. In 1886 Paul Héroult and Charles Martin Hall independently invented **molten salt electrolysis**. From 1888 the Aluminium Industrie AG in Neuhausen am Rheinfall used it to make aluminium, with the electricity supplied by the water power of the Rhine. This made Neuhausen one of the first aluminium smelters in Europe.

Batteries in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars are rechargeable galvanic cells, mostly **lithium ion batteries**. Fuel cells produce electricity from hydrogen and oxygen. In electroplating, objects are coated with a thin layer of metal, for example chromium or gold. The rusting of iron is also an electrochemical process.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrode at which oxidation takes place.
The electrode at which reduction takes place.
The chemical breaking down of a substance with the help of electric current.
An arrangement in which a chemical reaction produces electricity.
The giving up of electrons.

gewusst: In the 19th century, aluminium was at times more expensive than gold.
A lemon with a piece of copper and a piece of zinc becomes a small battery.
Making aluminium takes a great deal of electricity, but recycling it needs only a small part of that.

teile.einleitung: Ammonia is a colourless gas with the formula NH₃ that has a pungent smell. It is one of the most important substances in the chemical industry, because most of the world's fertilisers are made from it. Without ammonia, humanity could not feed so many people today.
wichtigste: Ammonia consists of one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.
The gas has a pungent smell and is lighter than air.
A solution of ammonia in water is alkaline.
When ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion, the ammonium ion NH₄⁺ is formed.
On an industrial scale, ammonia is made by the Haber Bosch process.
Most ammonia is made into fertilisers.
Ammonia is used as a refrigerant in artificial ice rinks and large cold stores.

abschnitte.text: At room temperature, ammonia NH₃ is a **colourless gas** with a pungent smell. Even small amounts irritate the eyes and airways. The gas is lighter than air and therefore rises. Under pressure or in the cold it becomes liquid; it boils at about minus 33 °C.

Ammonia dissolves very well in water. In doing so it takes up a hydrogen ion and becomes the **ammonium ion** NH₄⁺, leaving hydroxide ions behind. That is why the solution is **alkaline**. A solution of ammonia in water is called household ammonia, “Salmiakgeist” in German, and was often used in the past as a cleaner for windows and greasy stains.

In the **Haber Bosch process**, nitrogen from the air and hydrogen react with each other to form ammonia. This needs high pressure, high temperatures and an iron **catalyst**. Fritz Haber developed the method in the laboratory, and Carl Bosch made it suitable for industry. Both received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, Haber in 1918 and Bosch in 1931.

Plants need nitrogen to grow but cannot take it directly from the air. That is why **nitrogen fertilisers** such as urea or ammonium nitrate are made from ammonia. Most of the ammonia produced worldwide ends up in fertilisers. Experts estimate that without this artificial fertiliser only about half as many people could be fed.

When liquid ammonia evaporates, it takes up a lot of heat. That is why it is an excellent **refrigerant**. In Switzerland, many **artificial ice rinks** and large cold stores are cooled with ammonia. It does not harm the ozone layer and does not add to the greenhouse effect, but because it is poisonous it has to be monitored carefully.

Ammonia is poisonous and in high concentrations can damage the lungs. In nature it is formed when protein breaks down, for example in dung and slurry. The typical smell in a cowshed comes to a large extent from ammonia. If too much of it gets into the environment, it can over fertilise forests and waters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The positively charged particle NH₄⁺, formed from ammonia and a hydrogen ion.
A solution of ammonia in water, once a popular cleaning product.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
A substance that takes up heat in cooling systems and carries it away.

gewusst: A large part of the nitrogen in your body comes from ammonia that was made in factories.
The word ammonia goes back to the Egyptian god Amun, near whose temple sal ammoniac was found.
Ammonia is not only found on Earth; the atmosphere of the planet Jupiter also contains it.

teile.einleitung: Ceramics is a hard material that is shaped from clay and then fired in a kiln. Whether plates, flowerpots, roof tiles or bathroom tiles: we come across ceramics every day. It is one of the oldest materials that people have made themselves.
wichtigste: Ceramics are made mainly from clay.
Only firing in the kiln makes soft clay hard and firm.
Someone who makes crockery from clay is a potter by trade.
Round vessels are shaped on the spinning potter’s wheel.
Porcelain is a particularly fine, white ceramic.
A shiny glaze makes ceramics watertight and beautiful.
Bathroom tiles and red roof tiles are usually made of fired clay.

abschnitte.text: **Ceramics** is a collective term for objects made of fired, non-metallic raw materials. The most important raw material is **clay**, a fine, mouldable earth made of tiny mineral particles. Clay is kneaded with water, shaped and dried. The word ceramics comes from the Greek word “keramos”, which means potter’s clay.

After shaping, the clay must first dry slowly, otherwise it cracks. Then it is fired in a special kiln, depending on the type at about 900 to over 1400 degrees Celsius. At this heat the minerals in the clay change, and the material becomes rock hard. Often a second firing with **glaze** follows, a glassy layer that makes the vessel watertight and shiny. Unfired clay, on the other hand, would go soft again in water.

Roughly speaking, there is **earthenware**, **stoneware** and **porcelain**. Earthenware, such as flowerpots or roof tiles, is porous and is fired at fairly low temperatures. Stoneware is denser and is often used for sturdy crockery. Porcelain is made from kaolin, feldspar and quartz, fired at very high temperatures and is white and sometimes even slightly translucent.

As early as the Stone Age, people shaped figures from clay and fired them in the fire. The oldest known clay vessels come from China and are about 20,000 years old. The **potter’s wheel** was invented about 5000 to 6000 years ago in the Near East. Porcelain was invented in China; in Europe it was only successfully made at the beginning of the 18th century in Meissen.

In the kitchen we use cups, plates and bowls made of ceramics. Houses are built with bricks and roofed with tiles, and floors and walls are covered with tiles. Washbasins and toilet bowls are also made of ceramics, because it is hard, smooth and easy to clean. Modern technical ceramics are found in spark plugs, knife blades, dental crowns and heat shields.

In the Thun and Heimberg region in the canton of Bern, pottery has a long tradition; the colourful Thun majolica is well known. In Langenthal, porcelain was made for many decades. Today there are small pottery studios and courses in many Swiss places, where children can also work at the potter’s wheel.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine, soft earth that can be kneaded and shaped with water.
Strong heating in a kiln so that the shaped clay becomes hard.
A glassy, shiny layer on ceramics that makes them watertight.
Very fine, white and hard ceramic made from kaolin, feldspar and quartz.
A spinning disc on which round vessels are shaped from clay.

gewusst: Porcelain was once so valuable in Europe that it was called “white gold”.
NASA’s space shuttles were protected from the heat of re-entry by thousands of ceramic tiles.
Because clay shrinks when it dries and is fired, a potter has to make pieces a little larger.

teile.einleitung: The Arrhenius equation describes how strongly the speed of a chemical reaction depends on temperature. It is k = A·e^(-Ea/(R·T)) and was set up by the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius. It explains why food stays fresh longer in the fridge and why catalysts speed up reactions so much.
wichtigste: The Arrhenius equation is k = A·e^(-Ea/(R·T)).
k is the rate constant, Ea the activation energy, R the gas constant and T the temperature in kelvin.
The factor A is called the pre exponential factor.
Svante Arrhenius from Sweden set up the equation and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903.
Reactions with a large activation energy are particularly sensitive to changes in temperature.
In an Arrhenius plot, ln k against 1/T gives a straight line with gradient −Ea/R.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy and so makes the reaction faster.

abschnitte.text: **Svante Arrhenius** was a Swedish scientist who lived from 1859 to 1927. In 1889 he published the equation that bears his name today. For his theory of ions in solutions he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1903. He was also one of the first to calculate that carbon dioxide can warm the Earth.

In the equation k = A·e^(-Ea/(R·T)), k stands for the **rate constant**, that is, how fast a reaction takes place. Ea is the **activation energy**, the energy barrier that particles must overcome when they collide. R is the universal gas constant, about 8.314 J/(mol·K), and T is the temperature in kelvin. The **pre exponential factor** A depends on how often and how favourably the particles collide.

At higher temperatures, particles move faster. As a result, many more collisions have enough energy to overcome the **activation energy**. A rule of thumb, the **van 't Hoff rule**, says: 10 degrees warmer makes many reactions about two to three times faster. If a reaction becomes twice as fast from 298 K to 308 K, its activation energy is about 53 kJ/mol.

If you take the natural logarithm of both sides of the equation, you get ln k = ln A minus Ea/(R·T). If you plot ln k against 1/T, you get a **straight line**. Its gradient is −Ea/R. In this way the activation energy of a reaction can be found from measurements at different temperatures.

A **catalyst** lowers the activation energy. Just 10 kJ/mol less makes a reaction at 298 K about 57 times faster, if A stays the same. In the fridge the opposite happens: the cold slows down the reactions that make food go off. The **enzymes** in our body are catalysts too; without them, many life processes would run far too slowly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The minimum energy particles need for a reaction to start.
A number that shows how fast a reaction takes place at a particular temperature.
A unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero; 0 °C is about 273 K.
A fixed natural constant R that appears in many formulas in chemistry.

gewusst: A reaction with an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol becomes almost twice as fast just from warming it from 300 K to 310 K.
Crickets chirp faster in warm weather, because their body chemistry also depends on temperature.
Arrhenius worked not only on reactions but also on climate, heavenly bodies and the origin of life.

teile.einleitung: Infrared spectroscopy, IR spectroscopy for short, is a method chemists use to find out which building blocks a molecule contains. A substance is irradiated with infrared light and you measure which parts of it the substance absorbs. Because every molecule shows its own pattern, it works almost like a fingerprint.
wichtigste: Infrared radiation mainly makes molecules vibrate.
Each type of bond absorbs infrared light at typical wavenumbers.
A C=O double bond shows a strong band at about 1700 cm⁻¹.
An alcohol O-H group shows a broad band around 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹.
The region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is called the fingerprint region.
Wilhelm Herschel discovered infrared radiation in 1800.
The heart of an FTIR spectrometer is a Michelson interferometer.

abschnitte.text: **Infrared radiation** is light that is invisible to our eyes because its waves are longer than those of red light. But we feel it as heat, for example from a radiator or in the sun. It was discovered by the astronomer **Wilhelm Herschel** in 1800. He split sunlight with a prism and put thermometers behind the colours. Next to the red end, where no light could be seen any more, it was warmest.

The atoms in a molecule are joined by bonds that behave like little springs. They can stretch, squash and bend; this is called **molecular vibration**. If infrared light with exactly the right energy hits a molecule, it is absorbed and the vibration becomes stronger. Light atoms vibrate faster than heavy ones, which is why a C-D bond with heavy **deuterium** lies at a lower wavenumber than a C-H bond. Strong bonds also vibrate faster than weak ones.

An **IR spectrum** shows at which wavenumbers a substance absorbs light. The **wavenumber** is given in cm⁻¹ and is the reciprocal of the wavelength, so 2000 cm⁻¹ corresponds to 5 µm. A C=O double bond, for example in acetone, produces a strong band at about 1700 cm⁻¹. Alcohols show a broad O-H band around 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹ because they form hydrogen bonds. Below about 1500 cm⁻¹ lies the **fingerprint region**, whose pattern is unique for every molecule.

Modern instruments are mostly **FTIR spectrometers**, which stands for Fourier transform infrared. Their heart is a Michelson interferometer with a moving mirror. Instead of measuring each wavenumber separately, the instrument records them all at the same time. A computer then converts the measurement into a spectrum using a mathematical method, the Fourier transform. So a measurement often takes only a few seconds.

Pharmaceutical companies use IR spectroscopy to check whether a medicine contains the right active ingredient. The police use it to examine paint chips, fibres or suspicious powders. In food testing and recycling, it is used to recognise different plastics. Atmospheric scientists also use it, because gases such as **carbon dioxide** and methane absorb infrared radiation and so contribute to the greenhouse effect. Space telescopes such as the James Webb Telescope also observe space in infrared light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible light with long waves that we feel as heat.
The back and forth movement of the atoms in a molecule.
The reciprocal of the wavelength, given in cm⁻¹.
A place in the spectrum where light is absorbed.
Part of the spectrum with a pattern that is unique for every molecule.

gewusst: Herschel actually discovered infrared radiation by chance with completely ordinary thermometers.
Snakes such as pit vipers can sense the infrared radiation of warm prey.
Remote controls send their signals with invisible infrared light.

teile.einleitung: The limewater test is a simple chemical test for detecting the gas carbon dioxide. If you bubble the gas into clear limewater, it turns milky and cloudy. With this experiment you can even show that the air we breathe out contains carbon dioxide.
wichtigste: The limewater test is used to detect carbon dioxide.
Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water.
Limewater is alkaline.
In a positive test, the limewater turns milky and cloudy.
The cloudiness is caused by finely spread calcium carbonate.
Exhaled air contains about 4 per cent carbon dioxide.
If you keep bubbling carbon dioxide in for a very long time, the solution becomes clear again.

abschnitte.text: **Limewater** is a clear, colourless solution of **calcium hydroxide** in water. Calcium hydroxide is also called slaked lime; it is used, for example, for mortar. Limewater is **alkaline**, that is the opposite of acidic, and can irritate skin and eyes. That is why pupils wear safety goggles when experimenting. It is made by stirring calcium hydroxide into water and filtering off the undissolved remains.

You bubble the gas you want to test into a test tube of limewater. If it contains **carbon dioxide**, this reacts with the calcium hydroxide. Water and **calcium carbonate**, that is chalk, are formed. Calcium carbonate hardly dissolves in water and floats in the liquid as tiny white particles. That is why the limewater turns milky and cloudy, and the test is positive.

A popular school experiment goes like this: you carefully blow breath into limewater through a small tube. After a short time it turns cloudy. This shows that exhaled air contains a lot of carbon dioxide, about **4 per cent**. The air we breathe in, on the other hand, contains only about 0.04 per cent. The body produces carbon dioxide during **cellular respiration**, when it burns nutrients to obtain energy.

If you hold a cold glass over a burning candle and then shake the collected gases with limewater, it turns cloudy. This shows that carbon dioxide is produced when something burns. Because carbon dioxide contains carbon, the **candle wax** must also contain carbon. So with the limewater test you can also find out which elements a substance is made of. The same applies to wood, paper or natural gas.

If you keep bubbling carbon dioxide into the cloudy limewater for a very long time, something surprising happens: the solution becomes clear again. The calcium carbonate turns into **calcium hydrogen carbonate**, which dissolves well in water. Exactly this reaction also takes place in nature when water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and forms caves. In a similar way, lime mortar in old walls hardens because it slowly takes up carbon dioxide from the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A check that shows whether a particular substance is present.
Slaked lime, which dissolved in water gives limewater.
Chalk, which comes out of solution as white cloudiness.
A colourless gas that we breathe out and that is produced when things burn.
The process by which body cells obtain energy and produce carbon dioxide.

gewusst: Exhaled air contains about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than fresh air.
Lime mortar in old walls hardens over many years through the same reaction.
You can neither see nor smell carbon dioxide itself; the limewater makes it visible.

teile.einleitung: Vinegar is a sour liquid that you find in almost every kitchen. It flavours salad dressings, keeps gherkins fresh and even helps with cleaning. It is made by tiny bacteria.
wichtigste: Vinegar tastes sour and has a sharp, sour smell.
The sour taste comes from acetic acid.
Bacteria turn the alcohol in wine, cider or beer into vinegar.
Cider vinegar is made from apples, wine vinegar from wine.
In the kitchen, vinegar is often used for salad dressing.
Gherkins are pickled in vinegar so that they keep longer.
Vinegar can be used to remove limescale from the kettle.

abschnitte.text: Vinegar is water in which **acetic acid** is dissolved. Table vinegar usually contains about 5 per cent acetic acid; the rest is mainly water with flavourings and colourings. That is why vinegar tastes sour and smells sharp. There is also vinegar essence, which is much stronger and has to be diluted before use. Undiluted vinegar essence can irritate the skin.

Vinegar is made when **acetic acid bacteria** use oxygen from the air to turn the alcohol in a drink into acetic acid. In this way wine becomes wine vinegar, and apple cider becomes cider vinegar. Sometimes a slimy skin of bacteria forms, the **mother of vinegar**. In the 19th century the Frenchman Louis Pasteur discovered that bacteria are behind vinegar making. In factories today, vinegar is made in large containers into which air is blown.

Vinegar gives salad dressings, sauces and soups a fresh, sour taste. Gherkins, onions or beetroot pickled in vinegar keep for a long time, because hardly any germs can grow in the sour liquid. This way of making food last is called **preserving**. Well known kinds are wine vinegar, cider vinegar, rice vinegar and the dark aceto balsamico from the area around Modena in Italy.

Vinegar dissolves **limescale**, which builds up in the kettle, in the coffee machine or on the tap. The acid reacts with the limescale, and little bubbles of carbon dioxide rise up. The same happens with a raw egg: if it lies in vinegar for days, the shell dissolves, because it is made of lime. What is left is a wobbly egg held together only by a thin skin.

Vinegar is one of humanity's oldest foods, because wine turns into vinegar by itself if it is left open to the air. It was already known in ancient Babylon and in Egypt. Roman soldiers drank a mixture of water and vinegar as a refreshment. The French word vinaigre means “sour wine”.

begriffe.erklaerung: The acid that gives vinegar its sour taste and sharp smell.
A slimy skin of acetic acid bacteria that can form on vinegar.
Treating food so that it keeps for longer.
A hard, white coating that builds up from hard water; chemically mainly calcium carbonate.

gewusst: An egg that has lain in vinegar for a few days can bounce a little if you drop it carefully.
Ants use an acid too, but that is formic acid, not acetic acid.
Some kinds of aceto balsamico mature for many years in wooden barrels.

teile.einleitung: In heterogeneous catalysis, a catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction even though it is in a different phase from the substances that react. The catalyst is usually a solid, and the starting substances are gases or liquids. The best-known example is the catalytic converter in a car, which turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.
wichtigste: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
In heterogeneous catalysis, the catalyst and the reaction mixture are in different phases.
The reaction takes place on the surface of the catalyst in three steps: adsorption, reaction, desorption.
A three-way catalytic converter in a car contains mainly platinum, palladium and rhodium.
It breaks down carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides at the same time.
Many important substances such as ammonia, sulphuric acid and nitric acid are made with heterogeneous catalysis.
Gerhard Ertl received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2007 for his studies of reactions on solid surfaces.

abschnitte.text: A **catalyst** is a substance that makes a chemical reaction run faster but itself remains unchanged at the end. It lowers the energy needed for the reaction to start. In **heterogeneous catalysis**, the catalyst and the reacting substances are in different **phases**, for example a solid catalyst and gases. The advantage: the solid catalyst can easily be separated from the products and reused for a long time. That is why this kind of catalysis is particularly important in industry.

The reaction takes place on the **surface** of the catalyst, in three steps. First the particles stick to the surface; this is called **adsorption**. Then they react with each other there, because their bonds have been loosened. Finally the new particles come away again; this is called **desorption**. According to the Sabatier principle, the particles must stick neither too weakly nor too strongly, otherwise the catalyst works badly.

In the exhaust of petrol cars there is a **three-way catalytic converter**. It consists of a ceramic block with many fine channels coated with the precious metals platinum, palladium and rhodium. There, poisonous carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides are turned at the same time into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen. Cars with a catalytic converter must not be filled with leaded petrol, because lead poisons the active surface. In Switzerland the catalytic converter became practically compulsory for new petrol cars at the end of the 1980s, and leaded petrol is banned today.

Many basic chemicals are made by heterogeneous catalysis. In the **Haber-Bosch process**, ammonia for fertiliser is made from nitrogen and hydrogen on an iron catalyst. In the Ostwald process, ammonia is oxidised on a platinum-rhodium gauze to nitrogen monoxide, which is used to make nitric acid. In the contact process for sulphuric acid, vanadium(V) oxide oxidises sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide. And in the **hydrogenation of fats** for margarine, nickel serves as the catalyst.

Catalysis has been honoured several times with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Wilhelm Ostwald received it in 1909, among other things for his work on catalysis, and Paul Sabatier in 1912. The German chemist **Gerhard Ertl** received the Nobel Prize in 2007 for his studies of chemical processes on solid surfaces. He showed step by step exactly what happens on the surface of a catalyst. Today research is being done on catalysts for producing hydrogen and environmentally friendly fuels.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up in it.
A region with a uniform state, for example solid, liquid or gas.
Particles sticking to the surface of a solid.
Particles coming away from a surface.
A substance such as lead that blocks the surface of a catalyst.

gewusst: A catalyst must have an enormous surface area, which is why the precious metals are spread out in tiny particles on the support.
A catalytic converter only works properly once it is a few hundred degrees hot, which is why exhaust gases are dirtiest just after starting.
Because platinum, palladium and rhodium are very valuable, old catalytic converters are collected and recycled.

teile.einleitung: Entropy is a physical quantity that, put simply, describes how many ways there are to arrange the particles and the energy of a system. It is often called a measure of “disorder”. It explains why hot tea cools down by itself but never gets hot again by itself.
wichtigste: The physicist Rudolf Clausius introduced the term entropy in 1865.
According to Ludwig Boltzmann, entropy measures the number of possible microstates.
Molar entropy is given in J/(mol·K).
The second law states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
The third law states that a perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy.
If a gas is formed from a solid in a reaction, entropy increases considerably.
The entropy of vaporisation of water is about 109 J/(mol·K).

abschnitte.text: Imagine a box of coins that you shake. All the coins showing heads is possible in only one single way, but a mixture is possible in very many ways. It is similar with particles: states that can come about in many ways are much more likely. **Entropy** measures this number of possibilities. The physicist **Ludwig Boltzmann** called the individual arrangements **microstates**.

The German physicist **Rudolf Clausius** introduced the term in 1865. He formed it from the Greek word “trope” for turning or transformation. Clausius studied steam engines and wanted to understand why heat only ever flows from warm to cold. Later the Austrian Ludwig Boltzmann explained entropy in terms of the motion of atoms and molecules. His famous formula S = k·log W is on his gravestone in Vienna.

The **second law of thermodynamics** states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. That is why a drop of ink spreads out in water by itself but never gathers back into a drop. The **third law** states that a perfect crystal at absolute zero, that is, at 0 kelvin or minus 273.15 °C, has zero entropy. There, only one single arrangement is possible. Entropy is measured in joules per kelvin, and molar entropy in J/(mol·K).

Gases have a much higher entropy than liquids, and liquids a higher one than solids. If a gas is formed from a solid in a reaction, entropy therefore increases greatly. One example is lime burning: CaCO₃ breaks down into CaO and gaseous CO₂. Whether a reaction happens by itself depends on enthalpy and entropy together. This is described by the **Gibbs free energy**, using the formula ΔG = ΔH minus T·ΔS.

abschnitte.titel: Evaporation and the Pictet Trouton rule
abschnitte.text: When a liquid evaporates, entropy increases greatly, because the particles get much more room. The **entropy of vaporisation** is found by dividing the enthalpy of vaporisation by the boiling temperature in kelvin. For water this gives 40,700 J/mol divided by 373 K, so about 109 J/(mol·K). Many other liquids are at about 85 to 88 J/(mol·K); this is what the **Pictet Trouton rule** says. It is named after the Geneva physicist Raoul Pictet and the Irishman Frederick Trouton. Water lies well above it because of its hydrogen bonds.

begriffe.erklaerung: One particular, exact arrangement of all the particles and their energy.
A system that exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
Basic rules that describe how energy and heat behave.

gewusst: An untidy bedroom is often given as an example of entropy, but strictly speaking it is about particles and energy, not socks.
Living things build up ordered structures, but in doing so they increase the entropy of their surroundings, for example through the heat they give off.
In 1877 Raoul Pictet from Geneva was one of the first researchers to liquefy oxygen.

teile.einleitung: Hazard symbols are pictures that warn of dangers at a glance. On chemicals and cleaning products, they show in a diamond with a red border whether a substance is, for example, poisonous, corrosive or highly flammable. If you know them, you can protect yourself and others.
wichtigste: Hazard symbols on chemicals are shaped like a diamond with a red border.
A flame means highly flammable.
A skull means poisonous.
An exploding bomb means explosive.
Drops attacking a hand mean corrosive.
A dead tree with a fish means dangerous to the environment.
At home, hazard symbols are often found on cleaning products.

abschnitte.text: A **hazard symbol** is a simple picture that warns of a danger without words. You can understand it even if you do not know the language or cannot read yet. Today, chemicals carry black pictures on a white background in a **diamond** with a red border. These signs belong to the worldwide GHS system.

A **flame** warns of substances that are highly flammable, such as methylated spirit or petrol. A flame over a circle means oxidising: such substances make other things burn more fiercely. An exploding bomb warns of explosive substances. A gas cylinder shows that there is gas under pressure in a container.

The **skull** and crossbones stands for poisonous substances that are dangerous even in small amounts. Drops attacking a hand and a surface mean **corrosive**, as with drain cleaners and some descalers. An exclamation mark warns of irritating or harmful substances. A person with a star on their chest warns of serious health hazards.

A dead tree and a dead fish mean **dangerous to the environment**. Such substances harm animals and plants, especially in water. That is why they must never go down the sink, into the toilet or out into nature. Leftovers are taken back to the shop or to a collection point for hazardous waste.

Many cleaning products, paints and garden products in the household carry hazard symbols. They are kept in their original packaging and out of reach of small children. In Switzerland the symbols used to be black on **orange squares**; today the new diamonds apply. Anyone who has swallowed something dangerous can get help round the clock from **Tox Info Suisse** on the number 145.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture that warns of a danger.
Destroys skin, eyes or materials on contact.
Catches fire easily.
Dangerous waste that has to be collected and disposed of separately.

gewusst: As well as the chemical symbols, there are many other warning signs, such as the yellow triangle with a lightning bolt for high voltage.
Hazard symbols work the same way worldwide so that they are understood in every country.
Even seemingly harmless things such as dishwasher tablets often carry a hazard symbol.

teile.einleitung: A blast furnace is a huge plant in which liquid pig iron is obtained from iron ore. It is as tall as a building of several storeys and works day and night, often for many years without a break. The pig iron is later turned into steel for bridges, cars and rails.
wichtigste: In a blast furnace, iron ore is turned into liquid pig iron with coke.
Coke serves both as fuel and as a reducing agent.
It is mainly the gas carbon monoxide that removes the oxygen from the iron oxide.
Hot air is blown in at the bottom so that the coke burns fiercely.
Limestone binds the waste rock into slag, which floats on top of the pig iron.
Letting the liquid iron run out is called tapping.
Pig iron contains about 4 per cent carbon.

abschnitte.titel: How a blast furnace is built
abschnitte.text: A blast furnace is a tall, round steel shaft lined inside with fireproof bricks. At the top, the **throat**, layers of iron ore, coke and limestone are loaded in turn. At the bottom, nozzles blow in hot air that has first been heated to over 1000 °C in large **hot blast stoves**. Right at the bottom, in the hearth, the liquid iron and the slag collect.

The coke burns with the oxygen of the hot air, and it gets very hot, in places around 2000 °C. This produces the gas **carbon monoxide**, which rises upwards. It takes the oxygen away from the iron oxide in the ore; this process is called **reduction**. What is left is iron, which melts and drips downwards.

Iron ore also contains rock without iron, which is called waste rock. The limestone that is added combines with it to form **slag**. Because the slag is lighter than the iron, it floats on top and can be let out separately. Later it is used as a building material, for example for cement or in road building.

Several times a day a hole is drilled into the bottom of the furnace, and the glowing pig iron flows out. This spectacular moment is called **tapping**. The iron is about 1450 °C hot and glows bright orange. It is then taken to the steelworks in large ladles or wagons.

Because of its high carbon content, pig iron is brittle and cannot be forged. In the steelworks, oxygen is therefore blown into it, which burns off a large part of the carbon. This produces tough, flexible **steel**. There are no blast furnaces in Switzerland any more today; here steel is made mainly from scrap metal in electric furnaces.

As early as the Middle Ages there were simple blast furnaces in Europe that were fired with charcoal. In 1709 the Englishman Abraham Darby used **coke** made from coal for the first time. That was an important step for industrialisation. Iron ore used to be smelted in Switzerland too, for example from the Gonzen mine near Sargans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Iron straight from the blast furnace with a lot of carbon, still brittle.
Almost pure carbon, made by strongly heating coal.
A chemical process in which oxygen is removed from a substance.
Melted rock produced as a by-product of smelting.
Letting the liquid iron run out of the blast furnace.

gewusst: A modern blast furnace can produce several thousand tonnes of pig iron a day.
If a blast furnace is switched off, the iron inside can solidify and destroy the furnace, which is why it runs without a break.

teile.einleitung: Verdigris is a green to bluish green coating that forms when copper comes into contact with vinegar. It is poisonous and must not be eaten or licked. In the past, painters even used verdigris as a bright green paint.
wichtigste: Verdigris forms on copper and metals containing copper, such as brass.
It forms mainly when copper is in contact with vinegar for a long time.
Verdigris is poisonous.
The green layer on old copper roofs is properly called patina.
Patina protects the copper underneath and is therefore not removed.
In the past, painters used verdigris as a green paint.
The German word comes from “Spanish green”.

abschnitte.text: Verdigris is a chemical substance formed from **copper** and **acetic acid**. Chemists call it copper acetate. It forms green to bluish green crusts or powder. Verdigris can form on pure copper and on **brass**, a mixture of copper and zinc. That is why it is sometimes found on old door handles, taps or musical instruments made of brass.

Verdigris is **poisonous**, because copper compounds harm the body in larger amounts. Anyone who swallows it can get stomach ache, nausea and vomiting. So you should not lick greenish spots on copper pans or cutlery. In the past people often cooked in copper pans that were coated with tin inside, so that no verdigris formed in the food. Acidic foods such as pickled gherkins should never be kept in bare copper.

The green layer on old copper roofs, church towers and statues is often called verdigris. Its correct name, however, is **patina**, and it consists mainly of other copper compounds that form with air, rain and carbon dioxide. It usually takes many years for a new copper roof to turn green. Patina is useful, because it protects the copper underneath from further weathering. A famous example is the Statue of Liberty in New York, which is made of copper and is therefore green.

As early as ancient times, people made verdigris on purpose by hanging copper sheets over vinegar. The bright green powder was used as a **pigment** for paintings, book illuminations and murals. Many Renaissance painters also used it. Over time, however, verdigris can turn brown or dark in paintings. Today less poisonous and more durable green pigments are used.

The German word “Grünspan” comes from the medieval expression **“Spanish green”**. It is thought that the pigment was often imported from Spain at that time. In Latin it was called viride hispanicum, which also means Spanish green. In English it is called verdigris, which goes back to the old French “vert de Grèce”, that is “green from Greece”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reddish metal that conducts electricity well and is used for roofs and cables.
A mixture of copper and zinc with a golden yellow colour.
A protective layer that forms on metals over time.
A coloured powder from which paints are made.

gewusst: When it was unveiled, the Statue of Liberty in New York was copper red and only turned green later.
To make verdigris as a paint, people used to hang copper plates over pots of vinegar.
Many church towers in Switzerland have green copper roofs with patina.

teile.einleitung: Jacques Dubochet is a Swiss biophysicist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017. He found a way of freezing water so quickly that it becomes solid like glass instead of forming ice crystals. This makes it possible to see tiny building blocks of life in the electron microscope.
wichtigste: Jacques Dubochet was born in Aigle in the canton of Vaud in 1942.
In 2017 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry together with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
His contribution was to freeze water so quickly that it becomes glassy.
This technique is called vitrification and was developed around 1980 at the EMBL in Heidelberg.
For it, his team plunged thin films of water into liquid ethane.
From 1987 Dubochet was a professor at the University of Lausanne.
His work made cryo-electron microscopy possible.

abschnitte.text: Jacques Dubochet was born in **Aigle** in the canton of Vaud in 1942. As a child he had a reading and spelling difficulty, **dyslexia**, and often found school hard. Even so, he studied physics at what is now the EPFL in Lausanne and then molecular biology in Geneva. Later he did research in Heidelberg and in 1987 became a professor at the **University of Lausanne**. He is known as a researcher with a sense of humour who is committed to society.

An **electron microscope** works with electrons instead of light and can show much smaller things than a normal microscope. So that the electron beam is not disturbed, there is a **vacuum** inside the instrument. Biological samples such as viruses or proteins, however, consist largely of water and dry out in a vacuum. If you freeze them normally, **ice crystals** form. These scatter the electron beam and destroy the fine structures.

Around 1980 Dubochet and his team at the **EMBL** in Heidelberg found a solution. They put the sample in a very thin film of water on a small grid. Then they plunged it in a flash into **liquid ethane**, which had been strongly cooled with liquid nitrogen. The water solidified so quickly that the molecules had no time to form crystals. Glassy ice was formed, and this process is called **vitrification**.

In 2017 Dubochet received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** together with the German-American Joachim Frank and the Briton Richard Henderson. Together they had made **cryo-electron microscopy** possible. Frank developed computing methods to produce a sharp 3D image from many blurry pictures. Henderson showed that this way proteins can be imaged down to individual atoms. This made Dubochet one of the few Swiss Nobel Prize winners in chemistry.

With cryo-electron microscopy, researchers can study the shape of viruses, proteins and other tiny building blocks of life in detail. In 2020, for example, it was used to reveal the structure of the coronavirus very quickly. Such knowledge helps to develop medicines and vaccines. Today there are cryo-electron microscopes in many laboratories all over the world, including at Swiss universities. Dubochet also campaigns for science to be used responsibly for society.

begriffe.erklaerung: A microscope that works with electrons instead of light and shows tiny things.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.
Freezing water in a flash into glassy ice without crystals.
Electron microscopy of deep-frozen samples.
A difficulty with reading and writing that has nothing to do with intelligence.

gewusst: Dubochet liked to say that he was the first officially recognised dyslexic in the canton of Vaud.
The liquid ethane into which the samples are plunged is colder than minus 150 degrees Celsius.
Glassy ice also occurs in space, for example on comets.

teile.einleitung: In hot dip galvanising, steel parts are dipped into a bath of liquid zinc. This gives them a coating that protects them from rust for many decades. Crash barriers, electricity pylons and railings in Switzerland are typical examples.
wichtigste: In hot dip galvanising, steel parts are dipped into liquid zinc.
The zinc bath is about 450 degrees Celsius hot.
Beforehand, the parts are cleaned and pickled in acid so that the zinc sticks well.
At the boundary between steel and zinc, an iron zinc alloy forms.
Zinc is a less noble metal than iron and corrodes first, which is why it protects scratched steel too.
Crash barriers on Swiss roads are typically hot dip galvanised.
Hot dip galvanising usually protects steel outdoors for several decades.

abschnitte.text: Steel is strong and cheap, but it rusts when it comes into contact with water and oxygen. To protect it, it is coated with **zinc**. In hot dip galvanising this is done by dipping the parts into molten zinc. A distinction is made between **batch galvanising** of individual components and strip galvanising, in which sheet steel runs through the zinc bath as a long strip. Galvanised sheet is used, for example, for car bodies.

First the steel parts are degreased and then **pickled** in dilute hydrochloric acid, which removes rust and scale. Then they are dipped into a flux, which keeps the surface clean. After that they go into the zinc bath, at about 450 degrees, for a few minutes. Once pulled out, they cool in the air or in water.

In the hot zinc, the steel surface reacts with the zinc, and several thin layers of an **iron zinc alloy** form. On top of these lies a layer of pure zinc. These layers have grown firmly into the steel and are not just stuck on like paint. Freshly galvanised steel has a silvery shine and often shows a crystal pattern, the so called spangle. Over time, the surface becomes a dull grey.

To begin with, the zinc layer shields the steel from water and air. In addition, zinc is a **less noble** metal than iron. If the layer is scratched, the zinc therefore corrodes first and the steel is spared. This effect is called **cathodic corrosion protection**. A thin protective layer of zinc compounds, the patina, also forms on the surface.

In Switzerland, **crash barriers** on motorways and pass roads are almost always hot dip galvanised. Electricity pylons, noise barriers, railings, balconies, gratings and screws are also protected in this way. Outdoors, the protection usually lasts for several decades without any need for repainting. Zinc can also be recycled well. The process was invented in France in the 19th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bluish silver metal that is used to protect steel from rust.
Cleaning metal with acid to remove rust and dirt.
The destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with its surroundings, for example rusting.
A mixture of two or more metals.
The term for metals that react easily with oxygen and water.

gewusst: Zinc melts at only about 420 degrees Celsius, whereas iron melts only at over 1500 degrees.
The zinc layer sacrifices itself for the steel, which is why it is also called sacrificial protection.
After decades, galvanised steel parts can have the zinc removed and be galvanised again.

teile.einleitung: A solid is a substance in the solid state, like a stone, a wooden spoon or a piece of glass. Solid substances keep their shape, even when you pick them up. Along with liquid and gas, solid is one of the three most important states of matter.
wichtigste: A solid is a substance in the solid state.
It is typical of solid substances that they keep their shape.
Stones, wood, glass and metals are solid substances.
Sand is solid too, even though you can pour it.
Glass is a hard and transparent solid substance.
Many substances become liquid when warmed, like chocolate.
In solids, the tiniest particles sit firmly in their place.

abschnitte.text: A **solid** has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. You can pick it up and it keeps its shape. Examples are a stone, a wooden spoon, a nail or chocolate from the fridge. Liquids, in contrast, flow, and gases spread out through the whole room.

All substances consist of tiny particles. In a solid, they sit close together and hold on to each other. They cannot move freely, but can only **vibrate** in their place. That is why a solid keeps its shape and can hardly be squeezed together.

In many solids, the particles are arranged quite regularly; this is called a **crystal**. Examples are table salt, sugar, ice and rock crystal. In **glass**, on the other hand, the particles are disordered, which is why it is called amorphous. Glass is hard, transparent and breaks easily. In the Swiss Alps you can find beautiful rock crystals, which crystal hunters look for.

You can pour **sand** like a liquid, but it is still solid. That is because every single grain of sand is a tiny solid with a fixed shape. The same goes for flour, sugar and salt. If you pour out sand, it forms a heap, whereas water runs apart.

If you warm a solid, its particles vibrate more and more strongly until it **melts** and becomes liquid. Ice melts at 0 degrees, chocolate already at about body temperature, which is why it melts in your mouth. Iron only melts at over 1500 degrees. If you cool a liquid, it becomes solid again; this is called **solidifying**.

Solid substances can be very different: hard like diamond or soft like wax. **Diamond** is the hardest natural substance. Metals can be bent, whereas glass breaks. Rubber is elastic and springs back into shape.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in the solid state with a fixed shape.
The state of a substance: solid, liquid or gas.
A solid whose particles are arranged regularly.
The temperature at which a solid becomes liquid.
Without a regular order of particles, as in glass.

gewusst: Dry ice, frozen carbon dioxide, does not become liquid when warmed but turns straight into a gas.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals, over 3400 degrees.
A solid can expand when warmed, which is why bridges and rails have small gaps.

teile.einleitung: A substance is biodegradable if living things such as bacteria, fungi or worms can break it down. In the end what is mainly left is water, carbon dioxide and humus. In this way a banana skin disappears after a while, whereas a glass bottle stays lying around almost for ever.
wichtigste: Biodegradable means that living things can break a substance down.
A banana skin or a sheet of paper is biodegradable.
Fungi are particularly good at breaking down dead wood in the forest.
A glass bottle takes the longest to disappear in nature.
Discarded chewing gum is a problem, because it hardly breaks down.
Biodegradable plastic can be made, for example, from maize starch.
A wooden spoon is biodegradable, a plastic spoon is not.

abschnitte.text: In nature, dead plants and animals are constantly being broken down. This work is done by **decomposers** such as bacteria, fungi, earthworms and woodlice. They eat the material and turn it into simple substances such as water, carbon dioxide and **humus**. A substance that disappears in this way is considered **biodegradable**.

Breaking down takes very different lengths of time. A sheet of paper or a banana skin disappears after weeks or months. A piece of wood takes years, because it consists of tough **lignin** and cellulose. Plastic, on the other hand, breaks into small pieces only after hundreds of years, and **glass** practically does not break down at all.

Fungi are the best decomposers of **dead wood**, because they can even crack the hard parts of wood. Bacteria work mainly where it is warm and damp. Earthworms pull leaves into the soil and loosen it. Without these helpers, the forest would be smothered under mountains of old leaves.

Ordinary plastic is made from **crude oil** and is hardly broken down by living things. **Chewing gum** today is also mostly made of plastic and stays stuck on streets and squares for a long time. But there is **bioplastic**, for example made from maize starch. However, many of these plastics break down properly only in an industrial composting plant, not in the garden or in nature.

abschnitte.titel: Compost and green waste in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Vegetable peelings, leaves and grass cuttings can be **composted** in the garden or put in the green waste. In many Swiss municipalities, a green waste collection picks up this waste. In plants it is made into compost or **biogas**, which is used to produce electricity and heat. In this way waste becomes valuable soil for new plants again.

Never throw rubbish carelessly into nature, not even chewing gum or cigarette ends. Use **reusable** cups, wooden cutlery or your own boxes instead of throwaway plastic. Glass, PET and aluminium belong in the **recycling**, not in the forest. That way meadows, lakes and rivers stay clean.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living things such as bacteria, fungi and worms that break down dead material.
Dark, fertile soil formed from decomposed plant remains.
A heap of plant waste that rots down into soil.
Plastic that is made from plants or is biodegradable.

gewusst: A single teaspoon of good garden soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
Chewing gum used to be made from the sap of a tropical tree and was therefore natural.
Pieces of glass from Roman times are still found today in excavations in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The yield tells you how much product a chemical reaction actually delivered, compared with the amount that would be possible in theory. It is usually given as a percentage. In the laboratory and in industry a high yield is important, because it saves raw materials, energy and money.
wichtigste: The percentage yield is the amount of product obtained divided by the theoretically possible amount, times 100.
If you get 40 g of product instead of a theoretical 50 g, the yield is 80 per cent.
In the laboratory the yield is almost always below 100 per cent, because of side reactions and losses during work up.
A yield above 100 per cent usually points to a damp or impure product.
In multi step syntheses, the yields of the individual steps multiply.
Atom economy shows what share of the mass of the reactants ends up in the desired product.

abschnitte.text: From the reaction equation you can calculate the most product that can be formed; this is the **theoretical yield**. In reality you usually get less. If you divide the amount obtained by the theoretical amount and multiply by 100, you get the **percentage yield**. You can calculate with masses or with amounts of substance in moles.

If 0.50 mol of reactant in a 1 to 1 reaction produces 0.35 mol of product, the yield is **70 per cent**. When limestone is burned, 100 g of calcium carbonate gives a theoretical 56 g of **quicklime**. If you get only 42 g, that is 75 per cent. It is always important first to work out the theoretical amount using the **molar masses**.

Often **side reactions** take place alongside the desired reaction and produce other substances. Some reactions reach an **equilibrium** and never run to completion. In addition, something is always lost when filtering, pouring and purifying. If you nevertheless measure more than 100 per cent, the product is probably still damp or impure.

Medicines are often made in many steps. The yields multiply: three steps of 80 per cent each give 0.8 times 0.8 times 0.8, only about **51 per cent**. With ten such steps, only about a tenth would be left. That is why chemists look for the **shortest possible synthesis routes**.

A high yield on its own does not tell you whether a reaction is environmentally friendly. **Atom economy** shows what part of the atoms from the starting materials ends up in the desired product. The rest becomes by products or waste. **Green chemistry** tries to develop reactions with a high yield and high atom economy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A starting material that is used up in a reaction.
A substance newly formed in a reaction.
The largest possible amount of product according to the reaction equation.
An unwanted reaction that happens at the same time and forms other substances.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams.

gewusst: There is a kind of yield in baking too: depending on the recipe, a kilogram of flour makes different amounts of bread.
In large industrial plants, one per cent more yield can save many tonnes of raw materials every year.
Some natural substances are made in more than twenty steps, and in the end often only a tiny part is left.

teile.einleitung: The electron is a tiny, negatively charged particle and one of the three building blocks of the atom. Electrons surround the atomic nucleus and decide how atoms react with each other. When current flows through a cable, electrons are moving.
wichtigste: The electron is a negatively charged elementary particle.
In 1897 Joseph John Thomson showed that the electron is a separate particle.
Robert Millikan determined the elementary charge with the oil drop experiment.
According to the formula 2n², the second shell holds at most 8 electrons.
According to the Pauli principle, two electrons in an atom never have all four quantum numbers the same.
According to Hund's rule, orbitals of equal energy are first filled singly with the same spin.
Sodium has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.
A sulphur atom has 6 valence electrons.

abschnitte.text: In 1897 the British physicist **Joseph John Thomson** studied cathode rays in glass tubes with the air pumped out. He showed that they consist of tiny, negatively charged particles that are much lighter than an atom. This was the discovery of the **electron**, the first elementary particle. Thomson received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1906.

From 1909 Robert **Millikan** determined the charge of an electron with the oil drop experiment. He watched tiny, charged drops of oil between two electrically charged plates. The charge was always a multiple of a smallest charge, the **elementary charge** of about 1.6 times 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs. An electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton.

In the shell model, the electrons sit on **shells** around the nucleus. According to the formula 2n², the first shell holds 2, the second 8 and the third 18 electrons. More precisely, electrons are described with orbitals and four quantum numbers. The sodium atom with 11 electrons has the **electron configuration** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.

The **Pauli principle** of Wolfgang Pauli from 1925 says that two electrons in an atom never have all four quantum numbers the same. That is why at most two electrons fit in one orbital, with opposite spin. **Hund's rule** says that orbitals of equal energy are first filled singly with the same spin. By the way, Wolfgang Pauli taught at ETH Zurich for a long time.

The outermost electrons are called **valence electrons**; sulphur, for example, has six of them. They decide which chemical bonds an atom forms. In metals electrons can move freely, which is why metals conduct electricity. Lightning and the static charge that makes your hair stick to your jumper also have to do with electrons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest freely occurring electric charge, carried by an electron.
A statement of how the electrons of an atom are spread over the orbitals.
A property of an electron that, put simply, can be imagined as a kind of spinning.
Electrons in the outermost shell, important for chemical bonds.
Rays made of electrons in a tube with the air pumped out.

gewusst: The word electron comes from the Greek word for amber, because rubbed amber attracts small particles.
Old cathode ray televisions made their picture with a beam of electrons.
Wolfgang Pauli received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945 for his principle.

teile.einleitung: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is a formula for calculating the pH of a buffer solution. Buffers are solutions whose pH hardly changes when you add a little acid or alkali. Our blood is also such a buffer.
wichtigste: The equation is: pH equals pKa + lg(c(A⁻) / c(HA)).
It calculates the pH of a buffer solution made of a weak acid and its base.
Karl Albert Hasselbalch formulated the logarithmic form in 1916.
It is derived by taking the logarithm of the expression for the acid dissociation constant.
If acid and base have the same concentration, the pH equals the pKa.
With very dilute buffers or a very uneven ratio it becomes inaccurate.
An acetate buffer with ten times more acetate than acetic acid has a pH of 5.76.

abschnitte.text: A **buffer** is a solution of a weak acid and its matching base, for example acetic acid and acetate. If you add acid, the base mops it up. If you add alkali, the acid mops it up. That is why the **pH** stays almost the same. So buffers work like shock absorbers for the acidity of a solution.

The equation says that pH equals pKa plus the logarithm of the ratio of base to acid. The **pKa** shows how strong an acid is: the smaller it is, the stronger the acid. The base 10 **logarithm** turns a factor of 10 into the number 1. That is why the pH rises by exactly 1 when there is ten times more base than acid. The equation is derived by taking the logarithm of the expression for the acid dissociation constant and rearranging it.

An acetate buffer with a pKa of 4.76 and ten times more acetate than acetic acid has a pH of 4.76 + 1 = 5.76. An ammonia buffer with a pKa of 9.25 and ten times more ammonium than ammonia has a pH of 9.25 minus 1 = 8.25. If you add 0.05 mol of hydrochloric acid to one litre of acetate buffer containing 0.2 mol each of acid and acetate, you get 0.25 mol of acetic acid and 0.15 mol of acetate. The pH then only falls to about 4.54. For a phosphate buffer with a pH of 7.51 and a pKa of 7.21, you need **hydrogen phosphate** and dihydrogen phosphate in a ratio of about 2 to 1.

In 1908 the American chemist and biologist **Lawrence Joseph Henderson** described a formula for the acidity of buffers. In 1916 the Danish doctor **Karl Albert Hasselbalch** rewrote it in the logarithmic form known today. For this he used the pH scale, which the Dane Søren Sørensen had introduced in 1909. Hasselbalch used it above all to study the acidity of blood. That is why the equation is particularly important in medicine and biochemistry.

Human **blood** has a pH of about 7.4 and must stay very precisely at that level. This is ensured mainly by a buffer of carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate. Doctors use the equation to understand blood values. In laboratories it is used to make buffers for experiments, medicines and measurements. The equation becomes inaccurate with very dilute solutions and when one component is much more common than the other; it usually works well in the range of pKa plus or minus 1.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
A solution whose pH hardly changes even when acid or alkali is added.
A measure of the strength of an acid.
A type of calculation that shows how many times you must multiply 10 by itself to get a number.

gewusst: Even a small deviation of the blood pH from 7.4 can become dangerous.
The equation bears the names of two scientists who never worked on it together.
Shampoos and skin creams also contain buffers so that their pH stays stable.

teile.einleitung: In electrolysis, a substance is broken down chemically with the help of electric current. In this way, for example, water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen. Electrolysis is also enormously important in industry, for example for making aluminium, which has a long history in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Electrolysis is a redox reaction forced by electricity.
It uses direct current.
The positive pole is called the anode, and the negative pole the cathode.
In the electrolysis of water, hydrogen and oxygen are produced in the ratio 2 to 1.
Electrical energy is turned into chemical energy.
From 1888, aluminium was made by electrolysis in Neuhausen am Rheinfall.
The fuel cell reverses the electrolysis of water and produces electricity.

abschnitte.text: In **electrolysis**, electric current is used to force a chemical reaction that would not happen by itself. Chemically it is a **redox reaction**, in which electrons travel from one substance to another. It needs direct current, which always flows in the same direction. Electrical energy is turned into chemical energy in the process.

For electrolysis, two **electrodes** are dipped into a conducting liquid. The positive pole is called the **anode**, and the negative pole the **cathode**. Positively charged particles travel to the cathode, negatively charged ones to the anode. In practice you need a little more voltage than calculated; this extra voltage is called overpotential.

At school, water is often split with the **Hofmann voltameter**. Because pure water conducts electricity poorly, a little acid or salt is added. Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, in a volume ratio of 2 to 1. This fits the formula H₂O, because a water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

Aluminium is obtained by electrolysis from molten aluminium oxide, which takes a great deal of electricity. In 1888 one of the first aluminium works in Europe started operating in **Neuhausen am Rheinfall**. The electricity came from the water power of the Rhine. This firm later grew into the large Swiss company Alusuisse.

The **chlor alkali electrolysis** produces chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide solution all at once from salt solution. These substances are needed, for example, for plastics, cleaning products and for disinfecting water. In electroplating, objects are coated with a thin layer of metal, such as chromium or gold. Very pure copper for cables is also obtained by electrolysis.

If the electricity comes from renewable energy such as the sun, wind or water, the hydrogen produced is called **green hydrogen**. It can store energy when there is plenty of electricity available. A **fuel cell** reverses electrolysis and produces electricity again from hydrogen and oxygen, with only water as a product. In Switzerland, lorries with fuel cells are already on the road.

begriffe.erklaerung: A conductor, usually made of metal or graphite, through which current flows into a liquid.
The positive pole in electrolysis.
The negative pole in electrolysis.
A chemical reaction in which electrons are given up and taken in.

gewusst: In the 19th century aluminium was as rare and expensive as gold, until it could be made cheaply by electrolysis.
The terms anode, cathode and electrolysis come from the English scientist Michael Faraday.

teile.einleitung: Along with carbohydrates and proteins, fats are among the three most important nutrients. They are found in butter, cheese, nuts and cooking oil and give our bodies more energy than any other nutrient. Chemically they are built from glycerol and fatty acids.
wichtigste: A fat molecule consists of glycerol and three fatty acids.
1 gram of fat supplies about 9 kilocalories, more than twice as much as sugar.
Oils are liquid at room temperature, solid fats such as butter are not.
Vegetable oils contain particularly many unsaturated fatty acids with double bonds.
The grease spot test can be used to detect fat in food.
If you boil fat with caustic soda solution, saponification produces soap.
Over time, fats go rancid because of oxygen, light and heat.

abschnitte.text: A fat molecule is made up of one molecule of **glycerol** and three **fatty acids**. That is why it is also called a triglyceride. Chemically, fat belongs to the esters. The fatty acids can be of different lengths and have different numbers of double bonds. This decides whether a fat is solid or liquid and how healthy it is.

Fats with many saturated fatty acids, such as butter, coconut fat or lard, are solid at room temperature. **Oils** such as rapeseed oil, olive oil and sunflower oil contain many unsaturated fatty acids and are liquid. Fats do not dissolve in water and are lighter than water, which is why blobs of fat float on soup. A lot of rapeseed is grown in Switzerland, and rapeseed oil is pressed from it.

Fat is the body's most important **energy store**: 1 gram supplies about 9 kilocalories. The fatty tissue under the skin insulates against cold, and layers of fat protect organs such as the kidneys from knocks. The body also needs fats so that it can take in vitamins A, D, E and K. The body cannot make some fatty acids itself; they have to come from food.

Fat can be detected with the **grease spot test**: you rub a food on paper and let it dry. If a see through spot remains that does not disappear, it contains fat; water would evaporate. If fat is boiled with caustic soda solution, it breaks down into glycerol and the salts of the fatty acids. These salts are soap, and the reaction is called **saponification**.

Butter and oil go **rancid** over time, because oxygen, light and heat break down the fat molecules. This produces unpleasant smelling substances. That is why oil is kept cool, dark and tightly closed. Experts recommend using mainly vegetable oils such as rapeseed oil and not eating too much highly processed, fatty food such as chips or crisps.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for a fat molecule made of glycerol and three fatty acids.
A sweetish tasting alcohol that forms the backbone of fats.
Smelling and tasting spoilt because the fat has broken down.
Splitting fat with an alkali, which produces soap.
A unit for the energy in food.

gewusst: Fat is lighter than water, which is why blobs of fat always float on top of soup.
Penguins and seals survive icy cold thanks to a thick layer of fat under the skin.
Thousands of years ago, people were already making soap from animal fat and plant ash.

teile.einleitung: Almost all substances become denser and shrink when they cool. Water is an exception: it has its greatest density at about 4 °C and even expands when it freezes. This peculiarity is called the density anomaly and is very important for life on Earth.
wichtigste: Water has its greatest density at about 4 °C.
Ice has a density of about 0.92 g per cm³ and is lighter than liquid water.
That is why ice floats on water.
When water freezes, its volume increases by about 9 per cent.
Lakes freeze from the top, so fish can survive the winter at the bottom.
The cause is the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
Freezing water can split rocks and make glass bottles burst.

abschnitte.text: The word **anomaly** means a departure from the rule. Normally the particles of a substance move closer together when it cools, and the substance becomes denser. Water also becomes denser as it cools, but only down to about 4 °C. If it cools further, it expands again. When it freezes into ice, its volume suddenly increases by about 9 per cent.

Water molecules attract each other through **hydrogen bonds**. In ice they arrange themselves in a regular **crystal lattice** made of hexagonal rings. This lattice contains many hollow spaces, rather like a honeycomb. That is why ice needs more space than liquid water and has a lower density, about 0.92 g per cm³.

In autumn the surface water of a lake cools down. Water at 4 °C is heaviest and sinks to the bottom. Colder water stays on top and finally freezes into a sheet of ice. This layer of ice acts like a lid that protects the lake from further cold. At the bottom the water stays liquid at about 4 °C, and **fish** can survive the winter there.

Water gets into cracks and crevices in rocks. If it freezes at night, it expands and pushes the cracks apart. After many cycles of freezing and thawing, the rock breaks up; this is called **frost shattering**. The large scree slopes below rock faces in the Swiss Alps are formed largely in this way. Potholes in roads also often form like this in winter.

A full, closed glass bottle of water can shatter in the freezer, because the freezing water expands. For the same reason water pipes can burst in winter if they are not protected. **Icebergs** float in the sea, with about 90 per cent of their volume below the surface of the water. That is why an ice cube in a glass always floats on top.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example grams per cubic centimetre.
A departure from what is normal.
A force of attraction between water molecules, weaker than a real chemical bond.
The breaking up of rock by water freezing in cracks.

gewusst: Without the density anomaly, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, and many water animals could not survive the winter.
A few other substances such as silicon, gallium and bismuth also expand when they solidify.
The saying “only the tip of the iceberg” comes from the fact that most of an iceberg lies hidden under water.

teile.einleitung: The law of conservation of mass is one of the most important basic laws of chemistry. It states that in a chemical reaction no mass is lost and none is newly created. The atoms are only rearranged.
wichtigste: In a chemical reaction, the mass of the products equals the mass of the starting substances.
The atoms do not disappear; they are only joined in new ways.
In a chemical equation, the number of each kind of atom must therefore be the same on both sides.
If matches burn in a sealed jar, the scales show the same mass afterwards.
A candle gets lighter as it burns because mass escapes into the air as gases.
Steel wool gets heavier when it burns because it takes up oxygen from the air.
The law was recognised in the 18th century by Mikhail Lomonosov and Antoine Lavoisier.

abschnitte.text: In every chemical reaction the **total mass** stays the same. The substances present before weigh exactly as much as those present afterwards. The reason: the **atoms** are conserved; they only break old bonds and form new ones. No atom disappears, and none appears out of nowhere. That is why it is called the law of conservation of mass.

A burning candle gets lighter, and yet the law still holds. The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, and these **gases** escape into the air. With steel wool it is the other way round: it gets heavier when it burns because the iron takes up oxygen from the air. If you carry out such experiments in a **closed system**, for example matches in a sealed jar, the scales show exactly the same mass afterwards.

With the law you can calculate missing masses. If 56 g of iron react completely with 32 g of sulphur, 88 g of iron sulphide are formed. If 12 g of carbon burn with 32 g of oxygen, 44 g of carbon dioxide are formed. If you heat 10 g of limestone and get 5.6 g of quicklime, 4.4 g of gas must have escaped. If a product weighs 50 g and one of the two starting substances 30 g, the other weighed 20 g.

The Russian scholar **Mikhail Lomonosov** described the basic idea as early as the middle of the 18th century. The law became famous mainly through the Frenchman **Antoine Laurent de Lavoisier**, who worked with very precise scales. He carried out combustions in closed vessels and weighed everything before and after. In this way he disproved the phlogiston theory that was widespread at the time, according to which a mysterious substance escapes during burning. Lavoisier is therefore regarded as one of the founders of modern chemistry.

Because atoms are conserved, a correct **chemical equation** must be balanced. To the left and right of the arrow, the number of each kind of atom must be the same. For the formation of water you therefore write 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O: on the left and on the right there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms. Balancing such equations is a basic exercise in chemistry lessons.

Strictly speaking, the mass changes by a tiny amount in reactions that release energy. This follows from Albert Einstein’s famous formula E = mc², which shows that energy and mass are linked. In chemical reactions, however, this change is so small that no scales can measure it. In nuclear reactions in nuclear power stations or in the Sun, on the other hand, the effect is clear.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much an object or substance weighs, measured for example in grams.
An experiment in which no substance can get in or out.
A way of writing that shows which substances react and which are formed.
A substance that people used to wrongly believe was in all burnable things.

gewusst: For his experiments Lavoisier had scales built that were among the most precise of his time.
A tree consists largely of carbon, which it has taken in from the air as carbon dioxide.
