A nail also gets heavier when it rusts because it takes up oxygen and water from its surroundings.

teile.einleitung: The glowing splint test is a simple experiment that shows whether oxygen is present. A glowing wooden splint is held in a container: if it bursts into a bright flame, there is a lot of oxygen inside. It is one of the best-known experiments in chemistry lessons.
wichtigste: A glowing splint is a wooden splint that glows but does not burn with a flame.
In a positive glowing splint test, the glowing splint bursts into a bright flame.
In normal air the splint does not relight, because air contains only about 21 per cent oxygen.
In carbon dioxide a glowing splint goes out.
Oxygen is oxidising and carries the hazard symbol of a flame over a circle.
The valves of oxygen cylinders must never be oiled or greased.
Water plants produce oxygen through photosynthesis, which can be detected with the glowing splint.

abschnitte.text: You light a thin wooden splint and blow out the flame after a short time. The tip now goes on glowing red; it **smoulders**. You hold this glowing splint in a test tube in which you suspect there is oxygen. If the splint bursts into a bright flame, the test is **positive**: the tube contains pure oxygen or air with a lot of oxygen.

Burning needs fuel, heat and oxygen. Normal air consists of only about 21 per cent oxygen and about 78 per cent nitrogen, which does not burn. In pure oxygen, many more oxygen particles hit the hot wood, and burning is much more vigorous. That is why the glow suddenly turns back into a bright flame. In carbon dioxide, on the other hand, the splint goes out because there is no oxygen.

A classic school experiment shows that plants produce oxygen. You place a water plant such as **Canadian waterweed** under an upturned funnel filled with water and put it in the light. During **photosynthesis**, small gas bubbles rise and collect in a test tube. If you then hold a glowing splint in it, it bursts into flame. In the laboratory you can also obtain oxygen from hydrogen peroxide by adding a little manganese dioxide.

There are separate tests for other gases. **Hydrogen** is detected with the squeaky pop test: a test tube containing the gas is held to a flame, and there is a whistling or barking sound. Carbon dioxide turns clear limewater cloudy. So the glowing splint test is just one of several simple methods for telling gases apart.

Pure oxygen does not burn itself, but it is **oxidising**: it makes other substances burn much more fiercely. Cylinders of pure oxygen therefore carry the hazard symbol with a flame over a circle. Oil and grease can ignite violently in pure oxygen, so the valves of oxygen cylinders must never be lubricated. You always wear safety goggles during experiments.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wooden splint that glows but does not burn with an open flame.
Strongly helps other substances to burn without burning itself.
An experiment that shows that a particular substance is present.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.

gewusst: Oxygen was discovered independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Joseph Priestley in the 1770s.
In hospitals, patients are given pure oxygen, which is why open fire is strictly forbidden there.
A piece of steel wool that only glows in air burns with bright sparks in pure oxygen.

teile.einleitung: Steam is a substance in the gas state; usually water vapour is meant. It forms when water evaporates, for example when cooking. Real water vapour is invisible; the white clouds we see are already tiny droplets of water again.
wichtigste: Steam is a substance in gas form, usually water vapour.
When water is boiled, it evaporates and rises as steam.
Steam is very hot and can cause serious burns.
On a cold mirror or saucepan lid, steam turns back into drops of water.
This process is called condensation.
A cloud consists of many small droplets of water.
The white cloud when you breathe out in winter comes from condensed water vapour.

abschnitte.text: When you heat water, its particles move faster and faster. At 100 degrees Celsius, at sea level, the water starts to **boil**, and steam bubbles form all over the pan. The **water vapour** rises because it is lighter than the air. On high mountains water boils below 100 degrees, because the air pressure there is lower.

When steam meets something cold, it cools down and becomes liquid again. This is called **condensation**. That is why the mirror mists up after a shower and drops of water collect on the saucepan lid. In winter you see a little white cloud when you breathe out, because your warm, moist breath condenses in the cold air.

Steam from boiling water is at least 100 degrees hot. It can scald the skin worse than hot water, because it also gives off a lot of heat when it condenses. That is why you always open a saucepan away from your body. With the kettle and the oven too, you should not hold your face over the **steam outlet**.

As steam, water takes up about 1700 times more space than as a liquid. This expansion drives the **steam engine**, which James Watt greatly improved in the 18th century. Steam engines powered factories, locomotives and ships and set off industrialisation. Historic **paddle steamers** still sail on Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva today, and the Brienz Rothorn Railway runs with steam locomotives.

In the kitchen, vegetables are cooked gently in steam, and in a pressure cooker cooking is faster, because the higher pressure raises the boiling temperature. A steam iron makes clothes smooth. In many power stations, steam drives turbines that produce electricity. Clouds and fog also form from water vapour in the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in gas form.
The change from liquid to gas.
The change from gas to liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid boils; for water, 100 degrees at sea level.
A machine that works with the power of steam.

gewusst: Water vapour itself is transparent; you see it only when it condenses into droplets.
On the Brienz Rothorn Railway, steam locomotives climb to more than 2200 metres.
Water vapour in the air is also a greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid becomes solid. For water it is 0 degrees Celsius: if it gets colder, a puddle turns into ice. Every substance has its own freezing point.
wichtigste: Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.
At minus 5 degrees a puddle freezes, because minus means colder than 0 degrees.
Weather with temperatures below 0 degrees is called frost.
In the freezer, food is kept at about minus 18 degrees.
Salt and antifreeze lower the freezing point of water.
Freezing rain on cold ground forms dangerous black ice.
Frozen water expands, which is why ice floats.

abschnitte.text: When a liquid is cooled, its particles move more and more slowly. At the **freezing point** they settle into a fixed arrangement, and the liquid becomes a solid. For pure water this happens at 0 degrees Celsius. The other way round, ice melts again at exactly this temperature, so the freezing point is the same as the **melting point**. On a thermometer, “minus 10 degrees” means that it is 10 degrees colder than the freezing point of water.

In 1742 the Swedish scientist **Anders Celsius** proposed a temperature scale based on water. Today the rule is: 0 degrees is the freezing point and 100 degrees the boiling point of water at normal air pressure. Celsius himself originally set the scale the other way round, with 100 for the freezing point. In the USA people still use the Fahrenheit scale, where water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Most substances shrink when they solidify, but water expands, by about a tenth. That is why **ice** floats on water and lakes freeze from the top down. Fish survive the winter in the cool water underneath. However, the expansion can also burst water pipes and glass bottles and split rocks in the mountains.

If you dissolve salt or other substances in water, it only freezes at lower temperatures. This effect is called **freezing point depression**. That is why gritting crews spread salt on roads against black ice, and why antifreeze is added to the windscreen washer water in cars. Seawater only freezes at about minus 2 degrees. Other substances have completely different freezing points: mercury solidifies at about minus 39 degrees, and olive oil already turns cloudy and thick in the fridge.

Below 0 degrees we speak of **frost**. If rain freezes instantly on the cold ground, mirror-smooth **black ice** forms. In thunderclouds, water droplets freeze into hailstones, which are sometimes as big as walnuts. You should never touch an ice-cold metal pole with your tongue, because the moist tongue can freeze to it immediately. Then lukewarm water helps; do not pull!

In cold winters some lakes in Switzerland freeze over, for example the Lac de Joux in the Jura or mountain lakes in the Engadine. On frozen Lake St Moritz there are even horse races in February, the **White Turf**. Before you walk onto a lake, however, the ice must have been checked and declared safe by experts. Ice can be thin even where you do not expect it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Temperature at which a liquid becomes solid; for water 0 degrees Celsius.
Temperature at which a solid becomes liquid.
Temperatures below 0 degrees Celsius.
A smooth layer of ice that forms when rain freezes on cold ground.
The lowering of the freezing point when substances such as salt are dissolved in water.

gewusst: Very clean water can be cooled below 0 degrees without freezing, until a small jolt suddenly turns it into ice.
A full glass bottle in the freezer can burst because the freezing water expands.
Hoar frost on branches forms when water vapour in the air turns directly into fine ice crystals during frost.

teile.einleitung: Electron shells are the paths or levels on which, in the shell model, the electrons are arranged around the atomic nucleus. Each shell has room for only a certain number of electrons. This model explains why elements react so differently.
wichtigste: In the shell model, the electrons circle the atomic nucleus on shells.
The innermost shell is called the K shell, followed by L, M, N and more.
The nth shell holds at most 2n² electrons.
The K shell holds 2, the L shell 8, the M shell 18 and the N shell 32 electrons.
In 1913 Niels Bohr presented an atomic model with fixed electron orbits.
The electrons in the outermost shell decide how an element reacts.
An electron must take in energy to move to a shell further out.

abschnitte.text: An atom consists of a tiny nucleus and electrons that surround it. In the **shell model**, you imagine that the electrons lie in several layers around the nucleus, rather like the layers of an onion. These layers are called **electron shells**. The innermost shell is called the K shell, and going outwards come L, M, N, O, P and Q.

Each shell has room for only a certain number of electrons. It is calculated with the formula **2n²**, where n is the number of the shell. So the K shell holds 2 electrons, the L shell 8, the M shell 18 and the N shell 32. As a rule, the shells fill up from the inside outwards.

A sodium atom has 11 electrons, arranged as 2, 8 and 1, so 3 shells are occupied. An aluminium atom with 13 electrons has the arrangement 2, 8, 3. The number of occupied shells corresponds to the **period**, that is, the row in the periodic table. The electrons in the outermost shell are called **valence electrons** and decide how an atom reacts.

In 1913 the Danish physicist **Niels Bohr** presented an atomic model in which electrons circle the nucleus on fixed orbits. With it he explained why atoms give off light of only very particular colours. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work in 1922. Today we know that electrons do not have exact orbits, which is why experts use the more precise **orbital model**.

Atoms often aim for a full outer shell, like the one the noble gases have. That is why sodium readily gives up its single outer electron and chlorine readily takes one in, and this is how table salt is formed. If an electron takes in energy, it jumps to an outer shell, and when it falls back it gives off light. This explains the bright colours of fireworks and of flame tests.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of an atom.
The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
The idea that electrons are arranged in layers around the atomic nucleus.
A full outer shell, like the one the noble gases have.

gewusst: If an atomic nucleus were as big as a pinhead, the electron cloud would be as big as a football stadium.
The letters of the shells start with K because at first people did not know whether there were more shells further in.
From the third shell onwards, in reality the next shell is often started before the previous one is completely full.

teile.einleitung: Wood ash is the grey powder left behind when wood has burnt in a fireplace, stove or campfire. It consists of the minerals that cannot burn. Because embers can stay hidden in it for a long time, it must be handled carefully.
wichtigste: Wood ash is usually grey.
Ash is much lighter than the wood was before.
The still glowing remains of a fire are called embers.
There can still be embers in fresh ash, so you do not tip it straight into a rubbish bag.
The safest way to keep fresh ash is in a metal bucket with a lid.
Ash that has cooled down completely goes in the rubbish bag.
In the past, people made soap from wood ash and fat.
Some gardeners use wood ash as fertiliser.

abschnitte.text: Wood consists mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. When it burns, these substances turn into gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour and rise into the air. All that is left are the **minerals** that the tree took up from the soil. That is why the ash is much lighter than the wood, usually less than a hundredth of its weight. It contains mainly calcium, **potassium** and magnesium.

**Embers** can stay hidden in ash for a very long time, sometimes even several days. From the outside, the ash then looks quite harmless and grey. If you tip it into a plastic bag or a cardboard box too early, a fire can start. That is why fresh ash is put in a **metal bucket with a lid** and placed outside on ground that cannot burn. Only when the ash has cooled down completely does it go in the rubbish bag.

Wood ash is **alkaline**, that is the opposite of acidic. If you pour water over it, you get an alkaline solution that used to be called lye. People used it to wash clothes before there was washing powder. If you boil the lye with fat, you get **soap**. The potassium carbonate from the ash used to be called **potash**, because it was boiled down in pots.

Because ash contains potassium and calcium, some gardeners use it as **fertiliser** or sprinkle it against slugs. However, you should only use a little of it, because ash makes the soil less acidic and can also harm it. Wood ash can also contain heavy metals that the tree took up from the soil. Swiss specialist agencies therefore recommend always disposing of ash with the household rubbish. Ash from painted, varnished or treated wood never belongs in the garden.

Potash from wood ash used to be an important raw material for making **glass**. Glassmakers needed huge amounts of wood for it; whole forests were cut down. Ash was also used for dyeing fabrics and tanning leather. People also talk about ash from volcanoes, but this consists of finely ground rock and has nothing to do with burnt wood.

begriffe.erklaerung: The still glowing remains of a fire.
Substances such as potassium and calcium that plants take up from the soil.
The opposite of acidic; also called basic.
A salt from wood ash; chemically potassium carbonate.

gewusst: From a cubic metre of stacked wood, only a small bucket of ash is left.
In a heap of ash, embers can go on smouldering days after the fire.
The chemical element potassium takes its name from potash.

teile.einleitung: Petrol is a liquid fuel that mainly powers cars, motorbikes and lawnmowers. It is obtained from crude oil and is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons. Because it evaporates and burns easily, it is useful and dangerous at the same time.
wichtigste: Petrol is the usual fuel for the petrol engine.
It is made mainly from crude oil in refineries.
Most petrol molecules have about 5 to 12 carbon atoms.
The octane number tells you how knock resistant a petrol is.
At Swiss filling stations, unleaded petrol with an octane number of 95 is usual.
Burning it produces mainly carbon dioxide and water.
Even at room temperature, petrol vapour forms an explosive mixture with air.

abschnitte.text: Petrol is not a pure chemical but a mixture of hundreds of **hydrocarbons**. These are molecules made of carbon and hydrogen, most of them with about 5 to 12 carbon atoms. Petrol is colourless to slightly yellowish and has a strong smell. With a density of about 0.75 kilograms per litre, it is lighter than water and floats on it.

Petrol is obtained from crude oil in a **refinery**. First the crude oil is heated and separated by distillation into parts with different boiling points. Because this produces too little petrol, larger molecules are split into smaller ones by **cracking**. Today there is still one refinery in Switzerland, at Cressier in the canton of Neuchâtel, but most petrol is imported.

In the **Otto engine**, the petrol engine named after Nicolaus Otto, a mixture of petrol vapour and air is squeezed together in the cylinder. A spark plug lights it with a spark, and the hot gases push the piston down. If the mixture ignites by itself too early, the engine knocks and can be damaged. The **octane number** shows how knock resistant a petrol is; in Switzerland people usually fill up with unleaded 95 or 98.

In the past, lead compounds were mixed into petrol to make it more knock resistant. But lead is poisonous and also destroys cars' **catalytic converters**. That is why leaded petrol is now banned almost everywhere in the world. Burning petrol produces mainly carbon dioxide, which contributes to climate change, and water vapour.

Petrol evaporates very easily even at room temperature. Its vapour is heavier than air and forms an explosive mixture with it that even a small spark can ignite. That is why you must not smoke at a filling station and must switch off the engine. Petrol belongs only in approved cans and never in drinks bottles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance whose molecules consist only of carbon and hydrogen.
A number that shows how well petrol resists igniting by itself in the engine.
A factory in which crude oil is made into petrol, diesel and other products.
An internal combustion engine in which a spark plug ignites the petrol and air mixture.

gewusst: In 1888, on the first long car journey in history, Bertha Benz bought petrol at a pharmacy in Wiesloch, which is therefore considered the world's first filling station.
Burning one litre of petrol produces more than two kilograms of carbon dioxide, because the carbon combines with oxygen from the air.
Petrol used to be used as a stain remover for cleaning clothes too.

teile.einleitung: An ore is a rock from which so much metal can be extracted that mining it is worthwhile. Without ores there would be no iron for bridges, no copper for cables and no aluminium for bicycle frames. That is why people have been digging for ores for thousands of years.
wichtigste: An ore is a rock from which metal can be extracted profitably.
In most ores, the metals are present as chemical compounds, for example as oxides or sulphides.
Iron is obtained from haematite and magnetite, copper from chalcopyrite.
Bauxite is the most important raw material for aluminium.
The worthless rock that is separated from the ore is called gangue.
Ore is mined in huge open pits in opencast mining or underground in mines.
Iron ore was mined in the Gonzen near Sargans until 1966.

abschnitte.text: Ores consist of **minerals** that contain a metal. Whether a rock counts as an ore depends on how much metal it contains and whether extracting it pays off economically. If the price of a metal rises, poorer rocks can also become ores. Only a few metals, such as gold, often occur pure, that is, **native**, in nature. Most are firmly bound to other elements.

**Haematite** (red iron ore) and **magnetite** (magnetic iron ore) are iron oxides and the most important iron ores. Chalcopyrite is a compound of copper, iron and sulphur. Galena supplies lead, sphalerite supplies zinc. **Bauxite** is a reddish rock from which first aluminium oxide and then, with a lot of electricity, aluminium is obtained.

If an ore lies close to the surface, it is dug out by **opencast mining**, in pits that can be several kilometres wide. Deep deposits are reached by underground mining through shafts and tunnels. Huge excavators and lorries transport the rock. Today there are large ore mines in Australia, Brazil, Chile and Sweden, for example.

After mining, the ore is crushed and separated from the **gangue**; this is called ore processing. Then comes smelting: in the blast furnace, coke removes the oxygen from the iron oxide, so that liquid pig iron is produced. Sulphide ores such as chalcopyrite are first roasted, that is, heated in air. This produces sulphur dioxide, which today is captured and turned into sulphuric acid.

Switzerland is poor in ores, but in the past people still dug in many places. In the **Gonzen** near Sargans in the canton of St Gallen, iron ore was mined for centuries until the mine was closed in 1966. Today you can explore it as a show mine. Ore was also once mined in the Fricktal in Aargau and in the Grisons.

Metals from ores are found in cars, houses, mobile phones and solar panels. Mining changes landscapes greatly and can pollute water and soil. That is why **recycling** metals is becoming more and more important. Aluminium, for example, can be melted down again and again and needs only a small part of the energy required to make it from bauxite.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rock from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
The worthless rock that is separated from the actual ore when ore is mined.
Extracting metal from ore, for example in a blast furnace.
Extracting raw materials in an open pit at the Earth's surface.
A compound of an element with oxygen, such as rust.

gewusst: Haematite gets its name from the Greek word for blood, because its powder is red.
Magnetite is naturally magnetic and can attract small pieces of iron.
Today you can visit the former mine in the Gonzen on guided tours with a helmet and head torch.

teile.einleitung: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. These shared electrons hold the atoms together like a band. This is how molecules such as water, oxygen or sugar are formed, and even huge lattices such as diamond.
wichtigste: In a covalent bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons.
Another name for the covalent bond is the atomic bond.
Covalent bonds typically form between non metal atoms.
A double bond has 2 shared pairs of electrons, and a triple bond 3.
In the oxygen molecule O₂, the two atoms are joined by a double bond.
A hydrogen atom forms exactly 1 covalent bond.
In diamond, all the carbon atoms are joined by covalent bonds to form a huge lattice.

abschnitte.text: Atoms consist of a nucleus and a shell of **electrons**. In a covalent bond, two atoms each contribute one electron and share this **electron pair**. The pair then belongs to both atoms at once and holds them together. In German this is called an atomic bond; the usual term is **covalent bond**.

Atoms are particularly stable when their outermost shell is full, usually with eight electrons. This rule is called the **octet rule**. Non metal atoms such as chlorine, oxygen or nitrogen have almost full shells and are missing only a few electrons. By sharing electrons, both atoms reach a full shell without either having to give one up completely.

If two atoms share one electron pair, this is a **single bond**, as in the hydrogen molecule H₂. A hydrogen atom always forms exactly one bond. In the oxygen molecule O₂ the atoms share two pairs; this is a **double bond**. In the nitrogen molecule N₂ there are three pairs, a very strong **triple bond**.

When a few non metal atoms join through covalent bonds, **molecules** are formed. Examples are water H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂ and methane CH₄. If one atom pulls the shared electrons more strongly than the other, the bond becomes **polar**. In the water molecule the oxygen pulls the electrons towards itself, which is why water has a slightly negative and a slightly positive side.

Some substances do not form separate molecules but huge **atomic lattices**. In **diamond**, every carbon atom is joined to four neighbours by covalent bonds. That is why diamond is the hardest natural material. Quartz, the main component of many grains of sand and rock crystals, is built the same way.

abschnitte.titel: History and how it is drawn
abschnitte.text: In 1916 the American chemist **Gilbert Newton Lewis** described the idea of the shared electron pair. **Lewis formulas**, in which each bonding electron pair is drawn as a line, are named after him. So hydrogen is written H-H and oxygen O=O. As well as the covalent bond, there is the ionic bond, for example in table salt, and the metallic bond.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two electrons that belong together.
A particle made of several firmly joined atoms.
Atoms aim to have eight electrons in their outer shell.
An element such as oxygen, nitrogen or chlorine that does not have the properties of a metal.
Unevenly charged; one side is slightly negative and the other slightly positive.

gewusst: The triple bond in nitrogen is so strong that nitrogen gas in the air hardly reacts.
Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon, but they are joined differently.
A single diamond is really one giant molecule.

teile.einleitung: The rate constant k is a number that shows how fast a chemical reaction takes place. It appears in the rate law and links the reaction rate to the concentrations of the starting substances. The larger k, the faster the reaction.
wichtigste: The rate law for A + B → products is generally v = k·c(A)^m·c(B)^n.
The rate constant k does not depend on the concentration of the reactants.
However, k depends strongly on temperature and on catalysts.
For a first-order reaction k has the unit s⁻¹, for a second-order reaction L/(mol·s).
For first-order reactions the half-life is t½ = ln 2 / k.
The equilibrium constant is the ratio K = k(forward) / k(reverse).

abschnitte.text: The **reaction rate** v shows how fast the concentration of a substance changes during a reaction, for example in moles per litre and second. It usually depends on the concentrations of the starting substances, the **reactants**. The rate law describes this relationship: v = k·c(A)^m·c(B)^n. The number k is the **rate constant**; it is characteristic of each reaction at a particular temperature. The exponents m and n have to be determined by experiment.

The sum of the exponents is called the **reaction order**. For a first-order reaction v = k·c, and k has the unit s⁻¹. An example: with k = 0.05 s⁻¹ and c = 0.2 mol/L you get v = 0.01 mol/(L·s). For a second-order reaction such as v = k·c(A)·c(B), k has the unit L/(mol·s). With k = 2 L/(mol·s) and both concentrations 0.1 mol/L you get v = 0.02 mol/(L·s).

The **half-life** is the time after which only half of a substance is left. For first-order reactions it does not depend on the starting concentration and is t½ = ln 2 / k, or about 0.693 / k. With k = 0.0231 per minute this gives exactly 30 minutes. Radioactive substances decay according to the same law, and many medicines are also broken down in the body in roughly this way.

Concentration does not change k, but temperature certainly does. A rule of thumb is the **RGT rule** (reaction rate and temperature rule): if the temperature rises by 10 degrees, a reaction becomes about two to four times faster. This is described more precisely by the Arrhenius equation, named after the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius, who put it forward in 1889. A **catalyst** increases k because it offers the reaction an easier route with lower activation energy. That is why food keeps longer in a cool fridge: the reactions that make it go off run more slowly.

Many reactions run in both directions, forwards and backwards. In **chemical equilibrium** both rates are equal, and the concentrations no longer change. It follows that the equilibrium constant K equals the ratio of the two rate constants: K = k(forward) / k(reverse). If the forward reaction is much faster than the reverse reaction, the equilibrium lies far on the side of the products.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast the concentration of a substance changes during a reaction.
Starting substance of a chemical reaction.
Sum of the exponents in the rate law.
Time after which only half of a substance is still present.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

gewusst: The rate constants of different reactions can differ by many powers of ten, from fractions of a second to thousands of years.
The catalytic converter in a car speeds up reactions that turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.
Svante Arrhenius received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903.

teile.einleitung: The Grätzel cell is a special solar cell that uses a dye to turn sunlight into electricity. It was invented by the chemist Michael Grätzel at the EPFL in Lausanne. Its model is the photosynthesis of plants.
wichtigste: The Grätzel cell is also called a dye-sensitised solar cell.
Michael Grätzel developed it at the EPFL in Lausanne.
Its model was photosynthesis, in which leaf green captures light.
A dye captures the light and passes electrons to titanium dioxide.
The classic electrolyte contains iodide and triiodide.
Ruthenium complexes were the classic dyes used.
The cell also works well in diffuse light.
Michael Grätzel received the Millennium Technology Prize for it in 2010.

abschnitte.text: The Grätzel cell is a **dye-sensitised solar cell**. It turns light into electricity, much like the familiar blue solar cells on house roofs. Instead of silicon, however, it uses a dye that captures the light. The cells can be transparent and coloured, for example red, orange or green. This means they can easily be built into windows and façades.

Plants capture sunlight with the green pigment **chlorophyll** and use the energy in **photosynthesis**. Michael Grätzel transferred this idea to technology. In his cell, an artificial dye takes over the job of leaf green. That is why people sometimes speak of “artificial photosynthesis”. However, the cell does not make sugar but electricity.

Between two glass plates there is a layer of tiny grains of **titanium dioxide**, a white substance that is also found in toothpaste and paint. The dye sticks to the grains, classically a **ruthenium complex**. When light hits the dye, it passes an electron to the titanium dioxide, and this flows through a wire as electricity. A liquid, the **electrolyte** with iodide and triiodide, then gives the dye an electron back. In this way the cycle keeps going as long as light shines.

Michael Grätzel is a chemist who was born in Germany in 1944 and has done research at the **EPFL** in Lausanne for decades. In 1991 he presented the cell together with Brian O'Regan in the scientific journal Nature. For the invention he received the **Millennium Technology Prize** in Finland in 2010, one of the most important technology prizes in the world. On the EPFL campus, the SwissTech Convention Center has a coloured glass façade with dye-sensitised solar cells.

A big advantage is that the cell also works well in **diffuse light**, that is when it is cloudy or indoors. It is light, can be coloured and transparent and needs relatively simple materials. On the other hand, its efficiency is usually lower than that of good silicon cells. In addition, the liquid inside can leak or change over time. Today small Grätzel cells supply electricity, for example, to sensors or computer keyboards indoors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that turns light directly into electricity.
The process by which plants make sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.
A white substance that takes up the electrons in the cell and passes them on.
A liquid in which electrically charged particles can move.
How much of the light energy shining in is actually turned into electricity.

gewusst: In school lessons you can even build simple dye-sensitised solar cells with raspberry or blackberry juice.
The façade of the SwissTech Convention Center in Lausanne produces electricity with colourful glass panes.
Grätzel cells can produce electricity from the light of a room lamp.

teile.einleitung: Ice is frozen water, that is, water in the solid state. It forms when water cools below zero degrees Celsius. Ice comes as ice cubes in a glass, as snow, as hail and in huge glaciers.
wichtigste: Ice is frozen water.
Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.
Ice feels cold and hard.
Ice is lighter than water, which is why an ice cube floats.
Glacier ice forms from snow that is pressed together over many years.
A frozen lake is dangerous, because the ice can break.
Ice cubes are made by putting water in the freezer.

abschnitte.text: When water cools to **0 degrees Celsius**, its particles move more slowly and arrange themselves into a solid lattice. Ice forms, which is cold and hard. This process is called **freezing**. If ice warms above 0 degrees, it melts back into liquid water.

Almost all substances become denser when they solidify, but not water. When it freezes, water expands by about nine per cent, which is why ice is lighter than water and **floats**. With an iceberg, only about a tenth sticks out of the water. Because ice expands, a full glass bottle can burst in the freezer.

In the Alps, more snow falls high up than can melt in summer. Over the years the snow is pressed together into grainy **firn** and finally into solid glacier ice. The largest glacier in the Alps is the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais, about 20 kilometres long. Because of global warming, Swiss glaciers have been melting sharply for decades.

In winter some lakes freeze over, for example the Lac de Joux or lakes in the Engadine such as Lake St Moritz. But you may go onto the ice only when it has been officially declared safe. The ice can be thin in places, especially near inflows, reeds and bridges. If you fall through, the icy water is life threatening, so the rule is: **never alone** on the ice.

Ice cubes are made by putting water in a mould in the **freezer**. Ice cools drinks and helps against swelling after injuries. In the past, ice was cut from lakes in winter and stored in ice cellars to cool food in summer. Black ice on roads is dangerous, which is why roads are salted in winter: salt water freezes only below 0 degrees.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change from liquid water to solid ice.
The temperature at which water turns into ice, that is, 0 degrees Celsius.
Old, grainy snow that turns into glacier ice.
A large mass of ice that slowly moves down the valley.
A thin, slippery layer of ice on roads and paths.

gewusst: Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top, and the fish can survive underneath.
Snowflakes are made of ice crystals and almost always have six arms.
Glacier ice can have a bluish shimmer, because dense ice absorbs red light more strongly than blue.

teile.einleitung: Deoxyribonucleic acid, DNA for short, is a huge molecule in the cells of all living things. It stores the genetic information, that is, the plan for the whole body. It has the shape of a twisted rope ladder, the famous double helix.
wichtigste: DNA stores the genetic information of all living things and many viruses.
It consists of two strands that wind round each other to form a double helix.
The four bases are called adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine.
Adenine always pairs with thymine, and guanine always with cytosine.
The two strands are antiparallel, which means they run in opposite directions.
The human genome comprises about 3 billion base pairs.
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix, based on Rosalind Franklin's “Photo 51”.

abschnitte.text: DNA looks like a twisted rope ladder. The two sides are made alternately of a sugar and a phosphate group. The rungs are the **base pairs**, which hold together in the middle through **hydrogen bonds**. A building block of sugar, phosphate and base is called a **nucleotide**. The helix is only about 2 millionths of a millimetre thick.

There are four bases in DNA: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). They fit together in only one way; this is called **base pairing**. A and T form two hydrogen bonds, and G and C even three. That is why double stranded DNA always has as much A as T and as much G as C. So if a DNA contains 30 per cent adenine, it also has 30 per cent thymine, leaving 20 per cent each for guanine and cytosine.

The sugar in DNA is called **deoxyribose** and gives it its name. “Deoxy” means that one oxygen is missing. Compared with the ribose in RNA, a **hydroxyl group** is missing on the second carbon atom. This makes DNA more stable than RNA and well suited as a long term store.

Before a cell divides, it has to double its DNA. The double helix is opened like a zip. Enzymes build a new, matching strand for each old strand. So each new double helix contains one old and one new strand; this is called **semiconservative replication**. The order of the bases decides which proteins the cell can make.

In 1869 the Basel doctor **Friedrich Miescher** found a new substance in cell nuclei, which he called “nuclein”. Only much later did it become clear that this substance carries the genetic information. The X-ray image “Photo 51” by **Rosalind Franklin** showed that DNA has a spiral shape. In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published the model of the double helix, and in 1962 they received the Nobel Prize together with Maurice Wilkins.

With DNA analysis, the police can match traces to a person, because almost every person has their own sequence. In medicine, DNA helps to identify hereditary diseases. Researchers read the genetic material of animals and plants to understand how they are related. In 2003 the human genome was largely decoded in the **Human Genome Project**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shape of DNA: two strands that twist round each other like a spiral staircase.
A building block of DNA that carries the genetic information like a letter.
A section of DNA with the instructions for a particular feature or protein.
The whole genetic information of a living thing.
The doubling of DNA before a cell divides.

gewusst: If you unrolled the DNA from a single human cell, it would be about 2 metres long.
The discoverer of nucleic acids, Friedrich Miescher, came from Basel.
Rosalind Franklin died in 1958 and could therefore no longer receive the Nobel Prize of 1962.

teile.einleitung: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Every battery in a remote control and every rechargeable battery in a mobile phone is such a cell or is made up of several of them. It owes its name to the Italian doctor Luigi Galvani.
wichtigste: In a galvanic cell, chemical energy is converted into electrical energy.
It consists of two half cells with different metals or substances.
In the galvanic cell, the anode is the negative terminal; this is where oxidation takes place.
A salt bridge balances the charge through moving ions.
The Daniell cell consists of a zinc and a copper half cell; the electrons flow from the zinc to the copper.
Around 1800 Alessandro Volta built the first battery from zinc and copper discs.
A rechargeable galvanic cell is called an accumulator.

abschnitte.text: A galvanic cell consists of two **half cells**, for example a zinc rod in zinc sulphate solution and a copper rod in copper sulphate solution. The two metals give up electrons with different readiness. If you connect them with a wire, electrons flow from one to the other, and electric current is produced. A **redox reaction** takes place, which converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy.

Electrons are given up at the **anode**; in the galvanic cell it is the negative terminal. At the **cathode**, the positive terminal, particles take in electrons. If nothing else were done, charge would soon build up in the solutions. That is why a **salt bridge** or a porous wall connects the two solutions; ions move through it and balance the charge.

The best known example is the **Daniell cell**, which the English chemist John Frederic Daniell developed in 1836. Zinc is the less noble metal and gives up electrons, slowly dissolving as it does so. The electrons flow through the outer wire to the copper, where copper from the solution is deposited. The Daniell cell supplies a voltage of about 1.1 volts.

In the 18th century the Italian **Luigi Galvani** observed that frogs' legs twitched when they touched two different metals. He believed in a special animal electricity. His fellow countryman **Alessandro Volta** realised that the current came from the metals. Around 1800 he stacked zinc and copper discs with cardboard soaked in salt water and so built the first battery, the voltaic pile. The unit of voltage, the volt, is named after him.

abschnitte.titel: Batteries and rechargeable batteries in everyday life
abschnitte.text: An alkaline manganese battery of size AA has a nominal voltage of 1.5 volts. When it is flat, it cannot be recharged; such cells are called **primary cells**. An **accumulator**, on the other hand, can be recharged by applying an external voltage, because the reaction is reversed. Examples are lithium ion batteries in mobile phones and electric cars or lead acid batteries in cars. Fuel cells are galvanic cells too.

In Switzerland, used batteries and rechargeable batteries must be taken back; there are collection containers wherever they are sold. When you buy them, you pay an advance disposal fee, which pays for the **recycling**. Batteries contain valuable and partly poisonous metals such as zinc, manganese, nickel and lithium. In household waste they would harm the environment; in recycling, the metals are recovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrode in a solution that forms a galvanic cell together with a second half cell.
The electrode at which electrons are given up; in a battery, the negative terminal.
The electrode at which electrons are taken in; in a battery, the positive terminal.
A connection between two half cells through which ions can move.
A rechargeable battery.

gewusst: With a lemon, a galvanised screw and a copper coin, you can build a small galvanic cell.
A 9 volt battery contains several small cells inside, connected one after the other.
In 1801 Volta demonstrated his battery to the French ruler Napoleon Bonaparte.

teile.einleitung: Limestone and acid react vigorously with each other: if you drip acid onto limestone, it fizzes and gas bubbles form. The limestone dissolves and carbon dioxide is produced. Geologists use this reaction in the field and we all use it when descaling at home, and it even shapes whole caves.
wichtigste: Limestone consists mainly of calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3.
When an acid reacts with limestone, it fizzes and gas bubbles form.
Hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate give calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide.
Geologists use dilute hydrochloric acid to test whether a rock contains limestone.
A raw eggshell dissolves in vinegar within a day.
Limestone caves form when water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves limestone.
The Jura consists largely of limestone.
Chalk also consists mainly of calcium carbonate.

abschnitte.text: By **limestone** we usually mean calcium carbonate, chemically **CaCO3**. It consists of calcium, carbon and oxygen. Limestone, marble and **chalk** are made mainly of it, and so are mussel shells, corals and eggshells. Many limestones formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures that were deposited on the sea floor millions of years ago. The white coating in the kettle is also calcium carbonate from tap water.

If you put an acid on limestone, **carbon dioxide** is produced and fizzes up as gas bubbles. With hydrochloric acid the reaction is: calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid give calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. Calcium chloride dissolves in water, which is why the limestone disappears. If you put a raw egg in vinegar for a day, the shell dissolves, and what is left is an egg with a soft skin. The stronger and more concentrated the acid, the more vigorously it fizzes.

In the field, geologists often carry a small bottle of **dilute hydrochloric acid**. They drip a little of it onto a rock. If it fizzes, the rock contains limestone. Granite or gneiss from the Alps, on the other hand, do not fizz. This way rocks can be told apart quickly without needing a laboratory.

Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and soil and so becomes weak **carbonic acid**. When it seeps through limestone, it slowly dissolves it over thousands of years. This creates cracks, sinkholes and large caves; such a landscape is called **karst**. The **Jura** and many mountains of the Prealps, such as the Säntis or Pilatus, are made of limestone. In the Muotatal in the canton of Schwyz lies the Hölloch, one of the longest cave systems in the world.

abschnitte.titel: Limestone and acid in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Kettles, coffee machines and shower heads are descaled with vinegar or **citric acid**. Over time, acid rain can damage statues and buildings made of limestone or marble. In the sea, extra carbon dioxide makes the water a little more acidic, which makes it harder for corals and mussels to build their shells. Acids from food and drinks also attack tooth enamel, which is why brushing your teeth is important. In building, lime is an important raw material for cement and mortar.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical substance that limestone, chalk and marble are made of.
A substance that tastes sour and can dissolve limestone, for example vinegar.
A colourless gas produced when limestone reacts with acid.
A landscape with caves and sinkholes formed by dissolved limestone.

gewusst: More than 200 kilometres of the Hölloch in the Muotatal have been explored.
You can carefully bounce an egg without a shell from the vinegar experiment.
The White Cliffs of Dover in England consist of chalk, that is the shells of tiny sea creatures.

teile.einleitung: The alkaline earth metals form the second main group of the periodic table. They include beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium. They are reactive light metals and occur in nature only in compounds, for example in the limestone of the Jura.
wichtigste: The alkaline earth metals are in the second group of the periodic table.
They have 2 valence electrons, which they give up easily.
They include beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium.
Calcium reacts less violently with water than sodium.
Strontium colours fireworks red, barium colours them green.
Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light.
Radium was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898.

abschnitte.text: The alkaline earth metals are in the **second group** of the periodic table, right next to the alkali metals. Their name dates from the time when their oxides were called “earths” that react with water to form alkalis. All of them have two **valence electrons**, which they readily give up to form ions with a double positive charge. That is why they are base metals and never occur pure in nature. They are shiny, silvery **light metals**.

Alkaline earth metals react with water to form an alkali and **hydrogen**. Calcium reacts visibly, but less violently than the alkali metal sodium. Going down the group, the reaction becomes stronger, so barium reacts much more vigorously than magnesium. Magnesium hardly reacts with cold water, but it does with hot water. Beryllium is a special case and practically does not react with water.

Many alkaline earth metals give flames a typical colour, which is used in the **flame test** and for fireworks. **Strontium** glows red, **barium** green and calcium orange red. **Magnesium** burns with a dazzling white light and used to be used for flash in photography. So the red and green colours in the fireworks on 1 August come from these elements.

**Calcium** is one of the most common elements in the Earth's crust. Limestone, as found in the **Jura** and the limestone Alps, consists mainly of **calcium carbonate**, as do marble and chalk. Gypsum is calcium sulphate. Magnesium is found in the mineral dolomite, after which the Italian Dolomites are named. A lot of magnesium is also dissolved in seawater.

Calcium is an important building material for **bones and teeth**. That is why milk and cheese are considered good sources of calcium. **Magnesium** sits at the centre of the green leaf pigment **chlorophyll** and is therefore essential for photosynthesis in plants. Our muscles and nerves need magnesium too.

**Radium** is radioactive and was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898. It used to be used to paint glowing watch dials, until the dangers of radiation were recognised. Barium sulphate is used in hospitals as a contrast agent for X-rays of the stomach and intestines. Beryllium is poisonous, but because it is so light it is used in special components for space travel. Magnesium is very light and is combined with other metals to make parts for cars and bicycles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A vertical column in the periodic table with elements of similar properties.
A metal with a low density that feels light.
Identifying an element by the colour it gives a flame.
A solution of a base in water; it feels soapy and can be corrosive.
An electrically charged atom that has given up or taken in electrons.

gewusst: Strontium is named after the Scottish village of Strontian, near which it was found.
The rocks of many Jura ranges are made of lime that formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures.
Burning magnesium must not be put out with water, because it even keeps reacting with water.

teile.einleitung: Distillation is a process for separating or purifying liquids by evaporating them and turning them back into liquid. It makes use of the fact that different substances boil at different temperatures. In this way pure water, petrol from crude oil or fragrant oils from plants are produced.
wichtigste: In distillation, a mixture is heated until one component evaporates.
In the condenser the vapour becomes liquid again; this is called condensation.
The liquid collected is called the distillate.
The process uses the different boiling temperatures of substances.
Pure alcohol (ethanol) boils at about 78 °C, water at 100 °C.
If you distil salt water, you get pure water.
In refineries, crude oil is split into petrol, diesel and other parts by fractional distillation.

abschnitte.text: A liquid mixture is heated in a flask. The substance with the lower **boiling temperature** evaporates first. The vapour rises and flows into a cooled tube. There it gives off heat and becomes liquid again; this is **condensation**. The liquid collected at the end is called the **distillate**.

A simple distillation apparatus consists of a heat source, a round bottomed flask, a thermometer, a condenser and a collecting vessel. The thermometer bulb sits exactly level with the side arm leading to the condenser, so that it measures the temperature of the vapour. The **Liebig condenser** is a glass tube with cold water flowing round it. It is named after the German chemist **Justus von Liebig**, who made it well known. Anti bumping granules in the flask make sure the liquid boils calmly.

If you distil salt water, only the water evaporates, and the salt stays behind in the flask. In this way you get **distilled water**, which contains almost no dissolved substances. It is needed, for example, in the laboratory and used to be used often for steam irons. In very dry countries by the sea, huge amounts of drinking water are obtained from seawater by similar processes.

Crude oil is a mixture of many substances. In the refinery it is separated in a tall tower by **fractional distillation**. Light parts such as petrol collect at the top, diesel and heating oil further down, and a sticky residue for bitumen is left right at the bottom. Switzerland's only oil refinery is at Cressier in the canton of Neuchâtel. Liquid air is also split into nitrogen, oxygen and argon in this way.

Distilling fermented fruit is called **brandy making**, “Brennen” in German. A well known example is Kirsch from the Zug region, which is also in the Zug cherry cake. **Steam distillation** is used to obtain essential oils from plants such as lavender, peppermint or Swiss stone pine wood. These oils are used for scents, soaps and teas.

Simple distillation devices were already known in ancient times. In the Middle Ages, Arab scholars improved the distilling vessel, the **alembic**. Through the alchemists the art came to Europe. Today distillation is one of the most important processes in the chemical industry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil and evaporate.
When a gas cools and becomes liquid again.
The purified liquid collected after the condenser.
A part of a mixture that boils within a particular temperature range.
A cooled glass tube in which the vapour becomes liquid again.

gewusst: A distillation tower in a refinery can be several dozen metres high.
When water drips off a cold lid, you are seeing a mini distillation in the kitchen.
The word distillation comes from the Latin “destillare”, which means “to drip down”.

teile.einleitung: The air we breathe is the air we take in and let out with every breath. It brings vital oxygen into our body and carries carbon dioxide out again. The air we breathe out has a different make up from the air we breathe in.
wichtigste: We breathe with our lungs.
The air we breathe travels from the throat into the lungs through the windpipe.
It is best to breathe in through the nose, because it warms and cleans the air.
Breathed out air contains less oxygen, more carbon dioxide and a lot of water vapour.
Green plants make food and oxygen from carbon dioxide.
A classroom should be aired regularly so that stale air goes out.
Divers take their breathing air with them in a compressed air cylinder.

abschnitte.text: The air around us is a mixture of different gases. About 78 per cent is **nitrogen** and around 21 per cent **oxygen**. The small rest is made up mainly of the noble gas argon and about 0.04 per cent carbon dioxide. Depending on the weather, there is also more or less water vapour.

abschnitte.titel: The path of the air we breathe
abschnitte.text: When you breathe in, the air flows through the nose or mouth into the throat. In the **nose** it is warmed, moistened and cleaned of dust by little hairs and mucus. Then it passes through the larynx into the **windpipe** and on into the two lungs. There the airways branch into finer and finer tubes, down to tiny **air sacs**.

In the air sacs, **oxygen** passes into the blood and is carried to all the cells. The cells need it to get energy from food. This produces **carbon dioxide**, which flows back to the lungs with the blood and is breathed out. That is why breathed out air contains only about 16 per cent oxygen, but about 4 per cent carbon dioxide and a lot of **water vapour**.

Green plants take in carbon dioxide from the air. With the help of sunlight they make sugar from it as food and give off **oxygen**. This process is called **photosynthesis**. Forests, meadows and above all tiny algae in the sea supply the oxygen that people and animals need to breathe.

In a closed room with many people, the amount of carbon dioxide rises quickly. You get tired and find it harder to concentrate. That is why a **classroom** should be aired regularly, ideally with the windows wide open for a few minutes, called **burst airing**. Some schools in Switzerland use small CO₂ meters that show when it is time to open the windows.

People cannot breathe under water. Divers therefore carry a **compressed air cylinder**, in which air is squeezed together tightly. Fish, on the other hand, have **gills**, with which they take in the oxygen dissolved in the water. Whales and dolphins are mammals and have to keep coming up to the surface to breathe.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny sacs in the lungs in which oxygen passes into the blood.
The process by which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.
A colourless gas that we breathe out and that plants need to grow.
The breathing organs of fish, which take oxygen from the water.

gewusst: If you breathe on a cold window pane, it gets wet, because the water vapour from your breath condenses.
Breathed out air still contains so much oxygen that it can be used to help someone with mouth to mouth resuscitation.
High in the mountains the air is thinner, which is why you get out of breath faster there.

teile.einleitung: A functional group is a particular group of atoms in a molecule that shapes its properties and reactions. In organic chemistry there are millions of compounds but only a few dozen important functional groups. If you know them, you can predict how a substance will behave.
wichtigste: A functional group is a group of atoms that shapes the properties and reactions of a molecule.
Alcohols carry the hydroxyl group -OH, carboxylic acids the carboxyl group -COOH.
Aldehydes and ketones share the carbonyl group C=O.
Ethers have the structure R-O-R', amides carry the group -CONH₂.
Thiols carry the group -SH, nitriles the group -C≡N.
The carboxyl group has a high priority in IUPAC naming.
Lactic acid has a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group.

abschnitte.text: Organic molecules consist of a framework of carbon and hydrogen to which certain groups of atoms are attached. These groups, the **functional groups**, decide whether a substance is acidic, how it smells or whether it dissolves in water. Substances with the same functional group form a **class of compounds** and react in a similar way. In formulas, the carbon framework is often simply written as R, which stands for “rest”. This makes it possible to put the huge variety of organic substances in order.

The **hydroxyl group** -OH marks alcohols such as the ethanol in wine. The carbonyl group C=O is found in aldehydes such as formaldehyde and in ketones such as acetone, a solvent in nail varnish remover. The **carboxyl group** -COOH makes substances acidic, for example the acetic acid in vinegar. Ethers with the structure R-O-R' and esters with -COO- also belong to the groups containing oxygen.

The amino group -NH₂ occurs in amines, which often smell of fish. **Amides** carry the group -CONH₂; the building blocks of proteins are also linked by amide bonds. Nitriles have a triple bond between carbon and nitrogen, -C≡N. **Thiols** carry the group -SH and often smell extremely strong and unpleasant. Part of the stench of skunks comes from thiols.

The international chemistry union **IUPAC** has drawn up rules for how organic substances are named. The functional group often shows in the ending: alcohols end in -ol, aldehydes in -al, ketones in -one and carboxylic acids in -oic acid. If a molecule has several groups, the one with the highest priority decides the ending. The carboxyl group is near the top, ahead of aldehydes, ketones and alcohols.

Many important substances carry several functional groups. **Lactic acid**, which forms in yoghurt and in tired muscles, has a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group. **Amino acids**, the building blocks of proteins, have an amino group and a carboxyl group. Sugars such as glucose carry several hydroxyl groups and a carbonyl group. That is why they dissolve well in water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of substances with the same functional group and similar properties.
The group -OH, typical of alcohols.
The group -COOH, which makes carboxylic acids acidic.
A carbon atom with a double bond to an oxygen atom, C=O.
An international union that sets the rules for chemical names.

gewusst: Because natural gas itself has no smell, strong smelling sulphur compounds are added to it so that a leak is noticed at once.
Even a tiny trace of a thiol can be smelt; our nose is extremely sensitive to it.
Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same molecular formula but are completely different because of their functional group: one is a liquid, the other a gas.

teile.einleitung: Bases are substances that are the counterpart of acids. If you dissolve a base in water, you get an alkali, which feels slippery and can be corrosive. Bases are found in soap, drain cleaner and many cleaning products.
wichtigste: Bases are the chemical counterpart of acids.
An alkali is a solution of a base in water.
Hydroxide ions (OH-) are typical of alkalis.
Alkalis have a pH above 7.
Red litmus paper turns blue in an alkali.
In the right amounts, an acid and an alkali react to form a salt and water.
Drain cleaner often contains a strong alkali and is dangerous for skin and eyes.

abschnitte.text: According to the Swede Svante Arrhenius, bases are substances that form **hydroxide ions** (OH-) in water. Later, in 1923, Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry defined bases more generally as particles that take up protons. A solution of a base in water is called an **alkali**. Important bases are sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide and ammonia.

Alkalis have a **pH** above 7, and strong alkalis up to 14. They can be recognised with indicators: red **litmus paper** turns blue. Red cabbage juice turns green to yellow in an alkali, depending on its strength. Alkalis feel soapy and slippery, because they attack the fats in the skin.

If you dissolve sodium hydroxide in water, you get **sodium hydroxide solution**. It is found in drain cleaners and oven cleaners, because it breaks down grease and hair. For thousands of years soap has been made from fat and alkali. The lye pretzel also gets its brown crust because the dough is dipped briefly in dilute sodium hydroxide solution before baking.

If you put an acid and an alkali together in the right amounts, they cancel each other out. This reaction is called **neutralisation**. It produces a salt and water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution, for example, give table salt and water. Medicines with weak bases help against too much stomach acid.

Strong alkalis are **corrosive** and even more dangerous for the eyes than many acids. That is why you always wear safety glasses and gloves when working with alkalis. Household products containing alkali carry a hazard symbol and must be kept out of children's reach. If alkali gets into an eye, you must rinse it with water for a long time at once and get help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solution of a base in water.
A particle made of one oxygen and one hydrogen atom with a negative charge, OH-.
A number from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline something is.
The reaction of an acid and an alkali to form a salt and water.
A dye that shows by its colour whether something is acidic or alkaline.

gewusst: The German word for alkali, “Lauge”, comes from an old word for washing water.
Ammonia is a base with a strong smell that is found in some glass cleaners.
After baking, the lye pretzel is no longer corrosive, because the alkali reacts in the heat.

teile.einleitung: The GHS hazard pictograms are nine warning signs for dangerous chemicals that are the same all over the world. They show a black symbol in a white diamond with a red border. Together with signal words and hazard statements, they say exactly what danger a substance poses.
wichtigste: GHS stands for “Globally Harmonised System” for classifying and labelling chemicals.
There are nine different GHS hazard pictograms.
The labels carry the signal words “Danger” or “Warning”.
The standardised hazard statements are called H statements.
A drain cleaner often carries the pictogram for corrosive substances.
An exclamation mark means irritant or harmful to health.
Before, Switzerland used black symbols on orange squares.

abschnitte.text: **GHS** is the abbreviation for the Globally Harmonised System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals. It was drawn up by the United Nations and published in the early 2000s. The aim is for dangerous substances to be labelled in the same way all over the world. Switzerland and the EU have adopted the system and replaced the old orange symbols.

There are nine **pictograms**: exploding bomb, flame, flame over circle, gas cylinder, corrosion, skull and crossbones, exclamation mark, health hazard and environment. The gas cylinder stands for gases under pressure. The upper body of a person with a star on the chest warns of serious damage to health, such as cancer or lung damage. The exclamation mark stands for irritant or harmful substances.

Besides the pictograms, a GHS label contains a **signal word**. “Danger” is used for serious hazards, “Warning” for less serious ones. In addition there are the **H statements**, standardised hazard statements such as “Causes serious eye damage”. The **P statements** give safety advice, for example “Keep out of reach of children”.

A drain cleaner often carries the pictogram for **corrosive** substances, because it can injure skin and eyes. Methylated spirits and barbecue lighter fluid show the flame. Some spray cans carry the flame and the gas cylinder at the same time, because they contain a flammable gas under pressure. Plant protection products often show the environment pictogram with a tree and a fish.

Before you use a product with a GHS pictogram, read the label carefully. Often you need gloves or safety goggles, and you should air the room well. You must never mix different cleaning products, because poisonous gases can form. In case of an accident, Tox Info Suisse can help on the telephone number 145.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple picture symbol that communicates something without words.
A word on the label that shows how great the danger is: “Danger” or “Warning”.
Standardised sentences that describe the hazard of a substance.
Standardised sentences with advice on how to protect yourself.

gewusst: Each GHS pictogram has a number from GHS01 for the bomb to GHS09 for the environment.
For transport by road and rail there are separate hazard labels that look different from the GHS pictograms.
If you mix a cleaning product containing chlorine with an acidic descaler, poisonous chlorine gas can form.

teile.einleitung: Argon is a colourless, odourless noble gas that makes up almost one per cent of our air. We breathe it in and out with every breath without it doing anything in the body. Because it hardly reacts with other substances, it is very popular in technology as a shielding gas.
wichtigste: Argon has the chemical symbol Ar and the atomic number 18.
At just under 1 per cent, it is the third most common gas in dry air.
The Greek name argon means “the lazy one”.
Argon almost never reacts, because its outer electron shell is full.
Most of the argon in the atmosphere comes from the decay of radioactive potassium in rocks.
In welding, argon protects the hot metal from oxygen in the air.
Argon is used as a filling gas in light bulbs and double glazed windows.

abschnitte.text: Argon is a chemical **element** with the symbol Ar and the atomic number 18. It is one of the **noble gases**, the eighth main group in the periodic table, together with helium, neon, krypton, xenon and radon. At room temperature it is a colourless, odourless and non poisonous gas. Only at about minus 186 degrees Celsius does it become liquid.

The name comes from the Greek word for “lazy” or “idle”. Argon almost never reacts with other substances, because its outer **electron shell** is completely full. Atoms with a full outer shell are particularly **stable** and have no reason to form bonds. That is why argon occurs in nature only as single atoms.

Argon was discovered in 1894 by the British scientists **Lord Rayleigh** and **William Ramsay**. Rayleigh had noticed that nitrogen from the air was slightly heavier than nitrogen from chemical compounds. The two found out that an unknown gas was hidden in the nitrogen from the air. Both received a Nobel Prize for this discovery in 1904.

In dry air, argon makes up just under 1 per cent; after **nitrogen** and oxygen, it is the third most common gas. Most of it formed over billions of years as radioactive **potassium** in rocks decayed. Today argon is obtained by cooling air strongly, liquefying it and separating it into its components. This process is called air separation.

In **welding**, argon is blown around the weld so that the hot metal does not react with the oxygen in the air. Classic light bulbs were filled with argon instead of air so that the hot **filament** would not burn up. Argon also protects against unwanted reactions when making computer chips and storing sensitive substances. In fluorescent tubes it produces a bluish light, depending on the design.

Many **double glazed windows** have a filling of argon between the panes. Argon conducts heat less well than air and so gives better **thermal insulation**. In geology, the decay of potassium to argon is used to work out the age of rocks. This method is called potassium argon dating.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas that almost never reacts with other substances.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus; it determines the element.
A gas that protects sensitive substances from air.
Protection against heat being lost.

gewusst: In an ordinary classroom, several kilograms of argon float in the air.
Argon is much more common in the air than carbon dioxide.
Divers sometimes use argon to fill their drysuits, because it insulates well.

teile.einleitung: Fire safety covers everything that prevents fires and protects people in a fire. It includes smoke alarms, fire extinguishers and emergency exits, but also the right behaviour in an emergency. Anyone who knows what to do in a fire can save themselves and others.
wichtigste: In a fire, the first thing you do is raise the alarm; in Switzerland the fire brigade number is 118.
To leave a burning house, you use the stairs and never the lift.
When leaving a burning room, you close the door, because it holds back smoke and fire.
Emergency exits are marked with green signs.
If your clothes are on fire, you lie down and roll on the ground.
When escaping, you do not gather up toys or other things.
In a fire drill at school, everyone meets at the assembly point.
The fire brigade comes in red vehicles to put out fires.

abschnitte.text: For a fire to burn, it needs three things: a **fuel** such as wood or paper, **oxygen** from the air and enough **heat**. This is called the fire triangle. If one of the three parts is missing, the fire goes out. All methods of putting out fires are based on this, for example cooling with water or smothering with a fire blanket.

In a fire the order is **raise the alarm, rescue, extinguish**. In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on **118**, and the European emergency number 112 works too. You say calmly who is calling, where the fire is and what has happened. You should put out only small fires where you do not put yourself in danger.

When escaping, you always take the **stairs**, because a lift can get stuck or fill with smoke. Smoke is the greatest danger: it is poisonous and rises, so you move as low down to the floor as possible. You close doors behind you so that smoke and fire spread more slowly. Green **emergency exit** signs show the safe way outside.

A **smoke alarm** on the ceiling beeps loudly as soon as there is smoke and wakes even people who are asleep. A fire extinguisher and a **fire blanket** in the kitchen help with small fires. Burning fat in a pan must never be put out with water, otherwise it sprays out explosively. Candles and Advent wreaths should never be left burning unattended.

Schools hold regular **fire drills**. Everyone leaves the building calmly and quickly by the set escape route. Outside, you meet at the **assembly point** so that the teacher can check that everyone is there. In Switzerland, fire safety regulations set out, for example, how wide escape routes must be.

The fire brigade comes in red vehicles, with ladders, hoses and breathing apparatus. In Switzerland, most firefighters are members of the **volunteer fire brigade**, who turn out alongside their jobs. Large towns also have professional fire brigades. Many municipalities also offer a **youth fire brigade** for children and teenagers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The three things a fire needs: fuel, oxygen and heat.
A small device that sounds a loud alarm when there is smoke.
A fireproof blanket used to smother small fires.
A fixed meeting place outside where everyone gathers after escaping.

gewusst: In a house fire, it is usually not the flames but the poisonous smoke that is most dangerous.
Just one litre of burning oil put out with water can produce a fireball metres high.
Most firefighters in Switzerland volunteer alongside their actual jobs.

teile.einleitung: Benzene is a colourless liquid with a sweetish smell and the formula C₆H₆. Its six carbon atoms form a flat ring, which puzzled chemists for a long time. Benzene is an important basic material for industry, but it is also carcinogenic.
wichtigste: Benzene has the molecular formula C₆H₆.
Michael Faraday was the first to isolate benzene, in 1825.
In 1865 August Kekulé proposed the ring shaped structure.
The molecule is a flat, regular hexagon with bonds of equal length.
Benzene is the simplest aromatic compound.
It boils at about 80 °C.
Benzene is carcinogenic and is therefore hardly used as a solvent any more.

abschnitte.text: Benzene is a clear, highly flammable liquid that boils at about 80 °C and becomes solid at around 5 °C. It consists of six carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms. Benzene is the basic form of the **aromatic compounds**, a large group of substances that also includes toluene and naphthalene. The name aromatic comes from the fact that many of these substances have a strong smell.

The English scientist **Michael Faraday** first obtained benzene in 1825 from the residues of lighting gas. For a long time nobody knew how the atoms were arranged, because the molecule behaves differently from what was expected. In 1865 the German chemist **August Kekulé** proposed a ring of six carbon atoms. He later said that the idea came to him while half asleep, when he saw a snake biting its own tail.

Kekulé drew the ring with alternating single and double bonds. But measurements show that all six bonds are the same length, somewhere between a single and a double bond. The electrons are spread over the whole ring; this is called **resonance**. This makes benzene particularly stable; the resonance energy is about 150 kJ/mol.

Because of its stability, benzene does not react like ordinary double bonds. Instead of adding atoms, it usually exchanges a hydrogen atom for another atom; this is called **substitution**. If you want to react benzene with bromine, you need a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide. In this way the stable ring is kept.

Benzene is an important starting material for plastics such as polystyrene, for dyes, medicines and nylon. But it is **carcinogenic** and with longer contact can cause blood diseases such as leukaemia. That is why it is hardly used as a solvent any more. In Switzerland and the EU, petrol may contain at most 1 per cent benzene by volume.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances with a particularly stable ring of atoms, like the one benzene has.
When electrons do not sit in one fixed place but are spread over several atoms.
A reaction in which one atom in the molecule is exchanged for another.
Able to cause cancer in the body.

gewusst: The hexagon with a circle inside that chemists draw for benzene is one of the best known symbols of chemistry.
Benzene is also produced when tobacco burns and is therefore found in cigarette smoke.
The small amount of benzene left in petrol is one reason why you should not breathe in petrol fumes at a filling station.

teile.einleitung: An atomic model is a simplified idea of how an atom is built. Because nobody can look at an atom like an object, researchers have developed better and better models over time. Each model explains certain observations and was improved by new experiments.
wichtigste: An atomic model describes the structure of an atom in a simplified way.
From 1808 John Dalton published an atomic theory in which all atoms of an element weigh the same.
Thomson's atomic model is often called the plum pudding model.
From the scattering experiment with alpha particles and gold foil, Rutherford concluded that there is a tiny, positively charged nucleus.
In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed that electrons circle on orbits with fixed energies without giving off radiation.
In the orbital model, an orbital describes a region of space in which an electron is very likely to be.
An s orbital is spherical.

abschnitte.text: From 1808 the English scientist **John Dalton** published an atomic theory. According to it, every element consists of tiny, indivisible balls. All the atoms of one element weigh the same, while the atoms of different elements weigh different amounts. In chemical reactions, atoms are only joined in new ways, not destroyed or newly created.

In 1897 Joseph John Thomson discovered the electron. So the atom could no longer be indivisible. In his **Thomson atomic model**, he imagined the atom as a positively charged ball in which the negative electrons are stuck like raisins in a cake. That is why it is also called the **plum pudding model**; in German it is the “raisin cake model”.

From 1909, under the direction of **Ernest Rutherford**, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. Almost all of them simply flew through, but a few were strongly deflected or even bounced back. In 1911 Rutherford concluded that almost all the mass sits in a tiny, positively charged **atomic nucleus**. The electrons surround this nucleus in an otherwise almost empty space.

In 1913 the Dane **Niels Bohr** presented a new model for the hydrogen atom. In it, the electrons circle on particular orbits with fixed energies, without giving off radiation. If an electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit, it gives off light of one particular colour. In this way Bohr explained the coloured lines in the **spectrum** of hydrogen.

From 1926, researchers such as Erwin Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg developed **quantum mechanics**. According to it, you cannot say exactly where an electron is, only where it is likely to be. This region of space is called an **orbital**. The azimuthal quantum number l decides the shape: s orbitals are spherical, and p orbitals look like dumbbells.

Every atomic model is a simplification and not a true picture. At school the shell model is often used, because it is simple and explains a lot in chemistry well. For more precise questions you need the orbital model. The history of atomic models shows well how **science** works: experiments test ideas, and models are improved.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simplified idea that makes something invisible explainable.
