A positively charged particle made of two protons and two neutrons.
A region of space in which an electron is very likely to be.
Light split up into its individual colours.
A number that describes the state of an electron in the atom.

gewusst: Rutherford compared his surprise to a shell bouncing back off a piece of tissue paper.
Niels Bohr received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922.
Bohr's model works well for hydrogen but badly for atoms with many electrons.

teile.einleitung: A dipole is a particle with two differently charged ends, one slightly positive and one slightly negative. The best known dipole molecule is water. Because water molecules are dipoles, water dissolves so many substances and yet does not mix with oil.
wichtigste: A dipole molecule has a positive and a negative end.
The small charges at the ends are called partial charges.
The prefix “di” means two, so a dipole has two poles.
In the water molecule, the oxygen end is partly negatively charged.
Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is also a typical dipole molecule.
Oil and water do not mix, because water is polar and oil is non polar.
Substances that mix well with water are called hydrophilic.

abschnitte.text: A **dipole** has two poles with opposite charges, just as a magnet has a north and a south pole. In chemistry it usually means a molecule in which the electrons are unevenly spread. One end is then slightly negative and the other slightly positive. These weak charges are called **partial charges** and are written with the Greek letter δ (delta).

Atoms pull the shared electrons in a bond with different strengths. This ability is called **electronegativity**. In hydrogen fluoride (HF), the fluorine pulls the electrons strongly towards itself, so it is partly negative and the hydrogen partly positive. But a molecule is a dipole only if, because of its shape, the charges do not cancel each other out. Carbon dioxide (CO₂), for example, is straight and therefore not a dipole despite its polar bonds.

A **water molecule** (H₂O) is bent, rather like a V. The oxygen attracts the electrons more strongly and carries a negative partial charge. The two hydrogen atoms are partly positive. You can show this with a simple experiment: a thin stream of water is deflected to the side by a rubbed plastic rod or balloon.

Polar substances dissolve well in polar substances, and non polar ones in non polar ones. People say: **like dissolves like.** Oil consists of non polar molecules, which is why it does not mix with water and floats on top. Substances that like water are called **hydrophilic**, and substances that avoid water **hydrophobic**. Salt and sugar are hydrophilic and therefore dissolve well in water.

In a microwave oven, an electric field changes direction very fast. The water molecules in the food keep turning with it, and this movement warms the food. Soap has a hydrophilic and a hydrophobic end and can therefore link fat with water. There are dipoles in technology too, for example the **dipole aerial** for radio and television.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small charge at one end of a molecule, smaller than the charge of an electron.
A molecule with unevenly spread charges, that is, a dipole.
A molecule without a positive and a negative end, for example oil.
Water loving; mixes or dissolves well in water.
Water repellent; does not mix with water.

gewusst: Because water molecules are dipoles, water has a surprisingly high boiling point for such a small molecule.
A rubbed balloon can visibly bend a thin stream of water from the tap.
The angle in the water molecule between the two hydrogen atoms is about 104.5 degrees.

teile.einleitung: Helium is a colourless, odourless gas that makes party balloons float upwards. It is the second lightest element after hydrogen and belongs to the noble gases. It was named after the Sun, because that is where it was first discovered.
wichtigste: Helium has the atomic number 2 and is the second lightest gas after hydrogen.
It is colourless, odourless and tasteless.
Helium does not burn and reacts with practically no other substance.
The name comes from the Greek word “helios” for Sun.
Helium balloons shrink after a few days because the gas escapes through the skin.
Modern airships are filled with helium.
Breathing in helium from balloons is dangerous because you then get too little oxygen.

abschnitte.text: In 1868, during a solar eclipse, scientists observed a yellow line in the light of the Sun that did not match any known element. The Englishman Norman Lockyer suspected a new element and named it **helium** after the Sun. Only in 1895 did the chemist William Ramsay find helium on Earth too, in a mineral. In space, helium is the second most common element of all after hydrogen.

Helium is about seven times lighter than air. That is why it creates a strong **buoyancy** and makes balloons rise. In the past, airships were filled with hydrogen, but it burns very easily. Because helium is not flammable, today’s airships and weather balloons are much safer with it.

Helium belongs to the **noble gases**, which form almost no chemical compounds. Its atoms are so small that they slip through thin rubber skins. That is why a latex balloon sinks to the ground after one or two days, while foil balloons last longer. Helium only becomes liquid at about minus 269 °C; no other substance has to get this cold before it turns liquid.

Liquid helium cools the powerful magnets in hospitals that are used to make an **MRI** scan of the inside of the body. Divers breathe gas mixtures containing helium on very deep dives. In research too, for example at the CERN particle accelerator in Geneva, helium cools huge magnets. It also protects the hot metal from the air during welding.

If you breathe in helium, you suddenly speak with a high, funny voice. This is because sound travels about three times faster in helium than in air. Even so, it is dangerous, because there is then no **oxygen** in your lungs. You can faint, so you should never try it.

On Earth, helium forms very slowly when radioactive rocks decay. It collects underground together with **natural gas** and is extracted from it. Whatever escapes into the air rises all the way into space and is lost. That is why experts warn against wasting this valuable gas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas that hardly ever reacts with other substances, for example helium or neon.
A force that pushes a light object upwards in heavier surroundings.
The number of an element in the periodic table; it gives the number of protons.
A coloured line in split light by which an element can be recognised.

gewusst: Helium was discovered on the Sun almost 30 years before it was found on Earth.
At normal air pressure, helium does not become solid even at absolute zero.
The balloon Breitling Orbiter 3, in which Bertrand Piccard flew round the Earth in 1999, was partly filled with helium.

teile.einleitung: Iron is the metal that people use most. It is made into steel for bridges, cars, rails and tools. There is iron in our blood too, without which we could not carry oxygen.
wichtigste: Iron has the chemical symbol Fe, from the Latin word ferrum.
Iron is obtained from iron ore, which is melted in a blast furnace.
Steel consists mainly of iron.
Our blood needs iron to carry oxygen.
Iron is magnetic and can itself become a magnet.
In damp air, iron rusts.
The time when people learned to make iron is called the Iron Age.

abschnitte.text: Iron is a grey, shiny metal with the symbol **Fe** and the atomic number 26. It is almost eight times as heavy as water, which is why an iron nail sinks in water at once. Iron is attracted by magnets, and if you stroke a nail many times in the same direction with a magnet, it becomes magnetic itself. In damp air, reddish brown **rust** forms, which slowly eats away the iron.

In nature, iron is found almost only as **iron ore**, that is, rock containing iron compounds. In the **blast furnace** the ore is melted with coke at very high temperatures, producing liquid pig iron. Because pig iron is brittle, it is usually made into **steel** by removing carbon. Heavy, dark frying pans, on the other hand, are often made of cast iron.

In central Europe the **Iron Age** began around 800 BC and followed the Bronze Age. Iron tools and weapons were harder, and the ore was more common than copper and tin. Part of the Iron Age is called the La Tène period, named after a site on Lake Neuchâtel. There archaeologists found many swords and other iron objects of the Celts.

Our blood is red because it contains the pigment **haemoglobin**, with iron at its centre. In the lungs, oxygen binds to this iron, and the blood carries it to all parts of the body. If iron is lacking, you are often tired and pale. Iron is found, for example, in meat, lentils, beans and wholemeal products.

The **Eiffel Tower** in Paris was riveted together from thousands of iron parts in 1889. Today bridges, tower blocks, railway lines, cars and ships are made largely of steel. In Switzerland, iron ore was mined at the Gonzen near Sargans until the 20th century. Old iron can be melted down and recycled well.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rock that contains so much iron that the iron can be extracted from it.
A huge furnace in which iron ore is melted into liquid iron.
Iron with a little carbon, which is hard and tough.
The red pigment in blood, containing iron, which carries oxygen.

gewusst: The Earth's core probably consists mostly of iron and nickel.
Some of humanity's oldest iron objects were forged from meteorites that had fallen from the sky.
Mars is red because its dust contains a lot of iron oxide, a kind of rust.

teile.einleitung: Gold is a rare, shiny yellow precious metal that has fascinated people for thousands of years. It does not rust, is very heavy and can be beaten wafer-thin. To this day gold is used for jewellery, as an investment and in technology.
wichtigste: Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and the atomic number 79.
Pure gold shines yellow and does not rust.
Gold is very heavy: a cube with sides of 10 cm weighs over 19 kilograms.
Gold can be beaten into wafer-thin gold leaf.
A rectangular block of pure gold is called a gold bar.
The Swiss National Bank keeps Switzerland’s gold.
In the Napf area people still pan gold from the streams today.
The Vreneli is the best-known old Swiss gold coin.

abschnitte.text: Gold is a **precious metal**, which means it hardly reacts with air, water or acids. That is why it does not rust and still shines like new even after thousands of years. Its **density** is about 19.3 grams per cubic centimetre, almost twice that of lead. Gold melts at around 1064 degrees Celsius. It is very soft and stretchy; it can be drawn into fine wires or beaten into foils.

Coins were already being minted from gold over 2500 years ago. In Switzerland the **Vreneli** is famous, a 20-franc gold coin with the head of Helvetia, which was minted from 1897. Today gold coins are no longer used for everyday payments, but they are popular collector’s items and investments. The **Swiss National Bank** owns about 1040 tonnes of gold. A large part of it is stored in Switzerland, the rest in Great Britain and Canada.

Gold is found in veins of rock deep underground or as small grains in the sand of rivers. Large amounts are mined today in China, Australia, Russia and other countries. In Switzerland, hobby gold prospectors pan gold from the streams in the **Napf area** between Lucerne and Bern. For this they use a flat **gold pan**, in which the heavy gold stays behind while lighter sand is washed away. The flakes are usually tiny; you will not get rich this way.

Most pieces of gold jewellery are not made of pure gold but of an **alloy**, that is a mixture with silver or copper. This makes the jewellery harder. Purity is given in **carats**: 24 carats means pure gold. **Gold leaf** is so thin that light shines through it; it is used to gild picture frames, church domes and even cakes. The ancient Egyptians already made magnificent gold masks, for example for the pharaoh Tutankhamun.

Because gold conducts electricity very well and never rusts, it is found in almost every mobile phone and computer. There it coats tiny contacts and connectors. Gold is also used in space travel, for example as a thin layer on the visors of astronauts’ helmets to keep out solar radiation. Dentists used to use gold often for crowns and fillings. Old gold from electronic waste can be recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal that hardly reacts with air and water and therefore does not rust.
A measure of the purity of gold; 24 carats is pure gold.
A mixture of two or more metals.
Gold that has been beaten into wafer-thin sheets.
A rectangular block of pure gold.

gewusst: All the gold ever mined would fit into a cube with sides of only about 22 metres.
Gold leaf can be thinner than a ten-thousandth of a millimetre.
Gold from ancient graves still shines today just as it did thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: A battery is a small energy store that turns chemical energy into electric current. It is found in remote controls, torches, watches and toys. Because batteries contain valuable but also harmful substances, in Switzerland empty batteries do not go in the rubbish but back to the shop.
wichtigste: In a battery, a chemical reaction supplies electric current.
A rechargeable battery can be charged up again.
In Switzerland, empty batteries are taken back to a shop, and returning them is free.
Batteries do not belong in the rubbish bag, because they contain harmful substances.
Old lithium batteries in the rubbish can cause fires.
Metals such as zinc and iron can be recovered from old batteries.
A crossed out wheelie bin on the battery shows that it does not belong in the rubbish.
Button batteries must be kept away from small children, because swallowing them is very dangerous.

abschnitte.text: Every battery has a **positive terminal** and a **negative terminal** made of different materials. Between them is an **electrolyte**, a paste or liquid in which charged particles can move. If you connect the terminals through a device, electrons flow from the negative to the positive terminal. Meanwhile chemical reactions take place in the battery until the materials are used up.

Around the year 1800, the Italian **Alessandro Volta** built the first battery, the voltaic pile. It consisted of stacked discs of zinc and copper with layers soaked in salt water in between. The unit of voltage, the **volt**, is named after him. An ordinary AA battery supplies about 1.5 volts.

Ordinary batteries such as **alkaline batteries** can be used only once. A **rechargeable battery**, on the other hand, can be charged again many hundreds of times. Lithium ion batteries are found in mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and electric cars. They store a lot of energy in a small space but can get hot and catch fire if damaged.

In Switzerland, all shops that sell batteries must take empty batteries back **free of charge**. The recycling is paid for through an **advance recycling fee**, which is already included in the price. In special plants, metals such as zinc, iron, manganese and nickel are recovered. A crossed out wheelie bin on the battery is a reminder that it does not belong in the household rubbish.

Batteries contain substances that can pollute soil and water. **Lithium batteries** in the rubbish bag can cause fires in bin lorries or sorting plants. **Button batteries** are particularly dangerous for small children: if swallowed, they can cause serious injuries in the gullet within a short time. In such a case you must contact a doctor or the emergency number at once.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in the battery through which charged particles can travel.
In German “Akku”, short for accumulator, a battery that can be charged up again.
The unit of electric voltage.
Reusing materials from old objects.

gewusst: The unit volt is named after the inventor of the battery, Alessandro Volta.
A lemon with a piece of copper and a piece of zinc can also be a small battery.
Batteries do not last much longer in the fridge; a dry place at room temperature is enough.

teile.einleitung: The chemical bond is the force that holds atoms together. Without it there would be no molecules, no crystals and no metals, and so no water, no salt and no people. Depending on the kind of atoms, there are different kinds of bond.
wichtigste: Chemical bonds hold atoms together in molecules, salts and metals.
The three main kinds of bond are the covalent bond, the ionic bond and the metallic bond.
According to the octet rule, atoms aim for eight valence electrons.
Fluorine has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale.
From an electronegativity difference of about 1.7, it is called an ionic bond.
In metals, freely moving electrons hold the metal cations together.
Water boils at a much higher temperature than H₂S, because hydrogen bonds act between water molecules.
Between non polar molecules such as methane, mainly van der Waals forces act.

abschnitte.text: Atoms are particularly stable when their outermost shell is full. For most main group elements this means eight **valence electrons**, as in the noble gases. This **octet rule** explains why atoms give up, take in or share electrons. Hydrogen is an exception; two electrons are enough for it.

In a **covalent bond**, also called an electron pair bond, two non metal atoms share pairs of electrons. In the nitrogen molecule N₂ there is a triple bond with three pairs, that is, six electrons. If one partner pulls the electrons more strongly, a **polar covalent bond** forms, as in hydrogen chloride HCl. How strongly an atom attracts electrons is described by electronegativity, which Linus Pauling introduced in 1932. Fluorine has the highest value, about 4.0.

If the difference in electronegativity is very large, as a rule of thumb from about 1.7, one atom gives up electrons completely. Positive and negative **ions** are formed, which attract each other. This is how table salt, sodium chloride, is built. The ions form a regular lattice, which is why salts are often crystals with a high melting point.

In metals the atoms give up their outer electrons. The positively charged metal cations sit in a lattice, and between them the electrons move freely like an **electron gas**. These free electrons hold everything together. They also explain why metals conduct electricity and heat well and are shiny.

There are forces of attraction between molecules too, but they are much weaker. **Hydrogen bonds**, for example, link water molecules, which is why water boils only at 100 degrees, while the similar H₂S is already a gas at about minus 60 degrees. Between non polar molecules such as methane, only weak **van der Waals forces** act. That is why methane is a gas at room temperature.

begriffe.erklaerung: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
A measure of how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons.
A particle made of two or more firmly joined atoms.
A positively charged ion.
An attraction between a hydrogen atom and a strongly electronegative atom of another molecule.

gewusst: Geckos can walk on glass panes because millions of fine hairs on their feet use van der Waals forces.
Diamond is so hard because every carbon atom is joined to four neighbours by covalent bonds.
Without hydrogen bonds, water would be a gas at room temperature.

teile.einleitung: Many chemical reactions run not only in one direction but also back again. When the forward and backward reactions run equally fast, a chemical equilibrium has been reached. From the outside nothing then seems to happen any more, even though the particles keep on reacting.
wichtigste: In chemical equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions run equally fast.
It is a dynamic equilibrium; the reactions never stop.
An equilibrium constant K much greater than 1 means that the equilibrium lies on the side of the products.
According to Le Chatelier's principle, an equilibrium shifts to counteract an outside change.
In the synthesis of ammonia, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards more ammonia.
Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium of an exothermic reaction towards the reactants.
A catalyst makes the equilibrium form faster but does not change its position.
The ionic product of water at 25 °C is 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/L².

abschnitte.text: In a **reversible reaction**, the reactants react to form products, and at the same time products break down again into reactants. At the start the forward reaction dominates. Over time it gets slower and the backward reaction faster, until both are equally fast. Then **chemical equilibrium** has been reached, and the amounts of the substances no longer change.

In 1864 the Norwegians Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage described the **law of mass action**. It combines the concentrations of the substances at equilibrium into one number, the **equilibrium constant K**. If K is much greater than 1, mainly products are present. If K is much smaller than 1, the equilibrium lies on the side of the reactants.

In 1884 the Frenchman Henry Le Chatelier formulated an important rule: if an outside change is applied to an equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts to counteract it. If you add more reactant, more product is formed. If you raise the temperature, the direction that uses up heat is favoured, so for an **exothermic** reaction the backward reaction. If you increase the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer gas particles.

A famous example is making **ammonia** from nitrogen and hydrogen: N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃. On the left there are four gas particles, on the right only two, so high pressure favours the formation of ammonia. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed the process at the beginning of the 20th century. An iron catalyst makes sure that the equilibrium is reached quickly. Ammonia is used mainly to make fertilisers.

There is an equilibrium in pure water too: a tiny part of the water molecules breaks up into ions. The **ionic product of water** at 25 °C is 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/L², which gives a pH of 7 for neutral water. In a closed bottle of sparkling mineral water, dissolved carbon dioxide is in equilibrium with the gas above it. When you open the bottle, the pressure falls and the gas fizzes out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which the forward and backward reactions run equally fast.
A number that tells you on which side an equilibrium lies.
The rule that an equilibrium shifts to counteract an outside change.
A reaction that can run in both directions.

gewusst: Without the Haber Bosch process, farming today could feed only part of the world's population.
In our blood too, equilibria make sure that the pH almost always stays at about 7.4.
Fritz Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918 and Carl Bosch in 1931.

teile.einleitung: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not really mix, for example oil and water. Tiny droplets of one liquid float in the other. Milk, mayonnaise and skin cream are well known emulsions from everyday life.
wichtigste: An emulsion is a mixture of tiny droplets of one liquid in another.
Oil and water do not mix by themselves.
If you shake oil and water hard, many small droplets of oil form.
Without help, the two liquids separate again after a short time.
An emulsifier such as washing up liquid or egg yolk keeps the droplets spread out.
Milk is an emulsion of droplets of fat in water.
Mayonnaise is made of oil and egg yolk, which mix well together.

abschnitte.text: Some liquids do not get on with each other, like **oil and water**. If you pour them together, the lighter oil lies on top as a separate layer. If you shake hard, the oil breaks up into many small droplets that float in the water. Such a mixture is called an **emulsion**. The word comes from the Latin “emulgere”, which means “to milk out”, because milk is the best known example.

If you leave a shaken salad dressing of oil and vinegar to stand, it soon separates again. That is why you shake or stir it just before serving. For an emulsion to stay stable, an **emulsifier** is needed. An emulsifier has a water loving and a fat loving end and sits like a go between between oil and water. In **egg yolk**, the substance lecithin acts as an emulsifier, which is why mayonnaise holds together well.

**Milk** contains tiny droplets of fat spread out in water. If you leave raw milk to stand, the fat rises to the top and forms cream. That is why in the dairy the fat droplets are broken up finely; this is called **homogenising**. Mayonnaise and hollandaise sauce are oil in water emulsions. Butter, on the other hand, is a water in oil emulsion, with small droplets of water inside the fat.

An oil stain on a jumper cannot be washed out with pure water, because oil and water do not mix. **Washing up liquid** and detergents contain surfactants, which work like emulsifiers. They wrap round the droplets of fat so that the water can wash them away. Skin creams, sun creams and shampoos are emulsions too.

Burning oil in a pan must **never be put out with water**. The water sinks under the hot oil and evaporates suddenly. As it does so, it carries burning oil with it as a fine mist, and a dangerous flash of flame results. The right thing is to switch off the hob and put a lid or a **fire blanket** on the pan.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of tiny droplets of one liquid in another liquid.
A substance that links oil and water and keeps the emulsion stable.
A cleaning substance in soap and washing up liquid.
Breaking up droplets of fat so that they stay evenly spread.

gewusst: Milk looks white because the many droplets of fat and particles of protein scatter light in all directions.
Just one egg yolk is enough to bind a whole cup of oil into a creamy sauce for mayonnaise.
Oil paints and some medicinal ointments are emulsions too.

teile.einleitung: Enthalpy is a quantity from thermodynamics that chemists use to describe the heat involved in reactions. What matters most is its change ΔH: it shows how much heat a reaction gives off or takes in at constant pressure. With it you can calculate how much energy is released when natural gas is burnt.
wichtigste: Enthalpy is defined as H = U + p·V.
At constant pressure, the enthalpy of reaction is exactly equal to the heat exchanged.
A negative enthalpy of reaction ΔH means that the reaction is exothermic.
A positive enthalpy of reaction means that the reaction is endothermic.
The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable form is zero.
Liquid water has a standard enthalpy of formation of about minus 286 kJ/mol.
Burning one mole of methane releases about 890 kJ.

abschnitte.text: Every substance contains energy stored in its particles and bonds. This is called **internal energy** U. **Enthalpy** H adds to it the work needed to make room for the substance against the air pressure: H = U + p·V. Absolute enthalpy cannot be measured, but its change ΔH can. The name comes from the Greek “enthalpein”, which means roughly “to warm”.

In an **exothermic reaction**, the system gives off heat to its surroundings, and ΔH is negative. One example is burning wood or natural gas. In an **endothermic reaction**, the system takes in heat, and ΔH is positive. Because most reactions take place in open vessels at constant air pressure, ΔH is exactly the heat that is measured. It is measured in a **calorimeter**.

The **standard enthalpy of formation** states how much heat is released or needed when one mole of a substance is formed from its elements. For elements in their most stable form, such as O₂ as a gas, it is zero by definition. For liquid water it is about minus 286 kJ/mol. With such table values you can calculate ΔH for any reaction: you subtract the sum for the starting substances from the sum for the products. For burning methane this gives about minus 890 kJ/mol.

ΔH can also be estimated with **bond enthalpies**. Breaking bonds costs energy, and forming new bonds releases energy. In H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, one H-H bond (436 kJ/mol) and one Cl-Cl bond (242 kJ/mol) must be broken. In return, two H-Cl bonds of 431 kJ/mol each are formed. Overall, then, about 184 kJ is released, and ΔH is minus 184 kJ/mol.

The chemist **Germain Henri Hess** was born in Geneva in 1802 and later worked in Saint Petersburg. In 1840 he discovered that the total heat of a reaction does not depend on the route taken, only on the starting and final states. This **Hess's law** makes it possible to calculate enthalpies that cannot be measured directly. Changes of state have enthalpies too: melting one mole of ice at 0 °C needs about 6 kJ.

Food packaging states the **energy content** in kilojoules, for example per 100 grams. In principle, these values are found by burning the food in a calorimeter. Heating systems, gas cookers and car engines also use the enthalpy of reaction of combustion. Engineers use it to calculate how much fuel a plant needs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of physics and chemistry that studies heat and energy conversions.
An instrument for measuring the heat of a reaction.
A unit of energy, abbreviated kJ; 1 kJ is 1000 joules.
A unit of amount in chemistry; one mole contains about 602 sextillion particles.
The total energy stored in the particles of a substance.

gewusst: The term enthalpy was proposed at the beginning of the 20th century by the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes.
Evaporating one mole of water takes almost seven times as much energy as melting one mole of ice.
Hess's law is named after a man born in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: A chemical element is a basic substance made of only one kind of atom. All the atoms of an element have the same number of protons in the nucleus. Everything in the world is made up of the elements, just as words are made of letters.
wichtigste: A chemical element consists of atoms with the same number of protons.
Today 118 elements are known.
Each element has a chemical symbol of one or two letters.
Gold has the symbol Au, iron Fe and lead Pb.
Na stands for sodium and K for potassium.
Many symbols come from Latin names.
The elements are arranged in the periodic table.

abschnitte.text: A **chemical element** is a substance made of atoms with the same **number of protons**. This number is called the atomic number: hydrogen has 1, oxygen 8 and gold 79. Elements cannot be broken down further by chemical means. When different elements combine, compounds are formed, such as water from hydrogen and oxygen.

In the early 19th century the Swede Jöns Jakob Berzelius introduced today's **chemical symbols**. Many come from Latin: Au from aurum for gold, Fe from ferrum for iron and Pb from plumbum for lead. Na stands for sodium, from natrium, and K for potassium, from kalium. Other symbols are simpler, such as O for oxygen or C for carbon.

In 1869 Dmitri **Mendeleev**, and independently Lothar Meyer, arranged the elements in a table according to their mass and properties. Mendeleev even left gaps for elements that were not yet known and predicted their properties. In today's **periodic table**, the elements are arranged by atomic number. Elements in the same column behave similarly.

Most elements are **metals**, for example iron, copper and aluminium. There are also non metals such as carbon, sulphur and oxygen. At room temperature only mercury and bromine are liquid, and eleven elements are gases. The noble gases such as helium and neon hardly form compounds.

The most common element in the universe is **hydrogen**, followed by helium. Heavier elements such as carbon and iron were made in stars. In the Earth's crust, oxygen is the most common element, followed by silicon. About 90 elements occur in nature; the rest were made artificially in the laboratory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of atoms with the same number of protons.
A table in which all the elements are arranged.
A short sign of one or two letters for an element.
A substance made of two or more different elements.
An element that hardly reacts with other substances, for example helium.

gewusst: The element einsteinium is named after Albert Einstein, who worked in Bern for some years.
The element helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun and only afterwards on Earth.
About two thirds of the mass of the human body is oxygen.

teile.einleitung: Bronze is a mixture of copper and tin, that is, an alloy. It was so important that a whole age of humanity is named after it, the Bronze Age. To this day, church bells, statues and medals are cast in bronze.
wichtigste: Bronze is not a pure metal but a mixture of metals, usually copper with some tin.
New bronze has a golden brown shine.
Bronze is harder than pure copper and was therefore better for tools.
The time when people made tools from bronze is called the Bronze Age.
In the Bronze Age, people lived in pile dwellings on the shores of Swiss lakes.
Many church bells, monuments and statues are cast in bronze.
In competitions, third place gets the bronze medal.

abschnitte.text: Bronze is an **alloy**, that is, a mixture of several metals. It usually consists mostly of copper and about one tenth **tin**. New bronze is golden brown; over time a green layer, the **patina**, forms in the air. This layer protects the metal underneath from further decay.

Pure copper is fairly soft, and a blade made of it soon goes blunt. If you add tin, the metal becomes much harder and can still be worked well. In addition, bronze melts at a lower temperature than copper. That is why it could easily be **cast**, that is, poured into a mould as a liquid.

In central Europe the **Bronze Age** lasted roughly from 2200 to 800 BC. People made axes, swords, sickles, pins and jewellery from bronze. Because copper and tin are rarely found in the same place, a lively trade over long distances grew up. The Bronze Age was followed by the Iron Age.

In the Bronze Age many people lived in villages on the shores of Swiss lakes, for example Lake Zurich, Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel. These **pile dwellings** stood on wooden posts. Archaeologists have found many bronze objects there, which were well preserved in the damp ground. Since 2011 the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Many **church bells** are cast from a bronze particularly rich in tin, because it sounds beautiful and long. Large outdoor monuments and statues are also often made of bronze, as it stands up to the weather for a long time. In sports competitions, third place gets a bronze medal. Bronze is also used for ships' propellers, bearings in machines and musical instruments such as cymbals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of two or more metals.
A shiny silvery, soft metal that is mixed with copper to make bronze.
A green protective layer that forms on bronze and copper over time.
Houses on wooden posts on lake shores from the Stone Age and Bronze Age.

gewusst: Bronze medals at the Olympic Games are made mostly of copper.
On Lake Zurich and other Swiss lakes, remains of pile dwelling villages still lie under water today.
Cymbals and gongs in the orchestra are often made of bronze, because they ring on for a long time.

teile.einleitung: An electrophile is a particle that has too few electrons and therefore attacks electron rich places in other molecules. The name means “electron loving”. Electrophiles play the main part in many reactions of organic chemistry, for example in making dyes and medicines.
wichtigste: An electrophile is an electron poor particle that attacks electron rich places.
Its opposite is the nucleophile, an electron rich particle.
In Lewis's acid base concept, an electrophile is a Lewis acid.
The nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) is a typical electrophile.
With alkenes, an electrophile attacks the electrons of the C=C double bond.
A carbocation is a strong electrophile, because its positive carbon atom has only six valence electrons.
Catalysts such as iron(III) bromide or aluminium chloride make particles into stronger electrophiles.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of “electron” and the Greek “philos” for friend. An **electrophile** is positively charged or at least has a spot that is short of electrons. It therefore looks for electrons that it can use in a new bond. Typical electrophiles are the hydrogen ion H⁺, the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ and **carbocations**. The terms electrophile and nucleophile were coined in the 1930s by the British chemist Christopher Ingold.

Every electrophile has a reaction partner with a surplus of electrons, the **nucleophile**. The nucleophile provides a pair of electrons, and the electrophile accepts it. This creates a new bond. According to Gilbert Lewis's acid base concept, the electrophile is a **Lewis acid** and the nucleophile a Lewis base. You can picture it like a plug and a socket that fit together.

**Alkenes** such as ethene have a C=C double bond with many electrons. That is exactly where an electrophile attacks; this is called **electrophilic addition**. A well known example is the reaction with bromine: brown bromine water loses its colour when it is added to an alkene. In this way the laboratory can show whether a substance contains double bonds.

Benzene has a particularly stable ring of six carbon atoms. Here an electrophile swaps a hydrogen atom; this is called **electrophilic aromatic substitution**. In **nitration**, the nitronium ion is produced from concentrated nitric acid and sulphuric acid. In bromination, iron(III) bromide polarises the bromine molecule and makes it a stronger electrophile. With aluminium chloride, an alkyl group can be attached to the ring in **Friedel Crafts alkylation**.

Many everyday substances are made by reactions of electrophiles. They include dyes, plastics, detergents and medicines. The chemical industry in Basel has been using such reactions for more than a hundred years, for example to make dyes and active ingredients. Anyone who understands where electrophiles attack can predict which product will be formed.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electron rich particle that attacks positive or electron poor places.
A particle that can accept a pair of electrons.
A positively charged particle with a carbon atom that is short of electrons.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
A reaction in which an atom or group of atoms is exchanged for another.

gewusst: The explosive TNT is made by triple nitration, that is, by reaction with an electrophile.
The Friedel Crafts reaction is named after the Frenchman Charles Friedel and the American James Crafts, who discovered it in 1877.
Even the simple hydrogen ion H⁺ of an acid is an electrophile.

teile.einleitung: Crude oil as it comes out of the ground is a dark, thick liquid with which no car could drive and no aeroplane could fly. Only in a refinery is it turned into useful products such as petrol, diesel, kerosene and heating oil. This processing is called oil refining.
wichtigste: Crude oil is a mixture of very many hydrocarbons, that is, substances made of carbon and hydrogen.
First the crude oil is separated into different fractions by fractional distillation.
This happens in a tall tower, the distillation column.
Low boiling fractions such as gases and petrol are drawn off right at the top, heavy fractions further down.
Bitumen, which is used for road surfaces, is left at the bottom as a thick residue.
In cracking, long molecules are split into shorter ones so that more petrol is produced.
Oil products are desulphurised so that less sulphur dioxide is produced when they are burnt.

abschnitte.text: Crude oil formed over millions of years from the remains of tiny sea creatures, which were transformed under pressure and heat. It consists mostly of **hydrocarbons**, that is, molecules made of carbon and hydrogen. These molecules vary in length: some have only a few carbon atoms, others dozens. Short molecules boil at a low temperature, long ones only at a high temperature. The refinery makes use of exactly this difference.

The crude oil is heated in a furnace to about 350 to 400 degrees Celsius, so that a large part of it evaporates. The vapours rise up the **distillation column**, a tower that is often several dozen metres high. It gets cooler and cooler towards the top, and each substance condenses at the height that matches its boiling temperature. In this way the individual **fractions** are collected on many trays in the tower and drawn off. This process is called fractional distillation.

Right at the top, gases such as propane and butane escape; they are used, for example, as bottled gas for barbecues. Below them come petrol and naphtha, then **kerosene**, the fuel for jet aircraft. Lower still, diesel and heating oil are drawn off. At the bottom a heavy residue is left, from which lubricating oils and finally **bitumen** are obtained in a second distillation at reduced pressure. Bitumen is the thick, black substance in the asphalt of roads.

Distillation alone usually produces too little petrol and too much heavy oil. That is why long hydrocarbon molecules are split into shorter ones with heat and catalysts; this is called **cracking**. In what is known as reforming, molecules are rearranged so that the petrol burns better and more evenly in the engine. Naphtha is also used to make raw materials for plastics, paints and medicines.

Crude oil contains sulphur compounds that would turn into poisonous **sulphur dioxide** when burnt. This gas causes acid rain and irritates the airways. That is why the sulphur is removed from the products in the refinery with hydrogen; this is called **desulphurisation**. The sulphur obtained is sold on, for example to make sulphuric acid. Refineries themselves need a lot of energy and must keep to strict rules against air and water pollution.

Today there is only one refinery left in Switzerland, at **Cressier** in the canton of Neuchâtel. The refinery at Collombey in Valais was shut down in 2015. The crude oil reaches Cressier through a pipeline from the Mediterranean. However, a large share of fuels and heating oil is imported into Switzerland from abroad already processed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of a mixture whose substances boil in a similar temperature range.
A separation method in which a mixture is heated and the vapours are collected and cooled again.
Splitting long hydrocarbon molecules into shorter ones, for example to get more petrol.
A black, thick residue from crude oil that is found in the asphalt of roads.
An oil fraction from which fuel for jet aircraft is made.

gewusst: A single litre of crude oil contains hundreds of different hydrocarbons.
Many plastic objects, from a Lego brick to a toothbrush, begin their life as crude oil in a refinery.
The pipeline to the Cressier refinery runs from the Mediterranean through France to the canton of Neuchâtel.

teile.einleitung: In chemistry, chirality means that a molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image. It is like our hands: the left and right hands are mirror images, but they cannot be laid exactly on top of each other. The word comes from the Greek word for hand.
wichtigste: A molecule is chiral if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image.
The term chirality comes from the Greek word for hand.
A typical stereocentre is a carbon atom with four different substituents.
Butan-2-ol is an example of a chiral molecule.
The configuration of a stereocentre is given as R or S according to the CIP rules.
Glycine is the only proteinogenic amino acid that is not chiral.
A molecule with 3 stereocentres can have at most 8 stereoisomers.
Meso compounds have stereocentres but are achiral because of an internal mirror plane.

abschnitte.text: If you hold your left hand up to a mirror, the reflection looks like a right hand. Yet you cannot lay the two hands on top of each other so that everything matches. In science this **handedness** is called **chirality**, after the Greek word “cheir” for hand. Screws, snail shells and spiral staircases can also be chiral.

In organic molecules, chirality usually arises at a **stereocentre**. This is often a carbon atom to which four different atoms or groups are attached. In butan-2-ol these are a hydrogen atom, an OH group, a methyl group and an ethyl group. The two mirror image forms of such a molecule are called **enantiomers**.

To tell enantiomers apart, the **CIP rules** are used, named after the chemists Cahn, Ingold and Prelog. The four groups on the stereocentre are given ranks. Depending on the direction of rotation, the centre gets the letter **R** or **S**. Vladimir Prelog worked at ETH Zurich and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1975.

A molecule with n stereocentres can have at most 2 to the power n stereoisomers, so with 3 centres, 8. Sometimes there are fewer: if a molecule has an internal **mirror plane**, it is not chiral despite having stereocentres. Such substances are called **meso compounds**; one example is meso tartaric acid. Using tartaric acid crystals, Louis Pasteur discovered in 1848 that mirror image molecules exist.

Living things are full of chiral molecules. Almost all the amino acids in our proteins occur in only one form, the **L form**; only glycine is not chiral. Our receptors in the nose and on the tongue can tell enantiomers apart. So one form of the substance **carvone** smells of mint and the other of caraway.

Because the body itself is chiral, the two enantiomers of a medicine can act quite differently. Often only one form helps, while the other is weaker or has side effects. That is why pharmaceutical firms check very carefully which form they are making. A mixture of equal amounts of both forms is called a **racemate**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two molecules that relate to each other like an object and its mirror image.
An atom, usually carbon, to which four different groups are attached.
A mixture of equal amounts of both mirror image forms.
The term for a molecule that can be superimposed on its mirror image.

gewusst: Caraway and spearmint owe their scent to two mirror image forms of the same molecule.
The Swiss chemist Vladimir Prelog received the Nobel Prize for his research on the three dimensional shape of molecules.
A glove is chiral too: the left one does not fit the right hand.

teile.einleitung: A Brønsted acid is a particle that can give a proton, that is a hydrogen ion H⁺, to another particle. This idea comes from the Danish chemist Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted. With it, acids and bases can be described much more generally than before.
wichtigste: A Brønsted acid is a proton donor; it gives off a proton.
A Brønsted base is a proton acceptor; it takes up a proton.
The theory was set up independently in 1923 by Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted from Denmark and Thomas Martin Lowry.
A reaction with a transfer of protons is called protolysis.
When an acid gives off its proton, its conjugate base is formed.
Water can act as an acid or as a base, depending on its partner.
In water, a proton exists, put simply, as an oxonium ion H₃O⁺.

abschnitte.text: According to Brønsted's theory, an acid is any particle that can give off a **proton**. A base is any particle that can take up a proton. So an acid can get rid of its proton only if a base accepts it. Acid and base are therefore always partners, as when passing a ball.

The Danish chemist **Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted** published the theory in 1923. In the same year the Englishman Thomas Martin Lowry independently put forward the same idea, which is why it is also called the Brønsted Lowry theory. Before that, the theory of Svante Arrhenius applied, according to which acids form H⁺ ions in water and bases OH⁻ ions. The new theory is more general and also works without water.

When an acid gives off a proton, the **conjugate base** is left. So sulphuric acid H₂SO₄ becomes the hydrogen sulphate ion HSO₄⁻. The other way round, the base ammonia NH₃ becomes the acid NH₄⁺, the ammonium ion, by taking up a proton. That is why there are two such pairs in every protolysis.

When hydrogen chloride HCl dissolves in water, it gives its proton to a water molecule. The water acts as a base, and the **oxonium ion** H₃O⁺ is formed, which makes the solution acidic. With ammonia, on the other hand, water acts as an acid and gives off a proton itself. Particles that can do both are called **ampholytes**; the hydrogen carbonate ion HCO₃⁻ is one of them too.

When the gases ammonia and hydrogen chloride meet, white smoke of solid ammonium chloride forms. According to Arrhenius this is not an acid base reaction, because no water is involved, but according to Brønsted it is. In the reaction HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₂O, the hydrogen carbonate acts as an acid. Such proton transfers are also important in the body, for example so that the blood does not become too acidic.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle, a hydrogen atom without its electron.
A reaction in which a proton jumps from one particle to another.
A particle that can act both as an acid and as a base.
H₃O⁺, a water molecule with an extra proton.

gewusst: A single proton is tens of thousands of times smaller than a whole atom and never exists on its own in water.
In the same year, 1923, the American Gilbert Lewis set up an even more general acid base theory that does without protons.
The letter ø in Brønsted is typical of the Danish language.

teile.einleitung: The halogens are a family of chemical elements that includes fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. Their name comes from Greek and means “salt formers”, because with metals they form salts such as our table salt. Halogens are very reactive and are therefore almost never found in nature as pure substances.
wichtigste: The halogens are in main group 7 of the periodic table.
The group includes fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, radioactive astatine and the artificially made tennessine.
Fluorine is the most reactive halogen; reactivity decreases going down the group.
At room temperature fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is liquid and iodine is solid.
Halogens occur as molecules of two atoms, for example Cl₂.
If you dissolve hydrogen chloride in water, you get hydrochloric acid.
In the swimming pool, chlorine kills germs.

abschnitte.titel: A family in the periodic table
abschnitte.text: The halogens form main group 7, which today is also called group 17. All halogen atoms have seven electrons in their outermost shell. So they are missing only a single electron to reach the stable **noble gas configuration**. That is why they readily grab an electron from other atoms and become negatively charged **halide ions**.

Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine a yellowish green gas with a sharp smell. **Bromine** is a dark reddish brown liquid that gives off poisonous fumes even at room temperature. **Iodine** forms shiny greyish black crystals that turn directly into a violet vapour when warmed. Astatine is radioactive and so rare that only tiny amounts of it exist on the whole Earth.

When a halogen reacts with a metal, a salt is formed. The best-known example is **sodium chloride**, that is our table salt made of sodium and chlorine. Large amounts of chloride, bromide and iodide are also dissolved in seawater. Hydrogen chloride dissolved in water gives **hydrochloric acid**, which by the way is also found in our stomach.

In the swimming pool, **chlorine** makes sure that bacteria and other germs are killed. Fluoride in toothpaste hardens tooth enamel and protects against tooth decay. Our body needs iodine for the thyroid gland, which is why iodine is added to table salt in Switzerland. Chlorine is also used to make plastics such as PVC.

Pure halogens are poisonous and attack skin, eyes and airways. **Fluorine** in particular is so aggressive that it can even attack glass. Chlorine gas is heavier than air and therefore collects near the ground. You must also never mix chlorine cleaners with other cleaning products, because poisonous gases can form.

In 1774 the Swede Carl Wilhelm Scheele was the first to make chlorine. Iodine was discovered in 1811 in the ash of seaweed, bromine in 1826 in salt water. Fluorine could only be produced in pure form in 1886, by the Frenchman **Henri Moissan**, who later received the Nobel Prize for it. Before that, many chemists had been injured in experiments with fluorine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical element from main group 7 that forms salts with metals.
A negatively charged ion of a halogen, for example chloride.
A solution of hydrogen chloride in water, a strong acid.
Changing directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid.

gewusst: Switzerland was one of the first countries in the world to introduce iodised table salt to prevent goitre.
Apart from mercury, bromine is the only element that is liquid at room temperature.
Fluorine is so reactive that it even reacts with some noble gases.

teile.einleitung: A gas is a substance that spreads out freely through the whole space, like the air around us. Most gases can be neither seen nor felt. Along with solid and liquid, gas is one of the three most important states of matter.
wichtigste: A gas spreads out everywhere in a room.
Air is a mixture of different gases.
Many gases are invisible, but you notice some of them by their smell.
Gases can easily be squeezed together.
Helium is lighter than air, which is why a helium balloon flies upwards.
The bubbles in sparkling mineral water are the gas carbon dioxide.
People breathe out much more carbon dioxide than they breathe in.

abschnitte.text: A **gas** has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume. It spreads out everywhere in any container and any room. If you open a bottle of perfume, you soon smell the scent in the whole room. That is why you often notice invisible gases only by their **smell**.

In a gas, the particles are far apart and fly about fast in all directions. They bump into the walls of the container, and this creates **gas pressure**. Because there is a lot of empty space between the particles, gases can easily be **squeezed together**. That is how a diving cylinder holds a great deal of air, and how you pump air into a tyre with a bicycle pump.

**Air** is a mixture of gases: about 78 per cent nitrogen, 21 per cent oxygen and just under one per cent argon. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04 per cent. We need the oxygen for breathing. Breathed out air contains about a hundred times more **carbon dioxide** than breathed in air.

**Helium** is much lighter than air, which is why a helium balloon rises. Lighter still is hydrogen, the lightest gas of all, but it is flammable. Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects at the bottom, for example in wine cellars. Hot air balloons fly because warm air is lighter than cold air; at the balloon week in Château-d'Oex, many of them go up every year.

The bubbles in sparkling mineral water are the gas carbon dioxide, which has been dissolved in the water under pressure. Many households cook or heat with **natural gas**, which consists mainly of methane. Because methane has no smell, a strong smelling substance is added to it so that a leak is noticed at once. If it smells of gas, you must let in fresh air at once, must not use a light switch and must leave the house.

If you cool a gas strongly, it becomes liquid. Water vapour turns into water below 100 degrees, but air only at about minus 190 degrees. Liquid nitrogen is used for cooling in laboratories and hospitals. The other way round, liquids evaporate into gases when they are heated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that spreads out freely in a space and has no fixed shape.
The pressure produced when gas particles bump against walls.
A gas that we breathe out and that fizzes in sparkling mineral water.
A very light, non flammable noble gas used for balloons.
A flammable gas from the Earth that consists mainly of methane.

gewusst: If you breathe in a little helium, your voice sounds high and squeaky for a short while.
In 1999 Bertrand Piccard, together with Brian Jones, was the first to fly a balloon non stop around the Earth.
The word gas was invented in the 17th century by Johan Baptista van Helmont and comes from the word chaos.

teile.einleitung: In a chemical reaction, substances turn into new substances with different properties. This happens all the time around us, when cooking, when things rust or in our body. The atoms are kept; they are only rearranged.
wichtigste: In a chemical reaction, new substances are formed.
The starting substances are called reactants, and the new substances products.
The atoms are only joined in new ways; none is lost.
In a closed container, the total mass stays the same.
A reaction that releases heat is called exothermic.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up in the process.
Baking bread is a chemical reaction.

abschnitte.text: In a **chemical reaction**, bonds between atoms are broken and new ones are made. The starting substances are called **reactants**, and the substances formed **products**. In a reaction equation there is an arrow between them. One example is the burning of carbon: carbon and oxygen react to form carbon dioxide.

The sure sign is that a **new substance** is formed. Clues are a change of colour, gas bubbles, a new smell, light or heat. When ice melts, on the other hand, that is not a chemical reaction, because it is still water. But when bread is baked, new substances are formed, for example the brown, fragrant crust.

In the 18th century the Frenchman Antoine Laurent de **Lavoisier** showed by precise weighing that in reactions in a closed container the total mass stays the same. This is called the **law of conservation of mass**. When wood burns, it seems to get lighter, but the gases simply escape into the air. If you catch them, the mass adds up again.

If a reaction releases heat, it is called **exothermic**, for example burning or a hand warmer. If it constantly needs heat, it is called **endothermic**, as in baking. Many reactions first need a push, the activation energy. That is why you have to strike a match before it burns.

A **catalyst** makes a reaction faster and is still there unchanged afterwards. In a car, a catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. In our body, enzymes act as catalysts, for example in digestion. Without them, many life processes would run far too slowly.

Chemical reactions are everywhere: iron rusts, milk goes sour, an apple turns brown in the air. In photosynthesis, plants build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Our body burns food to obtain energy. A firework is also a chain of reactions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A starting substance in a chemical reaction.
A substance newly formed in a chemical reaction.
A reaction in which heat is released.
A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up.
The energy needed to start a reaction.

gewusst: The bright colours of a firework come from different metal salts, for example strontium for red.
The Maillard reaction between sugar and protein plays an important part in the browning of bread crust and Rösti.
Your body carries out millions of chemical reactions every second.

teile.einleitung: Amphoterism means that a substance can behave like an acid or like a base, depending on its partner. The word comes from Greek and means “both” or “on both sides”. The best known example of such an all rounder is perfectly ordinary water.
wichtigste: An amphoteric substance can react with acids and with bases.
A particle that can react as an acid and as a base is called an ampholyte.
Water is an ampholyte: towards ammonia it acts as an acid.
The ion H₂PO₄⁻ is also an ampholyte.
In neutral solution, amino acids exist mainly as zwitterions.
Aluminium hydroxide dissolves both in hydrochloric acid and in excess sodium hydroxide solution.
In excess sodium hydroxide solution, zinc hydroxide forms the ion [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻.

abschnitte.text: According to the acid base theory of **Brønsted**, an acid gives off protons and a base takes protons up. Some particles can do both; they are called **ampholytes**. Whether an ampholyte acts as an acid or as a base depends on its reaction partner. If it meets a stronger acid, it behaves as a base; if it meets a stronger base, it becomes an acid.

Water is the most important ampholyte. With hydrogen chloride it takes up a proton and becomes the **oxonium ion** H₃O⁺, so it acts as a base. With ammonia, on the other hand, it gives off a proton: NH₃ + H₂O gives NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, and here water acts as an **acid**. Water molecules even exchange protons among themselves; this is called autoprotolysis.

Many ions that still carry a hydrogen atom that can be split off are ampholytes. One example is **dihydrogen phosphate** H₂PO₄⁻: it can give off a proton or take one up. The **hydrogen carbonate ion** HCO₃⁻ from baking soda is also an ampholyte. Such ions help to keep the pH of the blood stable.

Amino acids have an acidic carboxyl group and a basic amino group. In neutral solution, the acid group passes its proton to the amino group. This creates a **zwitterion** with a positive and a negative charge in the same molecule. At a particular pH the amino acid is electrically neutral from the outside; this is its **isoelectric point**.

Some metal hydroxides are amphoteric too, for example **aluminium hydroxide** and **zinc hydroxide**. They dissolve in hydrochloric acid because they react as a base. They also dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide solution, forming complex ions such as [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻. This property is used in the laboratory to separate metals from one another.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that can give off or take up a proton.
A positively charged hydrogen ion H⁺.
A molecule with a positive and a negative charge at the same time.
The pH at which a particle has no charge from the outside.

gewusst: Water can be an acid and a base at the same time, which is why even the purest water contains a few ions.
This is also why aluminium in the kitchen is a problem with very acidic and very alkaline foods.
Without amphoteric particles in the blood, even an acidic drink would throw our body off balance.

teile.einleitung: A candle is a piece of wax with a wick in the middle that gives light and warmth when it burns. In the past it was one of the most important sources of light; today it is mainly used to create atmosphere. An amazing number of chemical processes take place in the small flame.
wichtigste: A candle is usually made of wax.
The wick is usually made of cotton.
Close to the flame, the wax becomes liquid.
In fact it is not the liquid wax that burns, but its vapour.
Bees supply wax for candles.
A candle is put on a firm candle holder and never next to a curtain.
Before leaving the room, you put out the candle.

abschnitte.text: A candle consists of a fuel, usually **wax**, and a **wick** of braided cotton. Today most candles are made of **paraffin wax**, which is obtained from crude oil. Others are made of stearin, which comes from plant or animal fats. Candles made of beeswax smell particularly nice.

The flame melts the wax right around the wick, so a small pool of liquid wax forms. The liquid wax rises up the wick, much like water in a paper towel; this is called **capillary action**. At the top, the heat turns the wax into **wax vapour**. This vapour combines with the oxygen in the air and burns, producing light, heat, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

abschnitte.titel: A close look at the flame
abschnitte.text: A candle flame has different zones. At the bottom by the wick it is bluish; there the gas burns with plenty of oxygen. The bright yellow part glows because tiny **soot particles** are glowing. The flame is hottest in the outer edge, where you can hardly see it.

The Romans already made candles from beeswax and from **tallow**, that is animal fat. Tallow candles smelt unpleasant and were sooty; beeswax was expensive and mainly for churches and rich people. In the 19th century stearin and paraffin candles came along, which were cheaper. The English scientist Michael Faraday gave famous lectures for children about the candle.

Candles burn on birthday cakes, on the Advent wreath and on the Christmas tree. In many religions, candles are lit during services and in remembrance. In Switzerland, **candle dipping** is popular during Advent: you dip a wick into liquid wax again and again. With every layer the candle gets a little thicker.

A candle is always placed on a firm **candle holder** that cannot burn. Curtains, paper and fir branches must be far enough away, because they can catch fire. Before you leave the room or go to sleep, you put out every candle. Children only light candles together with adults.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thread in the middle of the candle on which the flame burns.
A wax made from crude oil.
Liquid rising by itself in fine fibres or tubes.
Solid animal fat from which candles used to be made.

gewusst: If you blow out a candle and immediately hold a match to the smoke, the flame jumps back onto the wick.
A candle flame in weightlessness is not pointed but round and bluish.
In the past, people also measured time with marked candles, called candle clocks.

teile.einleitung: Chlorine is a chemical element with the symbol Cl, which at room temperature is a yellowish green, very poisonous gas. But we meet it every day in compounds, for example in table salt. In the swimming pool, chlorine compounds make sure the water stays free of germs.
wichtigste: Chlorine is a gas at room temperature.
Pure chlorine is yellowish green and very poisonous.
Table salt contains chlorine together with sodium.
Chlorine is added to swimming pool water because it kills germs.
An indoor pool smells particularly strongly of “chlorine” when there is a lot of sweat in the water.
Swimming goggles protect your eyes from chlorinated water.
Chlorinated water can bleach the colours of bright swimming costumes.

abschnitte.text: Chlorine has the **atomic number 17** and belongs to the **halogens**, together with fluorine, bromine and iodine. At room temperature it is a **yellowish green gas**, heavier than air and with a pungent smell. It reacts very violently with many other substances. That is why chlorine never occurs pure in nature, only in compounds.

The Swedish pharmacist **Carl Wilhelm Scheele** first made chlorine in 1774. But he did not yet think it was an element. Only the Englishman **Humphry Davy** realised in 1810 that it is an element in its own right. He named it after the Greek word “chloros” for yellowish green.

The most common chlorine compound is **table salt**, sodium chloride NaCl. In it, chlorine is bound as a **chloride ion** and is completely harmless. The sea contains huge amounts of it, and in Switzerland salt is obtained at saltworks on the Rhine and in Bex in Vaud. Our **gastric juice** also contains hydrochloric acid, a compound of hydrogen and chlorine.

In the swimming pool, chlorine kills **bacteria** and other germs so that diseases are not passed on. Usually chlorine compounds are added to the water, not pure chlorine gas. The typical indoor pool smell does not come from chlorine itself but from **chloramines**. They form when chlorine reacts with sweat and other substances from swimmers, which is why you should shower before swimming.

Chlorine is an important basic material in chemistry. It is used, for example, to make the plastic **PVC**, from which pipes, window frames and floor coverings are made. Many medicines and cleaning products are also produced with the help of chlorine. Bleach containing chlorine makes colours fade, which is why bright swimming costumes can be bleached in chlorinated water.

Pure chlorine gas is **very poisonous** and attacks the eyes and lungs even in small amounts. In the First World War it was used as a poison gas in 1915, which is banned internationally today. Care is needed at home: if you mix cleaners containing chlorine with acidic cleaners, **chlorine gas** can form. That is why you should never pour different cleaning products together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of very reactive elements to which chlorine belongs.
The negatively charged chlorine ion, as found in table salt.
Substances formed from chlorine and sweat that cause the indoor pool smell.
Killing germs that cause disease.

gewusst: If an indoor pool smells strongly of “chlorine”, there is probably too little clean chlorine in the water and too much dirt from swimmers.
A poisonous gas and a poisonous metal, chlorine and sodium, together make harmless table salt.
The name chlorine simply means yellowish green in Greek.

teile.einleitung: A fire extinguisher is a container, usually red, that can be used to put out small fires quickly. A gas under pressure pushes out the extinguishing agent, for example water, foam, powder or carbon dioxide. Fire extinguishers hang clearly visible on the wall in schools, shops and many blocks of flats.
wichtigste: A fire extinguisher is there to put out small fires.
Fire extinguishers are usually red.
A gas under pressure pushes out the extinguishing agent.
Before use, you have to pull out the safety pin.
You aim the jet at the bottom of the burning object, not at the flames at the top.
A small fire extinguisher sprays for only a few seconds.
In case of fire, children should fetch adults at once and alert the fire brigade on 118.

abschnitte.text: A fire extinguisher is a portable container with an **extinguishing agent**. It is usually red so that you can find it quickly in an emergency. In school buildings it hangs clearly visible on the wall, often near stairs or exits. It is meant only for small fires, such as a burning wastepaper basket.

Inside the fire extinguisher there is a gas under **pressure**, for example nitrogen or carbon dioxide. If you pull out the **safety pin** and press the lever, the gas forces the extinguishing agent through the hose. A small extinguisher is empty after just a few seconds. That is why you have to aim well and give short bursts.

A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat; if one of them is missing, it goes out. Water cools the fire, and a **foam extinguisher** covers it with foam and keeps the oxygen away. Powder extinguishers stop the burning chemically, and carbon dioxide pushes the oxygen away. For burning cooking fat there are special fat fire extinguishers, and burning oil must never be put out with water.

Every fire extinguisher has letters on it, the **fire classes**. A stands for solid materials such as wood and paper, B for flammable liquids such as petrol and C for gases. D refers to burning metals and F to burning cooking oils and fats. That way you know which fire the extinguisher is suitable for.

In case of fire, the rule is: first raise the alarm, then rescue, then put the fire out. In Switzerland you can reach the fire brigade on the number **118**. A fire extinguisher should be used by an adult, who aims the jet from below at the burning object. Children get themselves to safety, close the door if possible and fetch help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance used to put out a fire, such as water, foam or powder.
A small pin that stops the extinguisher from spraying by accident.
A group of fires sorted by the material that is burning.
A fire of hot oil or fat, for example in a pan.

gewusst: If you pour water onto burning oil, it evaporates explosively and throws up a huge flash of flame.
Fire extinguishers have to be checked regularly by experts so that they work in an emergency.
A carbon dioxide extinguisher gets so cold when it sprays that white snow forms on the horn.

teile.einleitung: Fine particulate matter consists of tiny particles that float in the air and are so small that you cannot see them with the naked eye. We breathe them in with every breath, and the smaller they are, the deeper they get into the lungs. That is why fine particulate matter is measured closely and limited in Switzerland.
wichtigste: PM10 refers to particles smaller than 10 micrometres.
Very fine particulate matter is particularly harmful, because it gets deep into the lungs.
Fine particulate matter comes from traffic, wood burning, industry and agriculture.
Electric cars also produce fine particulate matter through the wear of tyres and brakes.
During a temperature inversion in winter, a lot of fine particulate matter builds up in the Central Plateau.
The NABEL network monitors air quality in Switzerland.
In Switzerland, the annual average limit for PM10 is 20 micrograms per cubic metre (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: Fine particulate matter is a mixture of solid and liquid particles in the air, for example soot, dust, salts and worn off material. It is divided up by size: **PM10** are particles smaller than 10 micrometres, PM2.5 smaller than 2.5 micrometres. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. A hair is about 50 to 70 micrometres thick, so PM10 particles are much thinner. The abbreviation PM stands for the English particulate matter.

Fine particulate matter is produced when diesel, petrol, wood and waste are burnt. In road traffic, a large part comes not from the exhaust but from the **wear** of tyres, brakes and road surface; this applies to electric cars too. In winter in Switzerland, **wood burning** such as open fireplaces and old wood stoves contributes a great deal to the pollution. Some of it only forms in the air from gases such as ammonia from agriculture. Natural sources are Saharan dust, pollen and volcanic eruptions.

Coarse particles usually get stuck in the nose and throat. Very fine particles reach the air sacs of the lungs, and the finest even get into the blood. Fine particulate matter can make coughing, asthma and bronchitis worse and increase the risk of heart and circulatory diseases. Children, older people and people with lung diseases are particularly sensitive.

Normally the air gets colder higher up, and warm, polluted air rises. During a **temperature inversion**, however, a layer of warm air lies above cold air, like a lid. This often happens in winter in the Central Plateau, when there is high fog for days on end. The fine particulate matter cannot escape and builds up. At the same time, the air in the mountains is clear and sunny.

**NABEL**, the National Air Pollution Monitoring Network, is run by the Federal Office for the Environment and Empa. It takes measurements at stations in towns, in the countryside and in the mountains. The Ordinance on Air Pollution Control sets an annual average of 20 micrograms per cubic metre for PM10 and a daily average of 50 micrograms. For PM2.5 the annual average is 10 micrograms per cubic metre (as of 2025).

Thanks to **particle filters** on diesel engines, cleaner heating and stricter rules, fine particulate pollution in Switzerland has fallen considerably since the 1990s. Wood should only be burnt dry and untreated, and waste never belongs in the stove. People who travel by bike, on foot or by public transport cause less fine particulate matter. The fireworks on 1 August and on New Year's Eve also make the levels rise sharply for a few hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: Particles of fine particulate matter smaller than 10 micrometres.
A thousandth of a millimetre.
A weather situation in which warm air lies like a lid over cold air.
A filter in the exhaust that holds back the soot from diesel exhaust gases.
The federal measuring network that monitors air quality in Switzerland.

gewusst: Saharan dust can be blown over the Alps into Switzerland and sometimes turns the snow orange.
The finest particles in fine particulate matter are smaller than many viruses.
On New Year's Eve and 1 August, some stations measure many times the usual levels of fine particulate matter within hours.

teile.einleitung: A flame is the glowing, hot area in which a substance burns. It gives off light and heat and always points upwards. For a flame to burn, it needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat.
wichtigste: A flame gives off light and heat.
A flame needs fuel, oxygen from the air and heat.
These three things are shown by the fire triangle.
A candle flame points upwards and is blue at the bottom.
Blowing hard usually puts out a candle flame.
A small glowing bit that jumps out of the fire is called a spark.
A large fire that gets out of control is called a blaze.

abschnitte.text: A flame needs three things: a **fuel** such as wood or wax, the gas **oxygen** from the air and enough heat. They are drawn as the **fire triangle**. If one side is missing, the flame goes out. That is why a flame under a glass is smothered when the oxygen has been used up.

With a candle, the wax melts, rises up the wick and evaporates. It is the wax vapour that burns, not the solid wax. Right at the bottom the flame is blue; there the gas burns with plenty of oxygen. The bright, yellow part glows because tiny **soot particles** are glowing in it, hotter than 1000 °C.

The hot gases of the flame are lighter than the cool air around them. That is why they rise and stretch the flame out, while fresh air flows in from below. This movement of air is called **convection**. In the weightlessness of a space station there is no buoyancy, and there a candle flame is almost round and bluish.

The colour of a flame tells you quite a lot about what is burning in it. A blue flame gets plenty of oxygen, a yellow one contains glowing soot. Some substances colour flames brightly: sodium yellow, copper green and strontium red. This **flame colouring** is used for fireworks.

People have been using fire for hundreds of thousands of years for warmth, cooking and protection. A **campfire** is a fire in the open air; in Switzerland, bonfires burn on hills in many places on 1 August. However, a spark can set dry grass alight and start a blaze. That is why you never leave a fire unattended and put it out completely at the end.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture of the three things a fire needs: fuel, oxygen, heat.
The thread in a candle that draws liquid wax up to the flame.
A small glowing particle that jumps out of a fire.
Black particles of unburnt carbon.

gewusst: If you hold a burning match in the rising smoke above a candle that has just been blown out, the flame jumps back onto the wick.
The hottest part of a candle flame is not the bright yellow part but the almost invisible outer edge.
Sunlight is not a flame either, because nothing burns on the Sun; instead, atomic nuclei fuse together.

teile.einleitung: A fuel cell produces electricity from a chemical reaction, usually between hydrogen and oxygen. The only exhaust is water. Fuel cells power lorries, buses and cars today and supplied electricity even on the way to the Moon.
wichtigste: A fuel cell turns chemical energy directly into electrical energy.
The principle was discovered in 1838 by the chemist Christian Friedrich Schönbein, who taught in Basel.
In a hydrogen oxygen fuel cell, the product is water.
At the anode hydrogen is oxidised, and at the cathode oxygen reacts.
The theoretical voltage of a cell is 1.23 volts at 25 °C.
Unlike in a battery, the reacting substances are supplied continuously.
On the Apollo Moon missions, alkaline fuel cells supplied electricity and drinking water.

abschnitte.text: A fuel cell has two electrodes, the **anode** and the **cathode**, separated by an electrolyte. At the anode, hydrogen gives up electrons; it is oxidised. The electrons flow through an outside wire to the cathode, driving a motor, for example, on the way. At the cathode they combine with oxygen and the hydrogen ions to form water.

A battery contains its substances from the start and at some point runs flat.
