A fuel cell, on the other hand, is supplied with hydrogen and oxygen continuously, so it supplies electricity as long as there is fuel. A single cell has a theoretical 1.23 volts, slightly less in practice. That is why many cells are connected into a **stack**.

The most common is the **PEM fuel cell**, in which protons travel through a thin plastic membrane. It works at about 80 °C and needs the precious metal platinum as a catalyst. The solid oxide fuel cell, SOFC for short, has a ceramic electrolyte and runs at over 600 °C. The alkaline fuel cell supplied the Apollo spacecraft with electricity and the astronauts with drinking water.

The German chemist **Christian Friedrich Schönbein** taught at the University of Basel and discovered the principle of the fuel cell in 1838. At almost the same time, the Englishman William Grove built a first working cell. For a long time the invention remained a curiosity, because steam engines and generators were cheaper. Only space travel in the 1960s made it well known.

Fuel cells power hydrogen cars, buses, trains and lorries that give off only water vapour. In Switzerland, hydrogen lorries have been running for retailers and logistics firms since 2020. But this is environmentally friendly only if the **hydrogen** is made with renewable electricity. Disadvantages are the expensive platinum and the difficult storage of the hydrogen.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrode at which electrons are given up.
The electrode at which electrons are taken up.
A substance through which charged particles can travel, but not electrons.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.

gewusst: The astronauts of the Apollo missions drank the water that their fuel cells produced as waste.
A fuel cell works entirely without a flame, even though the same reaction takes place as when hydrogen burns.
In Basel, Christian Friedrich Schönbein also discovered ozone and guncotton.

teile.einleitung: The Bunsen burner is a gas burner used in chemistry lessons to heat substances. With an air hole on the tube, its flame can be adjusted from yellow and luminous to blue and very hot. It is named after the German chemist Robert Wilhelm Bunsen.
wichtigste: The Bunsen burner is named after the chemist Robert Wilhelm Bunsen.
In the school laboratory it usually burns natural gas.
With the air hole closed, a yellow, luminous flame burns.
With the air hole open, the hot, blue roaring flame forms.
The roaring flame is hottest just above the tip of the inner cone.
When lighting it, the air hole is closed.
A similar burner with a turning disc at the base is called a Teclu burner.

abschnitte.text: A Bunsen burner consists of a heavy base, a gas connection and an upright **burner tube**. At the bottom of the tube there are openings through which air flows in, and a turning collar can open or close them. In the tube the gas mixes with the air, and the mixture burns at the top. In the school laboratory **natural gas** is usually used, sometimes propane from a cartridge.

When the air hole is closed, a yellow, calm **luminous flame** burns. It glows because tiny glowing soot particles are in it, and it leaves soot on cold objects. If you open the air hole, the blue, loudly hissing **roaring flame** forms. It is much hotter; at its hottest point, just above the inner blue cone, it reaches about 1500 °C.

**Robert Wilhelm Bunsen** was a German chemist who taught in Heidelberg. Around 1855, with the instrument maker Peter Desaga, he developed the burner that bears his name today. Bunsen needed an almost colourless flame for his experiments. With the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff he discovered spectral analysis in this way, and two new elements, caesium and rubidium.

If you hold certain salts in the blue flame, it glows in typical colours. Table salt colours it yellow to orange because of the sodium, copper compounds colour it green, potassium violet and strontium red. With these **flame tests** substances can be identified. The same substances also give fireworks their bright colours.

Before lighting, you close the air hole so that the flame does not strike back into the tube. Then you hold the burning match or lighter to the opening and open the gas tap. You wear safety glasses, tie back long hair and never leave the burner unattended. A similar device is the **Teclu burner**, in which the air supply can be controlled precisely with a turning disc at the base.

begriffe.erklaerung: A yellow flame with the air hole closed, in which glowing soot particles shine.
A hot, blue flame with the air hole open.
The typical colour that a substance gives to a flame.
A flammable gas from the ground, consisting mainly of methane.

gewusst: Bunsen lost the sight of one eye in an explosion in the laboratory.
The names caesium and rubidium come from Latin words for sky blue and dark red, after the lines in their spectrum.
In daylight the flame of a Bunsen burner is so pale that it is easy to overlook.

teile.einleitung: Enantiomers are molecules that behave like the left and the right hand: they are mirror images of each other but cannot be laid exactly on top of each other. Although they consist of exactly the same atoms, they can smell different or work quite differently in the body. This property is called chirality or handedness.
wichtigste: Enantiomers are stereoisomers that relate to each other as image and mirror image.
Physically they differ in the direction in which they rotate linearly polarised light.
This rotation is measured with a polarimeter.
A mixture of equal parts of both enantiomers is called a racemate.
In 1848 Louis Pasteur was the first to separate enantiomers, by sorting crystals by hand.
With carvone, one enantiomer smells of caraway and the other of mint.
The amino acids in the proteins of living things almost always have the L configuration.

abschnitte.text: Hold your hands side by side: they look the same, but you cannot lay them on top of each other so that they match exactly. **Enantiomers** behave in just this way. Molecules with this property are called **chiral**, from the Greek word for hand. Usually the reason is a carbon atom with four different partners, a so called **stereocentre**.

Enantiomers have the same melting point, boiling point and density. They can be told apart with **linearly polarised light**, that is, light that vibrates in only one plane. One enantiomer turns this plane to the right, the other turns it just as much to the left. This is measured with a **polarimeter**. A **racemate** of equal parts of both forms does not rotate the light at all, because the effects cancel each other out.

In 1848 the French chemist **Louis Pasteur** studied crystals of a salt of tartaric acid. Under the microscope he noticed that there were two kinds, which were mirror images of each other. He patiently sorted them by hand with tweezers. Solutions of the two kinds rotated polarised light in opposite directions. Later Pasteur became famous above all for his research on bacteria and vaccines.

Our nose and tongue work with receptors that are themselves chiral, like a glove for a particular hand. That is why enantiomers can have quite different effects. With **carvone**, one form smells of caraway, the other of peppermint. This also matters for medicines: with the painkiller ibuprofen, it is mainly one of the two forms that works.

Nature usually prefers only one form. The amino acids in the **proteins** of living things almost always have the **L configuration**, whereas natural glucose has the D configuration. Why this is so has still not been fully explained. Chemists have developed methods for making just one form on purpose. Nobel Prizes in Chemistry were awarded for this in 2001 and 2021.

Enantiomers belong to the **stereoisomers**, that is, molecules with the same atoms and the same connections but a different arrangement in space. Stereoisomers that do not relate to each other as image and mirror image are called **diastereomers**. Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers have different melting and boiling points. That is why they are much easier to separate.

begriffe.erklaerung: Not able to match its own mirror image exactly, like a hand.
A mixture of equal amounts of both enantiomers.
An instrument that measures how much a solution rotates polarised light.
Molecules with the same atoms and connections but a different arrangement in space.
Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other.

gewusst: The word enantiomer comes from the Greek “enantios”, which means “opposite”.
Snail shells have a handedness too; most Roman snails coil to the right.
Many fragrances and flavourings in food occur in two mirror image forms that smell different.

teile.einleitung: Aromatic compounds are ring shaped molecules with a particularly stable electron system. The best known example is benzene with its six membered ring of carbon atoms. They got their name because many of the first known examples had a strong smell.
wichtigste: Aromatic compounds are flat rings with 4n + 2 π electrons; this is Hückel's rule.
The most important aromatic compound is benzene with the formula C₆H₆.
Typical of aromatic compounds is electrophilic substitution, not addition.
Methylbenzene has the common name toluene, and dimethylbenzene (xylene) has 3 isomers.
Naphthalene, made of two benzene rings, used to be used in mothballs.
Styrene is the building block of polystyrene, and pyridine is an aromatic ring containing nitrogen.
Benzo[a]pyrene in tobacco smoke and charred barbecue food is strongly carcinogenic.

abschnitte.text: Aromatic compounds are **ring shaped**, flat molecules whose electrons are spread evenly over the whole ring. This electron system makes them particularly stable. The most important one is **benzene** with the formula C₆H₆, a ring of six carbon atoms. Whether a ring is aromatic is checked with **Hückel's rule**: it must be flat and contain 4n + 2 π electrons, for example 6.

Benzene was discovered by Michael Faraday in 1825, but its structure was a puzzle for a long time. In 1865 **August Kekulé** proposed a six membered ring with alternating single and double bonds. He later said that the idea came to him in a dream of a snake biting its own tail. Today we know that the electrons are spread evenly; this is called **resonance**.

Although benzene seems to have double bonds, it does not react with bromine water like an alkene. Instead of addition, **electrophilic substitution** takes place: a hydrogen atom on the ring is exchanged for another group. In this way the stable ring is kept. This usually needs a **catalyst**, such as iron bromide.

**Toluene** is methylbenzene and is used as a solvent, for example in paints. Dimethylbenzene, **xylene**, has three isomers, depending on where the methyl groups sit on the ring. **Naphthalene** consists of two joined benzene rings and used to be used in mothballs. Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by the ring, and pyridine is an aromatic six membered ring containing nitrogen.

Many substances are made from aromatic compounds: plastics, dyes, medicines and detergents. **Styrene**, with its vinyl group, is the building block of polystyrene, from which yoghurt pots and expanded polystyrene foam are made. Aspirin and the vanilla flavour vanillin also contain an aromatic ring. Aromatic compounds are even found in our body, for example in the amino acids phenylalanine and tryptophan.

Some aromatic compounds are poisonous or **carcinogenic**. Benzene itself is so dangerous that its share in petrol is strictly limited. Large ring systems made of many benzene rings are called polycyclic aromatic compounds. One of them, **benzo[a]pyrene**, is found in tobacco smoke and charred barbecue food, which is why you should not eat burnt food.

begriffe.erklaerung: The simplest aromatic compound, a ring of six carbon atoms.
A flat ring with 4n + 2 π electrons is aromatic.
A reaction in which one atom is exchanged for another.
Molecules with the same formula but a different structure.

gewusst: Not all aromatic compounds smell, and many substances that smell are not aromatic compounds at all.
The graphite in pencil leads consists of huge layers of joined six membered rings.
Kekulé's dream of the snake is one of the best known anecdotes in the history of chemistry.

teile.einleitung: Fluorides are chemical compounds of the element fluorine. They are best known from toothpaste, where they protect teeth from tooth decay. They also occur in small amounts in water, tea and rock.
wichtigste: The word fluoride comes from the element fluorine.
Pure fluorine is a gas at room temperature.
Fluoride in toothpaste hardens the tooth enamel.
Small children need only a pea sized amount of toothpaste.
After brushing your teeth, you spit out the foam.
In Switzerland there is table salt with fluoride.
Black tea naturally contains quite a lot of fluoride.

abschnitte.text: **Fluorine** is a chemical element with the symbol F. As a pure substance it is a pale yellow, poisonous gas that reacts extremely violently with almost everything. That is why fluorine never occurs pure in nature, only bound to other elements. When fluorine combines with metals, salts are formed that are called **fluorides**.

A well known fluoride is the mineral **fluorite**, also called fluorspar, which consists of calcium and fluorine. It forms beautiful crystals, often purple or green, which are also found in the Swiss Alps. Fluoride gets from rock into groundwater in small amounts. Tea plants take up fluoride from the soil, which is why **black tea** contains quite a lot of it.

**Tooth enamel** is the hardest substance in the human body. Acids from bacteria that feed on sugar can slowly dissolve it, and this is how **tooth decay** develops. Fluoride becomes built into the tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to acid. It also helps to repair small damage that is just starting.

Toothpaste for children and for adults contains different amounts of fluoride. Small children need only a **pea sized** amount of toothpaste. After brushing, you spit out the foam and do not swallow it. Brushing thoroughly twice a day protects teeth best.

In Switzerland you can buy **fluoridated table salt**, which contains added fluoride. This gives the teeth a little protection when you eat too. The city of Basel used to add fluoride to its drinking water, but stopped in 2003. Swiss school dental care has helped to ensure that children today have much less tooth decay than in the past.

As with many substances, it is the **dose** that matters. In small amounts, fluoride protects the teeth. If a child takes in too much of it over a long time, white spots can appear on the permanent teeth. That is why you should not eat toothpaste and should use fluoride products as stated on the packet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very reactive, poisonous gas and chemical element.
The hard outer layer of the teeth.
Holes in the teeth caused by acid from bacteria.
A mineral made of calcium and fluorine, also called fluorspar.

gewusst: The word fluorescence, the glowing of certain substances, comes from the mineral fluorite.
Fluorine is the most reactive of all chemical elements.
Fluorite used to be used in melting metals because it makes the melt flow more easily, hence the name fluorspar.

teile.einleitung: Wood is the solid material that the trunks, branches and roots of trees and shrubs are made of. It is one of humanity’s oldest materials and grows back again and again. We build houses and furniture with it, use it for heating and even make paper from it.
wichtigste: Wood is obtained from trees.
It consists mainly of cellulose and lignin.
You can read the age of a tree from the annual rings in its trunk.
Dry wood usually floats in water.
Wood conducts heat poorly, which is why a wooden spoon in a pan does not get hot.
The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.
Wood that stays wet for a long time rots.

abschnitte.text: Wood is built up from countless tiny **cells** that look like long little tubes. Their walls consist mainly of **cellulose**, which gives wood its tensile strength. **Lignin** glues the cells together and makes the wood hard and able to withstand pressure. Air is trapped in the hollow spaces, which is why wood is light and usually floats.

In spring a tree grows quickly and forms light, loose wood. In summer the wood becomes darker and denser. In this way a new **annual ring** forms every year, which you can see in a cross-section of the trunk. If you count the rings, you know the age of the tree, and wide rings show good growing years.

When wood burns, it reacts with the oxygen in the air, producing heat, light, water vapour and **carbon dioxide**. A little ash with minerals is left behind. While growing, the tree took in exactly as much carbon dioxide from the air. That is why wood is regarded as a renewable fuel that harms the climate less than oil.

Wood can be sawn, planed, carved and bent. The **joiner** makes furniture and windows from it, the carpenter whole roof structures and wooden houses. Wood conducts heat and electricity poorly and therefore insulates well. Damp wood, however, is attacked by fungi and rots if it is not protected.

About a third of Switzerland is covered with forest. The most common tree is the **spruce**, followed by the beech. The larch is a special conifer that turns golden in autumn and loses its needles. Famous wooden buildings are the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne and the old wooden houses in Valais and the Emmental.

Working with wood produces a lot of **sawdust**, on which Swiss wrestlers fight, for example. Wood chips are pressed into chipboard. Paper and cardboard are made from the wood fibres. Even bark and leftover wood are still used as fuel in wood-fired heating systems.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance that plant cell walls are made of; it gives wood its tensile strength.
A wood substance that glues the cells together and makes the wood hard.
A ring in the cross-section of a trunk that shows one year’s growth.
A raw material that is formed again and again in nature.

gewusst: There are woods so dense that they sink in water, for example ebony.
The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is regarded as one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
A large part of wood consists of carbon that the tree has taken from the air.

teile.einleitung: Fatty acids are the building blocks of fats. They are long chains of carbon atoms with an acid group at the end. Whether a fatty acid is saturated or unsaturated decides whether a fat is solid or liquid and how it benefits our health.
wichtigste: Fatty acids are carboxylic acids with a long carbon chain.
Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds; unsaturated ones have one or more.
The saturated palmitic acid has 16 carbon atoms; oleic acid has one double bond.
In omega-3 fatty acids, the first double bond is at the third carbon atom counting from the end of the chain.
Linoleic acid is essential for humans; the body cannot make it itself.
In Switzerland, since 2008 cooking oils and fats may contain at most 2 grams of trans fatty acids per 100 grams of fat.
In the mitochondria, fatty acids are broken down by beta oxidation.

abschnitte.text: A fatty acid consists of a chain of carbon atoms to which hydrogen atoms are attached, and a **carboxyl group** -COOH at the end. Most natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, often between 12 and 22. Important examples are **palmitic acid** with 16 and stearic acid with 18 carbon atoms. In fats, three fatty acids at a time are bound to one glycerol molecule.

A **saturated** fatty acid contains no double bond between carbon atoms; it is, so to speak, full of hydrogen. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds. Oleic acid from olive oil has one, linoleic acid two. In natural fats, these double bonds are mostly in the cis form, which bends the chain. Bent chains cannot be packed so tightly, which is why oils with many unsaturated fatty acids are liquid at room temperature.

The name **omega-3** means that the first double bond is at the third carbon atom counting from the end of the chain. Omega stands for the last letter of the Greek alphabet, that is, the end. Omega-3 fatty acids are found in oily sea fish such as salmon, but also in linseed oil, rapeseed oil and walnuts. Linoleic acid is an omega-6 fatty acid. It and the omega-3 fatty acid alpha linolenic acid are **essential**: we have to take them in with our food.

When vegetable oils are partly hardened industrially, **trans fatty acids** can be formed, in which the double bond has a stretched out shape. They are found mainly in some fried foods, baked goods and snacks. Trans fatty acids increase the risk of heart and circulatory diseases. Switzerland was one of the first countries to limit them: since 2008, at most 2 grams per 100 grams of fat have been allowed.

When the body needs energy, it takes fatty acids from the fatty tissue and transports them into the blood. In the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cells, the chains are shortened step by step, two carbon atoms at a time. This breakdown route is called **beta oxidation**. A lot of energy is released, which the cell can use. Especially during long endurance activities such as hiking or cross country skiing, the muscles burn many fatty acids.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fatty acid without double bonds between the carbon atoms.
A fatty acid with at least one double bond in the chain.
Vital and only available from food, because the body does not make it itself.
An unsaturated fatty acid with a stretched out double bond, formed mainly when oils are hardened.
Tiny parts in the cells that provide energy.

gewusst: Soap consists of the sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids.
Butyric acid is a short fatty acid with only four carbon atoms and smells unpleasantly of rancid butter.
Palmitic acid is named after the oil palm, in whose oil it is plentiful.

teile.einleitung: Aluminium foil, or kitchen foil, is aluminium rolled out extremely thin. In the kitchen it keeps food fresh, in the oven it protects the roast, and in packaging it protects chocolate and medicines. By the way, the first factory for aluminium foil was in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Aluminium foil is made of very thinly rolled aluminium.
Household foil is thinner than a sheet of paper.
You can use both sides of aluminium foil.
Aluminium foil does not belong in the microwave, because there can be sparks.
You should not wrap acidic or salty food in aluminium foil, because they dissolve aluminium.
The first aluminium foil factory opened in Switzerland in 1910.
In Switzerland, clean used aluminium foil goes into the aluminium collection.

abschnitte.text: Aluminium foil is aluminium that has been pressed between rollers until it is only hundredths of a millimetre thick. Household foil is usually about 0.01 to 0.02 millimetres thick, thinner than a sheet of paper. Even so, it lets through neither light nor air, water or smells; it is a very good **barrier layer**. You can press it into any shape without tools, and it keeps that shape.

It starts as thick aluminium bars, which are rolled thinner and thinner, first hot and then cold. In the last pass two foils are rolled at the same time on top of each other, because a single foil that thin would tear. The side that touches the smooth **rollers** becomes shiny, and the side where the two foils lay against each other stays matt. That is why it does not matter which side you use; both work the same.

In 1910 the firm Dr. Lauber, Neher & Cie. opened the first factory for aluminium foil in Emmishofen near **Kreuzlingen** in Thurgau. Robert Victor Neher had developed a process for rolling aluminium continuously into thin foil. Soon foods such as chocolate were being wrapped in aluminium foil. Before that, foil made of tin was used, called “Stanniol”, a word that older people in German speaking Switzerland sometimes still use for aluminium foil.

Aluminium foil stops food drying out and is used for grilling and baking. But you should not store acidic foods such as tomatoes, lemons or pickled gherkins, or very salty foods, in it, because they **dissolve the aluminium**, which then gets into the food. Aluminium foil must not go in the **microwave**, because the microwaves create currents in the metal and sparks can result. For grilled food there are also aluminium trays.

Making new aluminium takes a great deal of electricity. That is why it makes sense to use aluminium foil several times and to collect it clean. In Switzerland you can take clean aluminium foil, cans and aluminium trays to the municipal **aluminium collection points**. Recycling saves most of the energy that would be needed for new aluminium.

begriffe.erklaerung: Pressing something thinner between rotating steel cylinders.
An earlier foil made of tin; the word is still often used in German for aluminium foil.
A layer that does not let light, air or moisture through.
Reusing used materials.

gewusst: One kilogram of aluminium is enough for aluminium foil covering many dozens of square metres.
The matt and shiny sides of aluminium foil come only from rolling two foils at the same time.
You can shape works of art with aluminium foil, because it takes on any shape you give it.

teile.einleitung: Atoms are the tiny building blocks from which all substances are made. Air, water, stones and your body too are built from atoms. An atom consists of a nucleus and a shell of electrons.
wichtigste: Atoms are the basic building blocks of all substances.
An atom consists of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Protons are positively charged, electrons negatively, and neutrons are neutral.
Protons and neutrons form the atomic nucleus; the electrons are in the electron shell.
The atomic number tells you how many protons are in the nucleus.
An atom that has given up or taken in electrons is called an ion.
The word atom comes from the Greek atomos, which means indivisible.

abschnitte.text: Atoms are unimaginably small; an atom measures about a ten millionth of a millimetre. A drop of water contains more atoms than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth. You cannot see atoms with ordinary microscopes. Only with the **scanning tunnelling microscope**, invented in 1981 at IBM in Rüschlikon near Zurich, could individual atoms be imaged.

At the centre lies the **atomic nucleus**, made of protons and neutrons. It is tiny but contains almost the whole mass of the atom. Around the nucleus is the **electron shell** with the electrons. If an atom were as big as a football stadium, the nucleus would be only as big as a pea in the middle.

**Protons** are positively charged, **electrons** negatively, and neutrons have no charge. An ordinary atom has as many protons as electrons and is therefore neutral from the outside. If an atom gives up or takes in electrons, it becomes a charged **ion**. Table salt, for example, contains sodium ions and chloride ions.

The **atomic number** gives the number of protons in the nucleus. It decides which chemical element it is. Hydrogen has one proton, carbon six and gold 79. Today 118 elements are known, arranged in the periodic table.

As early as about 400 BC, the Greek philosopher **Democritus** suspected that everything is made of indivisible particles. He called them atomos, that is, indivisible. Around 1808 John Dalton developed a scientific atomic theory. Later it was discovered that atoms are in fact made of even smaller particles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A very light, negatively charged particle in the electron shell.
An atom with an electric charge because it has given up or taken in electrons.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it determines the element.

gewusst: An atom consists almost entirely of empty space.
The atoms in your body are much older than the Earth; many of them were made in stars.
The scanning tunnelling microscope was invented in Switzerland by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986.

teile.einleitung: The noble gases are a group of six naturally occurring chemical elements: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon. They are on the far right of the periodic table and hardly react with other substances. Even so, we come across them in everyday life, for example in balloons, neon signs and car headlights.
wichtigste: Noble gases are in group 18, the last column of the periodic table.
They hardly react, because their outermost electron shell is full.
Helium has 2 valence electrons, and the other noble gases have 8.
Helium has the lowest boiling point of all the elements.
Argon is the most common noble gas in the air.
Xenon is used for very bright car headlights and flash lamps.
Radon is radioactive and can get into cellars from the ground.

abschnitte.text: Like noble metals such as gold, noble gases hardly form compounds with other substances. The reason is their full outermost **electron shell**. For helium this means 2 **valence electrons**, for the other noble gases 8. This stable arrangement is called the **noble gas configuration**. In chemical reactions, other atoms often try to reach exactly this state.

Helium was first discovered in 1868 in the light of the **Sun**, hence its name from the Greek “helios”. In 1894 **Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay** found argon in the air. Shortly afterwards, in 1898, Ramsay and Morris Travers also discovered neon, krypton and xenon. The names come from Greek: neon means “new”, krypton “hidden” and xenon “stranger”. Ramsay received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904.

After hydrogen, **helium** is the lightest gas and fills balloons and airships without burning. It boils only at about minus 269 °C, just a few degrees above absolute zero. That is why liquid helium cools the strong magnets in hospital MRI scanners. **Neon** glows reddish orange in glass tubes when electricity flows through them and became famous through neon signs.

The air contains just under 1 per cent **argon**, more than all the other noble gases together. In welding, argon protects the hot metal from oxygen, and it fills light bulbs and double glazed windows. **Krypton** is also used in lamps and insulating windows. **Xenon** gives very bright, white light in car headlights, flash lamps and cinema projectors.

**Radon** is radioactive and forms in the ground when uranium in rock decays. It can get into cellars and living rooms through cracks. Anyone who breathes in a lot of radon over a long time has a higher risk of lung cancer. The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) monitors radon levels and gives advice on protection. Levels can be raised especially in parts of the Alps and the Jura; regular airing helps.

For a long time people believed that noble gases could not form any compounds at all. In 1962 the chemist **Neil Bartlett** succeeded for the first time in making a xenon compound. Today several compounds of xenon and krypton are known, mostly with fluorine or oxygen. Hardly any stable compounds of helium, neon and argon are known to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom; they decide its chemical behaviour.
A completely full outer electron shell, a particularly stable state.
A substance whose atomic nuclei decay and give off radiation as they do so.
The temperature at which a substance changes from liquid to gas.

gewusst: If you breathe in helium, your voice sounds high because sound travels faster in helium, but this is not without danger.
Helium is the only element that does not become solid at normal pressure, even at absolute zero.
Many “neon tubes” contain no neon at all, but other gases that glow in other colours.

teile.einleitung: Isotopes are different kinds of atoms of the same chemical element. They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus. That is why they differ in weight but react almost the same way chemically.
wichtigste: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The word isotope comes from Greek and means “same place”.
Chemically, isotopes of an element hardly react differently.
Deuterium is hydrogen with one neutron; tritium has two neutrons.
Carbon-12 is the most common carbon isotope.
Carbon-14 is used to find out the age of finds.
Isotopes that decay and give off radiation are called radioactive isotopes.
In nuclear power stations, uranium-235 is split.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has an **atomic nucleus** made of protons and neutrons. The number of **protons** decides which element it is: hydrogen has one, carbon six, uranium 92. The number of **neutrons**, however, can vary. Atoms with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons are called isotopes. They are written with the mass number, for example carbon-12 with six neutrons and carbon-14 with eight neutrons.

The name comes from Greek: isos means “same” and topos means **“place”**. This is because isotopes are in the same place in the periodic table. The term was introduced by the British chemist Frederick Soddy in 1913. Studying radioactive substances, he had noticed that there are atoms that are chemically the same but differ in weight. Today several thousand different isotopes are known; most of them are unstable.

Hydrogen has three natural isotopes: normal hydrogen without a neutron, **deuterium** with one and **tritium** with two neutrons. Water containing deuterium is called heavy water and is about ten per cent heavier than normal water. Tritium is radioactive and is used, for example, in glowing watch hands. In nature, carbon consists of about 99 per cent carbon-12. A tiny part is radioactive carbon-14.

Some isotopes are unstable and decay over time, giving off **radiation**. They are called radioactive isotopes. The time it takes for half of the atoms to decay is called the **half-life**. For carbon-14 it is about 5730 years. Uranium-235 makes up only about 0.7 per cent of natural uranium and is split in nuclear power stations, as it used to be at Mühleberg and still is at Gösgen and Leibstadt.

The **radiocarbon method** is used to find the age of wood, bones or fabrics up to about 50,000 years old. It was developed around 1949 by the American Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize for it. In medicine, radioactive isotopes help to detect and treat diseases, for example iodine-131 for thyroid diseases. With stable isotopes, scientists can find out where a food comes from or what the climate was like long ago. The glacier mummy Ötzi was also dated with the radiocarbon method.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The sum of protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus.
The time after which half of the radioactive atoms have decayed.
The decay of unstable atomic nuclei, which produces radiation.

gewusst: Heavy water looks just like normal water, but an ice cube made from it sinks in normal water.
Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element.
The age of the glacier mummy Ötzi, over 5000 years, was determined with carbon-14.

teile.einleitung: Methylated spirit, in Switzerland often called “Brennsprit”, is alcohol for burning and cleaning. It consists mainly of ethanol but has been made undrinkable on purpose. Many people know it from the fondue burner, but great care is needed when handling it.
wichtigste: The main component of methylated spirit is ethanol, with the formula C2H5OH.
Methylated spirit is denatured so that nobody uses it as drinking alcohol.
To denature it, the extremely bitter denatonium benzoate is often mixed in.
Methylated spirit feels cold on the skin, because it evaporates quickly and takes heat from the skin.
In Switzerland, methylated spirit is often used at home as fuel for the fondue burner.
The flame of burning spirit is almost invisible in daylight.
You must never pour spirit into a burning or hot burner, otherwise a flash of flame shoots out.

abschnitte.text: Methylated spirit is a clear, colourless liquid that consists mostly of **ethanol**. Ethanol has the formula C2H5OH and is the same alcohol found in wine or beer. It boils at only about 78 °C and therefore evaporates quickly. Burning it produces mainly water vapour and **carbon dioxide**, which is why spirit burns almost without soot.

Drinking alcohol is heavily taxed in many countries. So that nobody drinks cheap methylated spirit, it is **denatured**. Substances are mixed into it that make it undrinkable, for example **denatonium benzoate**. This substance is one of the most bitter known; even tiny amounts make a liquid disgustingly bitter.

In Switzerland, methylated spirit is known above all from the **fondue burner**, on which the cheese is kept warm. It is also used to clean windows and glass, because it dissolves grease and dries without streaks. Camping stoves and small spirit stoves also run on it. Many burners today use **fuel paste**, which does not spill so easily.

If you drip spirit onto your skin, it immediately feels cool. The alcohol **evaporates** very quickly and needs heat to do so. It takes this heat from the skin; this is called **evaporative cooling**. But after evaporating, the skin is left dry, because alcohol also removes fat from it.

Methylated spirit is highly flammable, and its **vapours** catch fire very quickly. The flame is almost **invisible** in daylight, so sometimes you do not notice that something is still burning. If you pour spirit into a burning or hot burner, the vapours ignite and a dangerous **flash of flame** shoots out. So always wait until the burner has cooled down, and children should never refill it with spirit themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: An alcohol with the formula C2H5OH that burns easily and evaporates quickly.
Making an alcohol undrinkable on purpose.
The cooling that happens when a liquid evaporates and takes in heat as it does so.
A small warmer used, for example, to keep fondue warm; in Switzerland it is called a “Rechaud”.

gewusst: Denatonium benzoate is also painted onto some toys and cables so that children and pets do not chew them.
Because spirit burns almost without soot, the bottom of the fondue pot stays clean.
In the dark, a spirit flame can be seen as a faint bluish glow.

teile.einleitung: Aluminium is a silvery grey, very light metal found in drinks cans, aircraft, bicycles and window frames. It is the most common metal in the Earth's crust, but it never occurs pure. It is obtained from the rock bauxite using a lot of electricity.
wichtigste: Aluminium is a particularly light metal.
It has the chemical symbol Al and the atomic number 13.
It is obtained from the rock bauxite.
Aluminium does not rust like iron, because it forms a protective oxide layer.
Many drinks cans, aircraft parts and light bicycle frames are made of aluminium.
Recycling it saves a great deal of energy.
Switzerland was an important country for aluminium production early on.

abschnitte.text: Aluminium is a **light metal** with a density of about 2.7 grams per cubic centimetre, only about a third as heavy as steel. It is silvery grey, shiny and conducts electricity and heat very well. It melts at about 660 °C and can easily be rolled, cast and bent. If it is mixed with other metals to form **alloys**, it becomes much stronger.

In air, a very thin layer of **aluminium oxide** forms on aluminium at once. This layer is dense and protects the metal underneath from further damage. That is why aluminium does not rust like iron, which forms crumbly, reddish brown layers of rust. With the process of anodising, the protective layer can be strengthened artificially and even coloured.

In nature, aluminium occurs only in compounds, even though it makes up about 8 % of the Earth's crust. The most important raw material is **bauxite**, a reddish rock mined mainly in Australia, Guinea, China and Brazil. From it, aluminium oxide is first obtained, which is then broken down into aluminium by **molten salt electrolysis** using a great deal of electric current. This process was invented independently by Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult in 1886.

Because it is light and strong, a large part of many **aircraft** is made of aluminium alloys. Bicycle frames, car parts, trains, ladders and window frames are also built from it. In the kitchen you know drinks cans, kitchen foil, pans and coffee capsules. Because it conducts well, it is also used for high voltage power lines.

Aluminium can be melted down any number of times without losing quality. **Recycling** needs only about 5 % of the energy needed to make new aluminium from bauxite. In Switzerland, you can take cans, kitchen foil and other aluminium packaging to collection points. A very high proportion of aluminium drinks cans are collected and recycled here.

Pure aluminium was first made by Hans Christian Ørsted in 1825 and by Friedrich Wöhler in 1827. At first it was as expensive as gold, and the French Emperor Napoleon III is said to have used aluminium cutlery for special guests. In 1888 one of the first industrial aluminium productions in Europe began in **Neuhausen am Rheinfall**, powered by the water of the Rhine. Later, works in Valais, such as in Chippis, were added.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal with a low density that is lighter than iron.
A reddish rock from which aluminium is obtained.
Breaking down a substance with electric current.
A mixture of several metals.
A thin protective layer that forms on the metal in air.

gewusst: In 1884 the top of the Washington Monument in the USA was crowned with a small pyramid of aluminium, then a very precious metal.
After oxygen and silicon, aluminium is the third most common element in the Earth's crust.
Rubies and sapphires consist mostly of aluminium oxide.

teile.einleitung: An ion is an atom or a group of atoms that is electrically charged. This happens when an atom gives up or takes up electrons. Ions are found in table salt, in seawater and even in our nerves.
wichtigste: Ions are electrically charged atoms or groups of atoms.
Positively charged ions are called cations, negatively charged ones anions.
Metals usually form cations, for example Na⁺ or Al³⁺.
There are also ions made of several atoms, such as sulphate SO₄²⁻ or ammonium NH₄⁺.
Table salt consists of sodium ions and chloride ions.
Molten salt conducts electricity because the ions can then move freely.
Ionisation energy is the energy needed to tear an electron away from an atom.

abschnitte.text: A normal atom has as many positive **protons** as negative electrons and is therefore neutral. If it gives up an electron, it becomes positively charged and is called a **cation**. If it takes up an electron, it becomes negatively charged and is called an **anion**. The energy needed to tear an electron away from an atom in the gas state is called **ionisation energy**.

Atoms like to form ions that have the same number of electrons as a noble gas, because this is particularly stable. Sodium gives up one electron and becomes Na⁺, which has as many electrons as **neon**. The two are said to be **isoelectronic**. Chlorine takes up one electron and becomes the chloride ion Cl⁻ with the electron number of argon.

Cations and anions attract each other strongly and form a regular **ionic lattice**. This is how a salt such as table salt, that is sodium chloride NaCl, is formed. An aluminium ion typically carries the charge 3+, a calcium ion the charge 2+. That is why the **empirical formula** of calcium chloride is CaCl₂, because two chloride ions balance one calcium ion.

Some ions consist of several firmly joined atoms; they are called **polyatomic ions**. The sulphate ion SO₄²⁻, for example, is found in gypsum. The ammonium ion NH₄⁺ is found in many fertilisers. The carbonate ion CO₃²⁻ is also important, because together with calcium it forms the limestone of the Alps.

Solid table salt does not conduct electricity, because the ions are fixed in the lattice. In **molten salt** or in salt water, the ions can move freely and carry charge. That is why tap water with dissolved salts is dangerous near electricity. Our body also needs ions: sodium and potassium make sure that signals travel along the **nerves**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged ion; it has given up electrons.
A negatively charged ion; it has taken up electrons.
The regular arrangement of ions in a salt crystal.
The energy needed to take an electron away from an atom.
Having the same number of electrons as another particle.

gewusst: The word ion comes from Greek and means “going” or “wandering”, because ions move in an electric current.
The name was introduced in 1834 by the English scientist Michael Faraday.
Sports drinks contain ions because you lose salts when you sweat.

teile.einleitung: Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom in a chemical bond pulls the shared electrons towards itself. You can picture it as a tug of war over electrons. From it you can tell whether a bond is non polar, polar or ionic.
wichtigste: Electronegativity describes how strongly an atom attracts electrons in a bond.
Linus Pauling introduced the term in 1932 with a numerical scale.
Fluorine has the highest value, about 4.0, followed by oxygen.
Hydrogen has a value of about 2.2 on the Pauling scale.
Across a period, electronegativity increases from left to right.
Down a main group, it decreases from top to bottom.
Caesium is one of the elements with the lowest electronegativity.

abschnitte.text: In a **covalent bond**, two atoms share a pair of electrons. If both atoms are the same, as in the hydrogen molecule H₂, they pull equally hard, and the electrons lie exactly in the middle. The **electronegativity difference** is then 0. If the atoms are different, the stronger one pulls the electrons closer to itself. This creates a **polar bond** with a slightly negative and a slightly positive end.

In 1932 the American chemist **Linus Pauling** proposed a numerical scale. Fluorine, the most electronegative element, was given a value of about 4.0. Oxygen follows with about 3.4, and nitrogen and chlorine are at about 3.0. Hydrogen has roughly 2.2, carbon about 2.5. Alkali metals such as **caesium** have very low values below 1.

Within a **period**, electronegativity increases from left to right. The reason: the atomic nucleus has more protons and attracts the electrons more strongly. Within a **main group**, it decreases from top to bottom, because the atoms get bigger and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus. That is why fluorine is at the top right and caesium at the bottom left. Usually no value is given for the noble gases.

From the difference in electronegativities you can estimate the kind of bond. If it is very small, the bond is non polar, as between carbon and hydrogen. With medium differences, for example between oxygen and hydrogen in water, it is **polar**. If the difference is very large, about more than 1.7, one atom pulls the electrons completely to itself, and an **ionic bond** forms, as in table salt.

Linus Pauling lived from 1901 to 1994 and is considered one of the most important chemists of the 20th century. He studied how chemical bonds work and received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for it in 1954. In 1962 he also received the Nobel Peace Prize for his campaign against nuclear weapons tests. He is still the only person to have received two Nobel Prizes, each entirely on his own.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly an atom attracts the electrons in a bond.
A bond in which the electrons lie closer to one of the two atoms.
A bond between positively and negatively charged particles, the ions.
A horizontal row in the periodic table.

gewusst: Electronegativity has no unit; it is simply a number for comparison.
As well as the Pauling scale there are other scales, for example that of Allred and Rochow.
Because oxygen is so electronegative, water is a dipole and has many special properties.

teile.einleitung: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in all living things. Without them, most processes in the body, such as digestion, would happen far too slowly. That is why they are also called biocatalysts.
wichtigste: Enzymes are biocatalysts that usually consist of proteins.
An enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
The names of most enzymes end in “-ase”.
In 1894 Emil Fischer compared enzyme and substrate to a lock and key.
According to the induced fit model, the active site adapts its shape when it binds the substrate.
At too high temperatures an enzyme denatures and loses its three dimensional structure.
In 1897 Eduard Buchner showed that cell free yeast juice can ferment sugar.

abschnitte.text: An **enzyme** is a large molecule, usually a **protein**, that speeds up a chemical reaction. In doing so it is not used up itself and can work again and again. Enzymes work by lowering the **activation energy**, that is, the push a reaction needs. Some enzymes manage thousands of reactions per second. The substance an enzyme converts is called the **substrate**.

Every enzyme has a place where the substrate is bound, the **active site**. In 1894 the chemist **Emil Fischer** compared enzyme and substrate to a lock and key. Only the right substrate fits in, which is why every enzyme is very specific. Later Daniel Koshland developed the **induced fit model**: the active site is flexible and adapts its shape when it binds the substrate, like a glove to a hand.

Thousands of different enzymes work in our bodies. In saliva, **amylase** breaks starch down into sugar, which is why bread tastes slightly sweet after you have chewed it for a while. In the stomach, pepsin splits proteins, and in the intestine lipases break down fats. Most enzyme names end in “-ase”, for example lactase, which splits milk sugar. People who lack lactase do not tolerate milk well.

Every enzyme has an **optimum temperature** at which it works fastest; for many human enzymes this is about 37 °C. If it gets much hotter, the enzyme **denatures**: it loses its three dimensional shape and no longer works, rather like egg white when an egg is cooked. Enzymes can also be inhibited. In **competitive inhibition**, a similar substance occupies the active site, and more substrate can overcome this inhibition. The Michaelis constant gives the substrate concentration at which an enzyme works half as fast as the maximum possible.

For a long time people believed that fermentation was only possible in living yeast cells. In 1897 **Eduard Buchner** showed that cell free juice pressed from yeast can also ferment sugar. This proved that certain substances, and not life itself, cause the reaction. Buchner received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1907. The word enzyme comes from Greek and means roughly “in sourdough”.

Enzymes are used in many ways. To make **cheese** such as Emmental or Gruyère, you need rennet, which contains an enzyme that makes the milk curdle. Detergents contain enzymes that remove stains of protein, fat or starch even at low temperatures. Enzymes also play an important part in baking, brewing beer and in medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
The substance an enzyme converts.
The place on the enzyme where the substrate binds.
When a protein loses its shape and function through heat or acid.
A large molecule made of amino acids.

gewusst: Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme that splits protein, which is why a gelatine dessert with fresh pineapple does not set.
The enzyme catalase in potatoes makes hydrogen peroxide foam up strongly.
There are thousands of different enzymes in the human body, each with its own job.

teile.einleitung: Isomerism means that different substances are made of exactly the same atoms, but these are arranged differently. Such substances are called isomers; they have the same molecular formula but often completely different properties. You can compare it to Lego bricks: you can build different figures from the same bricks.
wichtigste: Isomers always have the same molecular formula.
For the formula C4H10 there are two isomers, n-butane and 2-methylpropane.
There are three structural isomers for C5H12 and five for C6H14.
Ethanol and dimethyl ether are isomers with the formula C2H6O.
Stereoisomers differ only in the arrangement of the atoms in space.
Because a C=C double bond cannot rotate freely, but-2-ene has a cis and a trans isomer.
In the E/Z naming system, Z stands for “zusammen” (together).

abschnitte.text: A **molecular formula** such as C4H10 only says how many atoms of which kind are in a molecule. But it does not reveal how the atoms are joined together. That is why there can be several different molecules for one molecular formula. These **isomers** often have different boiling points, smells or effects.

In **structural isomers** the atoms are joined in a different order. Butane can form a straight chain, which is n-butane, or a branched chain, which is 2-methylpropane. The more carbon atoms a molecule has, the more isomers there are: for C5H12 there are three, for C6H14 already five. A particularly clear example is ethanol, an alcohol, and dimethyl ether, a gas, which are both C2H6O.

Parts of a molecule can rotate freely around a single bond, but not around a **double bond**. That is why two identical groups can lie on the same side of the double bond, which is the **cis form**, or on opposite sides, which is the trans form. In but-2-ene there are thus two different substances. In the newer E/Z naming system, Z stands for the German “zusammen” (together) and E for “entgegen” (opposite).

Some molecules behave like our left and right hands: they are mirror images but cannot be laid exactly on top of each other. Such molecules are called **chiral**, and the two forms are called **enantiomers**. Our nose can sometimes tell them apart. The substance carvone smells of mint in one form and of caraway in the other.

At the beginning of the 19th century chemists believed that the same composition also meant the same substance. Then Friedrich Wöhler and Justus von Liebig found two substances with the same composition but different properties. In 1830 the Swede Jöns Jakob Berzelius gave this phenomenon the name **isomerism**. In 1848 Louis Pasteur separated mirror-image crystals from each other under the microscope for the first time.

In our body many substances fit like a key in a lock, and only the right isomer fits. That is why with medicines one form can heal while the other has no effect. Glucose and fructose are also isomers with the formula C6H12O6, but they taste differently sweet. Chemists must therefore know exactly which **isomer** they are making.

begriffe.erklaerung: Different substances with the same molecular formula but a different structure.
A formula that shows how many atoms of each kind a molecule contains.
Isomers whose atoms are joined in a different order.
Isomers with the same connections but a different arrangement in space.
Handed, that is mirror images like a left and right hand that cannot be laid exactly on top of each other.

gewusst: For the molecular formula C20H42 there are over 300,000 different structural isomers.
The two mirror-image forms of carvone smell of spearmint chewing gum in one case and of caraway in the other.
Glucose and fructose are made of exactly the same atoms.

teile.einleitung: A liquid is a substance that can flow, like water, milk or honey. Liquids have no shape of their own but take on the shape of their container. Along with solid and gas, liquid is one of the three most important states of matter.
wichtigste: A liquid is a substance that can flow.
Water, milk, juice and cooking oil are liquids.
A liquid takes on the shape of its container, for example the shape of the bottle.
You can pour liquids.
In a still glass, water has a flat surface.
Honey flows much more slowly than water; it is thick and sticky.
If you spill water on the table, it spreads out.

abschnitte.text: A **liquid** has a fixed volume but no fixed shape. If you pour a litre of milk from a bottle into a jug, it is still a litre, but the milk takes on the shape of the jug. That is why you can **pour** liquids and stir them with a spoon. If you spill water on the table, it spreads out until it forms a thin puddle.

The particles of a liquid lie close together but can slide past each other. They are like marbles in a bowl that are constantly moving. Because the particles lie so close together, a liquid can hardly be **squeezed together**. That is why brakes in cars and diggers work with liquids; this is called hydraulics.

Liquids flow at different speeds. Water is runny, whereas **honey** is thick and flows very slowly. Experts call this thickness **viscosity**. If honey is warmed, it flows faster; in the fridge, on the other hand, it becomes even thicker.

In a still glass, the surface of the water is flat and level, because gravity pulls all the particles downwards. At the surface, the particles hold together especially strongly; this is called **surface tension**. That is why round drops form and pond skaters can walk across a pond. Oil and water do not mix; the lighter cooking oil floats on top.

If you cool a liquid, at some point it becomes solid: water freezes into ice at 0 degrees. If you heat it, it evaporates and becomes a gas: at sea level water boils at 100 degrees. The metal **mercury** is liquid at room temperature, which is very rare for metals. Lava is molten rock that can be over 1000 degrees hot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that flows and takes on the shape of its container.
A measure of how thick a liquid is.
A force that holds the surface of a liquid together like a skin.
How much space a substance takes up, for example in litres.
Technology that uses liquids to transmit forces.

gewusst: Water is heaviest at 4 degrees, which is why the water at the bottom of a lake is about 4 degrees in winter.
Glass does not flow, even though old church windows are sometimes thicker at the bottom; this comes from the way they used to be made.
More than half of a human being is water.

teile.einleitung: An exothermic reaction is a chemical reaction in which energy is released, usually as heat. A campfire, a candle or a hand warmer are examples of it. The opposite is an endothermic reaction, which takes in heat from its surroundings.
wichtigste: An exothermic reaction gives off heat to its surroundings.
The prefix “exo” comes from Greek and means outside or out.
Burning wood is a typical exothermic reaction.
In the energy diagram, the products lie lower than the starting substances.
The enthalpy of reaction of an exothermic reaction has a negative sign.
Iron rusting is exothermic too, which is what disposable hand warmers make use of.
Many exothermic reactions still need a little energy to start, the activation energy.

abschnitte.text: In every chemical reaction, bonds between atoms are broken and new ones are formed. If the new bonds are stronger than the old ones, energy is released overall. Such a reaction is called **exothermic**, from the Greek exo for outside and thermos for warm. The energy usually goes to the surroundings as heat, sometimes also as light or sound.

In an **energy diagram**, you plot the energy of the substances before and after the reaction. In an exothermic reaction, the products lie lower than the starting substances, and the difference is given off. The **enthalpy of reaction** is therefore negative, since the substances have lost energy. Often, though, you first have to get over a small hill, the **activation energy**, as when you strike a match.

Burning is the best known kind of exothermic reaction. A candle flame feels hot because burning the wax releases energy. Disposable hand warmers contain iron powder, which rusts quickly in the air and gets warm as it does so. If you mix dilute hydrochloric acid with dilute caustic soda solution, the solution gets noticeably warmer; this is a **neutralisation**.

In the **thermite reaction**, aluminium powder reacts with iron oxide. This produces aluminium oxide and liquid iron, and the temperature rises to well over 2000 °C. This heat is used to weld railway rails together right on the track. The liquid iron runs into a mould between two rail ends and joins them firmly.

Reactions that take in heat from their surroundings are called **endothermic**. One example is cold packs, which go cold when you bend them. Energy is also taken in when baking with baking powder and during photosynthesis in plants. Exothermic reactions, on the other hand, supply us with heat, electricity from power stations and energy for the body.

begriffe.erklaerung: Gives off heat or other energy to the outside during the reaction.
Takes in heat from the surroundings during the reaction.
The energy needed to get a reaction going.
The amount of heat given off or taken in during a reaction.

gewusst: Our bodies also get their heat from a slow, exothermic reaction in which nutrients react with oxygen.
A compost heap can get warmer than 60 °C inside, because bacteria release heat as they work.
The thermite reaction is so hot that it even keeps burning under water.

teile.einleitung: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Like beads on a string, they join up into long molecules from which muscles, hair, enzymes and much more are made. Every amino acid has two typical groups: an amino group and a carboxyl group.
wichtigste: Every amino acid has an amino group and a carboxyl group.
The standard genetic code directly specifies 20 proteinogenic amino acids.
The body cannot make essential amino acids itself; it has to take them in with food.
Amino acids join through peptide bonds to form proteins.
At the isoelectric point, the net charge of an amino acid is zero.
Cysteine can form disulphide bridges, and in proline the amino group is part of a ring.
Amino acids can be made visible with ninhydrin, even in fingerprints.

abschnitte.text: An amino acid is a small organic molecule with two important parts: the basic **amino group** (NH₂) and the acidic **carboxyl group** (COOH). In the amino acids in proteins, both are attached to the same carbon atom. A **side chain** is also attached to it, which is different in every amino acid. The simplest amino acid is glycine, whose side chain is just a hydrogen atom.

The genetic code directly specifies **20 proteinogenic** amino acids, from which living things build their proteins. There are also two rare special cases, selenocysteine and pyrrolysine. The side chains make the difference: **tryptophan** carries an indole ring, and lysine has an extra amino group at the end. Cysteine contains sulphur and can form **disulphide bridges**, and in proline the amino group is part of a ring.

Two amino acids join when the carboxyl group of one reacts with the amino group of the other. Water is split off and a **peptide bond** is formed. Many amino acids one after another form a chain that folds into a particular shape. This shape decides whether the **protein** works as an enzyme, a muscle fibre or a building block of hair.

The human body can make some amino acids itself, but not others. These **essential** amino acids must come from food, for example from eggs, milk, meat, fish, pulses or cereals. In adults, eight are usually counted among them, including lysine, leucine and tryptophan. People who eat vegetarian food like to combine beans with cereals to get all the amino acids.

Because amino acids have an acidic and a basic group, in water they often carry a positive and a negative charge at the same time. They are then called **zwitterions**. The pH at which the total charge is exactly zero is called the **isoelectric point**. This property is used in the laboratory to separate amino acids and proteins from one another.

With the reagent **ninhydrin**, amino acids turn violet. This is how they are made visible on chromatography plates. The police use ninhydrin to find **fingerprints** on paper, because sweat contains traces of amino acids. In food chemistry too, the amino acid content is measured in this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large molecule built from many amino acids.
The bond that holds two amino acids together.
Vital for life and obtainable only from food.
A particle with a positive and a negative charge at the same time.

gewusst: The amino acid glutamic acid gives the taste called “umami”, which you can taste in Parmesan or tomatoes, for example.
From just 20 building blocks, tens of thousands of different proteins are made in the human body.
Hair and fingernails consist mainly of the protein keratin, which contains a lot of cysteine.

teile.einleitung: The ionic bond is one of the ways in which atoms hold together firmly. One atom gives up electrons and another takes them up; this creates positively and negatively charged particles that attract each other. All salts are built up in this way, for example our table salt.
wichtigste: An ionic bond typically forms between metal and non-metal atoms.
Electrostatic attraction holds the oppositely charged ions together.
A positively charged ion is called a cation, a negatively charged ion an anion.
A magnesium atom that gives up two outer electrons becomes the ion Mg²⁺.
A sulphide ion carries the charge 2-.
In a solid salt, the ions are arranged in a regular ionic lattice.
If struck hard, salt crystals shatter instead of changing shape.

abschnitte.text: Metal atoms such as sodium have only a few electrons in their outermost shell and give them up easily. Non-metal atoms such as chlorine, on the other hand, readily take up electrons. If sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine, both have a stable **noble gas configuration**. The atoms have thus become charged particles, the **ions**.

An atom that gives up electrons becomes positively charged and is called a **cation**, for example Na⁺ or Mg²⁺. An atom that takes up electrons becomes negative and is called an **anion**, for example Cl⁻ or O²⁻. Plus and minus attract each other like the poles of magnets. This **electrostatic attraction** is the ionic bond itself.

In a salt crystal, countless ions arrange themselves alternately in a regular **ionic lattice**. In table salt, each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions and vice versa. That is why grains of salt look like little cubes under a magnifying glass. The formula only gives the ratio of numbers; for magnesium oxide made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ it is therefore MgO.

Ionic compounds have very high melting points; table salt only melts at about 800 °C. They are hard but **brittle**: when struck, the layers shift, ions with the same charge end up next to each other and repel each other. As solids, salts do not conduct electricity. When molten or dissolved in water, however, they conduct well, because the ions can then move freely.

Table salt is sodium chloride, that is Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Limestone consists of calcium ions and carbonate ions. Gypsum, road salt and many minerals in rock are also **ionic compounds**. Mineral water contains dissolved ions such as calcium and magnesium, which are listed on the label.

Whether an ionic bond forms depends on how strongly the atoms attract electrons. This measure is called **electronegativity**. If the difference between two atoms is large, an ionic bond forms. If it is small, the atoms prefer to share the electrons, and then it is called a covalent bond.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrically charged particle formed from an atom by giving up or taking up electrons.
A positively charged ion.
A negatively charged ion.
A regular three-dimensional arrangement of ions in a solid salt.
A measure of how strongly an atom pulls electrons towards itself.

gewusst: Sodium is a violently reacting metal and chlorine a poisonous gas; together they make harmless table salt.
Salt water conducts electricity much better than pure water, because ions move in it.

teile.einleitung: In chemistry, an indicator is a substance that shows by its colour whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. You can even find some indicators in the kitchen, for example in red cabbage juice. Chemists use indicators to check acidity quickly and easily.
wichtigste: An indicator shows by its colour whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.
Litmus is obtained from lichens and is violet in a neutral solution.
Red cabbage juice turns red with vinegar and green to yellow in a strongly alkaline solution.
Phenolphthalein turns pink to violet in an alkali.
The hydrangea flowers blue or pink depending on how acidic the soil is.
Black tea gets lighter with lemon juice because its pigments act as an indicator.
Universal indicators show the approximate pH with many colours.

abschnitte.text: The word **indicator** comes from the Latin indicare, which means “to show”. An acid-base indicator is a dye that changes colour when the **pH** changes. The pH usually ranges from 0 to 14: below 7 a solution is acidic, at 7 neutral and above 7 **basic** or alkaline. An indicator changes its colour within a particular pH range, the transition range. So you can see at a glance whether lemon juice, soapy water or tap water is acidic or alkaline.

**Litmus** is one of the oldest indicators and is obtained from certain **lichens**. It turns red in acids, blue in alkalis and violet in neutral solutions. In the laboratory, people often use litmus paper, which is dipped briefly into the liquid. This is also where the expression “litmus test” for a decisive check comes from. Litmus only shows roughly whether something is acidic or alkaline.

The juice of **red cabbage** contains pigments called anthocyanins. If you add vinegar, the juice turns red; in water it stays violet, and in soapy water it turns blue to green. In strongly alkaline solutions it even turns yellow. Black tea is also an indicator: it gets lighter with lemon juice. Blueberry juice and red onions show similar colour changes.

**Phenolphthalein** is colourless in acidic and neutral solutions and turns pink to violet in alkalis. Methyl orange changes from red to yellowish orange in the acidic range. A **universal indicator** is a mixture of several dyes and shows many different colours for different pH values. In a titration, acid or alkali is added drop by drop until the indicator changes colour. Today the pH is also often measured electronically with a pH meter.

The **hydrangea** is a garden plant whose flowers turn blue on acidic soils and pink on chalky, alkaline soils. The reason is that the plant can take up more aluminium in acidic soil, which changes the colour of the flowers. Gardeners make use of this to grow blue hydrangeas. Many flower colours in roses, violets or cornflowers also come from anthocyanins. In schools in Switzerland, the red cabbage experiment is a popular first chemistry experiment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
The opposite of acidic; also called alkaline.
An indicator from lichens, red in acid and blue in alkali.
Red, violet and blue plant pigments, for example in red cabbage.
A method for finding out the exact amount of an acid or alkali.

gewusst: With red cabbage juice you can make a whole rainbow scale of colours at home.
The expression “litmus test” is also used for decisive checks outside chemistry.
In some regions red cabbage is called “Blaukraut” (blue cabbage) in German, because it turns bluish when cooked with alkaline water.

teile.einleitung: The law of definite proportions is a basic rule of chemistry. It states that a chemical compound always contains its elements in the same ratio by mass. Whether water comes from the Alps or from the laboratory, it is always made up in the same way.
wichtigste: A compound always contains its elements in the same ratio by mass.
The law was formulated at the end of the 18th century by the Frenchman Joseph-Louis Proust.
In water, hydrogen and oxygen are in a ratio of about 1 to 8.
So 3 g of hydrogen react with 24 g of oxygen.
A mixture such as salt water can vary, but the compound sodium chloride has a fixed composition.
Compounds with a variable composition are called berthollides.
John Dalton’s atomic theory explained the law.

abschnitte.text: The law says: in a pure **compound**, the masses of the elements involved are always in the same **ratio**. Water, for example, always contains about 1 gram of hydrogen for every 8 grams of oxygen. So if you want to make water, exactly 24 grams of oxygen react with 3 grams of hydrogen. If more oxygen is present, the rest is simply left over.

With the law you can calculate amounts as in a **rule of three** problem. 24 g of magnesium combine with 16 g of oxygen to form 40 g of magnesium oxide. If you take only 12 g of magnesium, that is half, you get 20 g of magnesium oxide. In copper(II) sulphide, 6.35 g of copper go with 3.21 g of sulphur, so 19.05 g of copper go with three times as much, namely 9.63 g of sulphur.

At the end of the 18th century the French chemist **Joseph-Louis Proust** examined many substances very precisely. He found that copper carbonate, for example, always has the same composition, no matter where it comes from. His fellow countryman **Claude-Louis Berthollet**, on the other hand, believed that compounds could form in any ratios. The dispute lasted for years; in the end Proust largely won.

Why the law holds was explained by the Englishman **John Dalton** at the beginning of the 19th century with his **atomic theory**. Every element consists of atoms with a particular mass. In a compound, the atoms combine in fixed number ratios, for example two hydrogen atoms with one oxygen atom. That is why the ratio by mass is always the same too.

The law helps to tell **compounds** apart from mixtures. Salt water is a mixture, because you can dissolve more or less salt in it. Sodium chloride, that is table salt itself, on the other hand always has the same composition. There are exceptions, however, such as certain iron oxides like wüstite, which are called **berthollides** in honour of Berthollet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pure substance in which different elements are firmly joined chemically.
Different substances that are only mixed and not chemically joined.
How many grams of one substance go with how many grams of another.
A compound with a slightly variable composition.

gewusst: The law of definite proportions helped to prove the existence of atoms long before they could be seen.
A water molecule from a glacier is made up in exactly the same way as one from the tap.
Proust worked in Spain for a time, where he carried out many of his investigations.

teile.einleitung: Sherbet powder is a sweet powder that fizzes in water and tingles on your tongue. The secret is a chemical reaction between bicarbonate of soda and an acid, which produces carbon dioxide. The same principle is used in effervescent tablets, for example vitamin tablets.
wichtigste: If you pour sherbet powder into water, it fizzes.
In sherbet powder, bicarbonate of soda and an acid react with each other.
Sherbet powder often contains citric acid.
Sugar makes sherbet powder sweet.
Sherbet powder tingles on your tongue because gas bubbles form in your saliva.
Sherbet powder must be kept dry, otherwise it starts fizzing in the tin.
Sherbet powder fizzes faster in warm water than in cold.
A pressed tablet that fizzes in water is called an effervescent tablet.

abschnitte.text: Sherbet powder has just a few ingredients. The important ones are **bicarbonate of soda**, chemically sodium hydrogen carbonate, and a solid acid such as **citric acid** or tartaric acid. Added to these are **sugar** for the sweet taste and flavourings and colourings. The colour and taste often show a fruit such as lemon, raspberry or woodruff.

As long as the powder is dry, nothing happens. But when the bicarbonate of soda and acid come into contact with **water**, they dissolve and react with each other. This produces **carbon dioxide** gas, which rises in lots of small bubbles. It is the same gas that fizzes in sparkling mineral water.

If you sprinkle sherbet powder on your tongue, it reacts with your **saliva**. The gas bubbles and the acid stimulate the nerves on your tongue, which is why it **tingles**. At the same time you taste the sweetness of the sugar and the sourness of the citric acid. Because it contains a lot of sugar, you should eat sherbet powder only now and then.

Chemical reactions usually run faster in warmth. That is why sherbet powder fizzes more strongly and quickly in **warm water** than in cold. Stirring also speeds up the reaction. You can try this yourself in a small **experiment** with two glasses.

If you press the powder into a solid tablet, you get an **effervescent tablet**. Such tablets are available, for example, with vitamin C or magnesium. The fizzing makes the tablet dissolve quickly and evenly. Here too, the tubes must be tightly closed so that no **moisture** gets in.

begriffe.erklaerung: A white salt that forms gas together with acid.
An acid found naturally in lemons that tastes sour.
The gas that rises in bubbles when something fizzes.
A pressed tablet made of fizzy powder that dissolves with a fizz.

gewusst: Sherbet powder and baking powder work on the same chemical principle.
With bicarbonate of soda, citric acid and water, you can launch a small rocket made from a film canister into the air.
Sherbet powder has been a popular sweet for about a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: Ketones are a group of organic substances that all have a special group of atoms: a carbon atom with a double-bonded oxygen that is attached to two other carbon atoms. The best-known ketone is acetone, which is found in many nail varnish removers.
wichtigste: Ketones contain a carbonyl group, that is a carbon atom with a double bond to an oxygen atom.
In ketones the carbonyl carbon atom is bonded to two other carbon atoms, so a ketone needs at least three carbon atoms.
The simplest ketone is called propanone according to IUPAC; better known is the name acetone.
The ketone with four carbon atoms is called butanone.
Ketones are formed when secondary alcohols are oxidised.
Ketones give a negative result in Fehling’s test.
Ketones and their enol form are in equilibrium with each other in keto-enol tautomerism.

abschnitte.text: All ketones have the **carbonyl group** C=O. In ketones this group is always in the middle of a carbon chain, because the carbonyl carbon atom has a carbon group on its left and on its right. If, on the other hand, the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain, it is called an aldehyde. According to the IUPAC rules, ketones are given the ending **-one**, for example propanone or butanone.

**Acetone** or propanone is a colourless, highly flammable liquid with a typical smell. It dissolves fats, varnishes and many plastics and is therefore used as nail varnish remover and as a solvent. Acetone mixes with water in any ratio. Industry produces millions of tonnes of acetone every year, mainly as a starting material for plastics.

If you oxidise a secondary alcohol, such as propan-2-ol, a ketone is formed. Ketones are hard to oxidise any further, which is why **Fehling’s test** and the silver mirror test are negative for them. This is how ketones can be told apart from aldehydes in the laboratory. Ketones can also exist in a form with a C=C double bond and an OH group, the enol; this is called **keto-enol tautomerism**.
