The carbonyl group is polar, which is why small ketones dissolve well in water. Acetone boils at 56 °C, lower than the similarly sized alcohol propan-2-ol at 82 °C. The reason: acetone molecules cannot form **hydrogen bonds** with each other, because they lack a hydrogen atom on an oxygen atom. With water, however, they can form hydrogen bonds.

abschnitte.titel: Ketones in nature and the body
abschnitte.text: Many ketones occur in nature. The fruit sugar fructose has a keto group, as do the fragrance camphor and the hormone cortisone. When the body fasts for a long time and breaks down fat, the liver forms so-called ketone bodies, one of which is acetone. That is why the breath can then smell slightly of acetone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of atoms made of a carbon atom with a double bond to an oxygen atom.
The simplest ketone, chemically propanone, known from nail varnish remover.
An alcohol in which the carbon atom with the OH group is bonded to two other carbon atoms.
An equilibrium between two forms of a molecule that differ by a moving hydrogen atom.

gewusst: The word ketone was derived from the name acetone in the 19th century.
Butanone is also called methyl ethyl ketone and is a common solvent in glues.
The human body also makes small amounts of acetone itself.

teile.einleitung: A boiled egg is a classic on the breakfast table and at Easter. But something amazing happens when it is cooked: the clear, runny egg white turns white and firm. This change is chemical and can never be reversed.
wichtigste: When cooked, the egg white turns white and firm.
The egg white sets first, then the yolk.
A hard-boiled egg is cooked for about 10 minutes.
A boiled egg can never be made raw again.
After cooking, eggs are put in cold water so that they stop cooking.
Eggs boiled for too long get a greenish ring around the yolk.
A hard-boiled egg spins quickly and evenly on the table.

abschnitte.titel: What happens when you boil an egg?
abschnitte.text: The egg white, also called **albumen**, consists mainly of water and **proteins**. Proteins are long, intricately folded molecules. The heat makes them unfold and clump together into a firm network. This process is called **denaturation** or coagulation. The network scatters the light, which is why the previously clear egg white turns white.

The heat travels from the outside inwards, so the egg white sets first and the yolk only later. After about 4 to 5 minutes in boiling water an egg is soft-boiled: the white is firm, the yolk still runny. After about 6 to 7 minutes the yolk is jammy. For a hard-boiled egg, allow about 10 minutes. Large eggs and eggs straight from the fridge need a little longer.

At the blunt end of every egg there is a small **air cell**. When heated, the air expands and can crack the shell, which is why eggs are often pricked before boiling. After boiling, the eggs are plunged into cold water so that they stop cooking. In the mountains water boils below 100 degrees, at 3000 metres at about 90 degrees. So eggs take longer there.

If you boil an egg far too long, the yolk gets a greenish grey ring. Sulphur is released from the egg white, and iron from the yolk. The two combine to form **iron sulphide**, which looks greenish. The egg is still edible, but it often tastes a little of sulphur. Cooling it in time prevents the green ring.

With a simple test you can tell a boiled egg from a raw one: you spin it on the table. A hard-boiled egg is solid inside and spins quickly and evenly. In a raw egg the liquid sloshes about and slows the spin, so the egg wobbles slowly. If you stop a raw egg briefly with your finger, it often keeps turning a little afterwards because the inside is still moving.

A hen’s egg provides valuable proteins, vitamins and minerals. In Switzerland, boiled eggs are traditionally dyed and hidden at **Easter**. In “Eiertütschen”, two people knock the tips of their eggs against each other; whoever’s egg stays whole wins. Boiled, unpeeled eggs keep for a few days in the fridge, and dyed Easter eggs without cracks often even longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A change in proteins caused by heat or acid, in which they lose their shape and become firm.
An important building block of living things and a nutrient.
The clear part of the egg around the yolk, also called albumen.
A small space filled with air at the blunt end of the egg.
To cool something hot quickly with cold water.

gewusst: The older an egg is, the easier it is to peel after boiling.
A fresh raw egg sinks in water; a very old egg can stand upright or float because its air cell has grown larger.
When frying an egg, the egg white also denaturates, only through the heat of the pan instead of water.

teile.einleitung: In an extraction, a substance is dissolved out of a mixture with the help of a solvent. That sounds complicated, but you do it every time you make tea. Sugar, vegetable oil and decaffeinated coffee are also obtained this way.
wichtigste: In an extraction, a substance is dissolved out with a solvent.
It makes use of solubility, that is, the fact that one substance dissolves in a liquid better than others.
Making tea is an extraction with hot water.
In the school laboratory, green leaf pigment is dissolved out of crushed leaves with methylated spirit.
Two liquids that do not mix are separated in a separating funnel.
In Aarberg and Frauenfeld, sugar is leached out of sugar beet chips with hot water.
In a Soxhlet extractor, a substance is leached again and again with fresh solvent.

abschnitte.text: An extraction is a **separation method** in which you dissolve a wanted substance out of a mixture. For this you choose a **solvent** in which this substance dissolves well, but the other components hardly at all. With tea, the hot water dissolves colourings, flavourings and scents out of the leaves, and the leaves themselves are left behind. The important property here is **solubility**. The word comes from the Latin extrahere, which means “to draw out”.

If a substance is dissolved out of a solid, this is called solid liquid extraction or **leaching**. Examples are tea, coffee and obtaining plant dyes. In the school laboratory, you crush leaves with sand and add methylated spirit, that is, ethanol. The liquid turns a strong green, because the leaf green chlorophyll dissolves in it. With water alone this hardly works.

You can also move a substance from one liquid into another if the two do not mix, such as water and oil. You shake both together, and the substance moves into the liquid in which it dissolves better. Then you separate the two layers in a **separating funnel**, a pear shaped glass vessel with a tap at the bottom. You simply let the lower layer run out.

In the sugar factories at **Aarberg** in the canton of Bern and at **Frauenfeld** in Thurgau, sugar beet is processed every autumn. The beet is washed and cut into thin strips, the chips. In a large tower, hot water leaches the sugar out of the chips. After cleaning and boiling down the raw juice that results, white granulated sugar is obtained. The leached chips are used as animal feed.

To make decaffeinated coffee, the **caffeine** is dissolved out of the unroasted beans with a solvent, today often with water or with carbon dioxide under high pressure. After pressing, cooking oil from rapeseed or soya is also extracted with a solvent to get more oil. Scents for perfumes and active ingredients from medicinal plants are also obtained by extraction.

The **Soxhlet extractor** was invented in 1879 by the chemist Franz von Soxhlet. The solvent is evaporated in a flask, rises, condenses on a condenser and drips onto the sample. When the chamber is full, the solution flows back into the flask, and everything starts again. In this way the sample is leached again and again with fresh solvent, and only a little of it is needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid in which other substances dissolve, for example water or ethanol.
How well a substance dissolves in a particular solvent.
Dissolving a substance out of a solid with a liquid.
A glass vessel with a tap used to separate two liquids that do not mix.
What has been dissolved out in an extraction.

gewusst: The first commercially decaffeinated coffee came onto the market from Bremen at the beginning of the 20th century.
Making a meat stock is an extraction too, because the water dissolves flavourings out of bones and vegetables.
Vanilla extract is made by leaving vanilla pods to steep in a mixture of alcohol and water.

teile.einleitung: Cotton is a soft natural fibre that grows on the seeds of the cotton plant. T-shirts, jeans, towels and cotton wool are made from it. It is the most important natural fibre in the world.
wichtigste: The fibres are fine hairs on the seeds of the cotton plant.
Cotton fibres are usually white.
Cotton needs a warm climate, which is why it is not grown in Switzerland.
Jeans are usually made of cotton.
Cotton clothes soak up sweat well and are pleasant in summer.
Cotton buds have soft tips made of cotton.
St Gallen became world famous for embroidery on cotton fabric.

abschnitte.text: Cotton belongs to the **mallow family** and grows as a shrub in warm regions. After flowering, the plant forms a seed capsule. When it is ripe, the **boll** bursts open and a white, fluffy tuft spills out. These fibres are fine hairs on the seeds, which once helped to spread them in the wind.

Cotton needs a lot of sun, warmth and water. Among the biggest growing countries are China, India, the USA and Brazil. In Switzerland it is too cold for it. After the harvest, a machine called a **cotton gin** separates the fibres from the seeds.

The fibres are cleaned, combed and **spun** into a thread. Fabrics are woven or knitted from the threads. For **jeans**, a strong cotton fabric called denim is used. Cotton consists almost entirely of **cellulose**, the same substance that wood and paper are mostly made of.

Cotton is soft, pleasant on the skin and can soak up a lot of water. That is why towels and summer T-shirts are often made of cotton. It is easy to wash and dye. However, it dries slowly and can shrink a little in a hot wash.

Although no cotton grows in Switzerland, processing it was an important industry for a long time. In eastern Switzerland and the Zurich Oberland there were many **spinning mills** and weaving mills. **St Gallen embroidery** on cotton fabric was world famous around 1900 and was exported to many countries. Today the Textile Museum in St Gallen tells this story.

Growing cotton takes a great deal of water and often pesticides. In Central Asia, the watering of cotton fields helped to make the **Aral Sea** shrink dramatically. In history, enslaved people were forced to work on cotton plantations in the southern states of the USA. Today there is organic cotton and fair trade labels that pay attention to the environment and fair wages.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fibre that comes from a plant or an animal.
Twisting fibres together into a long thread.
The building material of plant walls, of which cotton consists almost entirely.
A strong cotton fabric from which jeans are made.

gewusst: The banknotes of some countries, such as the US dollar, contain a lot of cotton.
There are also kinds of cotton with naturally brown or greenish fibres.
Growing the cotton for a single T-shirt often takes several thousand litres of water.

teile.einleitung: A sewage treatment plant cleans the dirty water from homes, schools and factories before it flows back into rivers and lakes. In Switzerland it is usually called an ARA, which stands for “Abwasserreinigungsanlage” (waste water treatment plant). Screens, tanks and billions of tiny bacteria help with the work.
wichtigste: A sewage treatment plant cleans waste water.
In Switzerland it is often abbreviated to ARA.
The water from the toilet flows through the sewers to the treatment plant.
A screen at the entrance holds back large objects.
Tiny bacteria eat the dirt in the water.
In the digester, biogas is produced from sludge.
The cleaned water flows into a river or lake, and in Switzerland the sewage sludge is burnt.

abschnitte.text: Everything we flush down the washbasin, shower and toilet flows through underground pipes, the **sewers**. In many places rainwater from roads and roofs is added too. In the end the waste water reaches the treatment plant. There it is cleaned in several stages, which often takes about a day.

First a **screen** holds back large objects such as cotton buds, wet wipes and plastic. In the grit chamber, sand and small stones sink to the bottom. Then the water flows slowly through the **primary settling tank**, where more dirt particles settle as sludge. Fat floats on top and is skimmed off.

In the **aeration tank**, billions of bacteria and other tiny organisms are at work. They eat the dissolved dirt in the water and multiply as they do so. So that they get enough oxygen, air is blown into the tank. In the secondary settling tank the flakes of bacteria sink, and the water at the top is now clean.

Iron salts are used to remove **phosphate** from the water, which would otherwise make too many algae grow in lakes. Many large Swiss treatment plants also have a fourth stage with ozone or activated carbon. It removes **micropollutants**, that is tiny residues of medicines, pesticides and cosmetics. Switzerland was one of the first countries to make this extra treatment compulsory.

The settled sludge goes into the **digester**, a large closed tank. There bacteria break down the sludge without oxygen, and biogas is produced. With the gas, the treatment plant generates electricity and heat for its own operation. In Switzerland the remaining sewage sludge may no longer be spread on fields; it is burnt.

abschnitte.titel: Clean lakes thanks to the ARA
abschnitte.text: In the 1960s many Swiss rivers and lakes were badly polluted, and in some places swimming was banned. Only after that were treatment plants built almost everywhere. Today nearly every house in Switzerland is connected to an **ARA**. That is why people can swim in the Aare, the Rhine or Lake Zurich again today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for “Abwasserreinigungsanlage”, the Swiss word for sewage treatment plant.
A network of underground pipes that collects and carries away waste water.
A tank in which bacteria clean the water with the help of air.
A closed tank in which biogas is produced from sewage sludge.
Tiny residues of medicines or chemicals in water.

gewusst: Cotton buds, wet wipes and food leftovers belong in the bin and not in the toilet, because they can block pumps.
A large treatment plant can cover a considerable part of its electricity needs itself with biogas.
Invisible to people and animals, millions of bacteria are at work in a single drop of activated sludge.

teile.einleitung: The electrochemical series is a ranking that shows how readily metals and other substances give up or take in electrons. At the top are noble metals such as gold, and at the bottom reactive ones such as lithium. With it you can predict which reactions will happen and how much voltage a battery will supply.
wichtigste: The electrochemical series arranges substances by their standard potential.
Noble metals such as gold have a positive standard potential.
Reactive metals such as lithium have a strongly negative standard potential.
A less noble metal gives its electrons to the ions of a more noble metal.
If you dip an iron nail in copper sulphate solution, copper is deposited on it.
Reactive metals such as magnesium dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off hydrogen.
Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent in the electrochemical series.

abschnitte.text: Every substance has a particular **standard potential**, measured in volts. The reference point is the **hydrogen electrode**, whose potential is fixed at 0 volts. Substances with a positive value are considered noble, and those with a negative value base or reactive. Lithium has about minus 3 volts, copper about plus 0.34 volts and gold about plus 1.5 volts. If you arrange all the values in order of size, you get the electrochemical series.

**Base metals** give up electrons easily, so they are readily oxidised. That is why they rust or corrode quickly, and many dissolve in acids, forming hydrogen. Magnesium, zinc and iron are among them. **Noble metals** such as silver, gold and platinum are reluctant to give up their electrons. That is why gold jewellery is still shiny after centuries.

If you put a bright **iron nail** in blue copper sulphate solution, it becomes coated with reddish brown copper. The less noble iron gives electrons to the copper ions, and the solution gradually becomes paler. But if you put a silver plate in copper sulphate solution, nothing happens, because silver is more noble than copper. The rule is: a metal can push out of a solution only the ions of a **more noble** metal.

Non metals such as the **halogens** also belong in the electrochemical series. Here the strongest oxidising agent is fluorine, which grabs electrons most strongly. It is followed by chlorine, bromine and iodine. That is why if you add chlorine water to a potassium bromide solution, elemental **bromine** is formed, which colours the solution yellowish brown.

If you connect two different metals through a solution, you get a **galvanic cell**, that is, a battery. The further apart the metals are in the electrochemical series, the greater the voltage. A zinc copper cell supplies about 1.1 volts. In **galvanising**, the less noble zinc protects iron from rust, because the zinc is attacked first. On the same principle, sacrificial anodes made of zinc or magnesium protect ships and boilers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number in volts that shows how easily a substance takes in or gives up electrons.
The giving up of electrons.
The taking in of electrons.
A substance that takes electrons away from other substances.
An arrangement of two metals and a solution that supplies electric current.

gewusst: You can build a small battery from a lemon, a piece of copper and a piece of zinc.
Lithium is so reactive that in lithium ion batteries for mobile phones it makes particularly high voltages possible.
Many devices and vehicles have parts made of zinc or magnesium that corrode first as sacrificial anodes and so protect the more valuable metal.

teile.einleitung: Iodised salt is table salt to which a small amount of iodine has been added. We need iodine for the thyroid gland, but there is too little of it in Swiss soils and food. That is why Switzerland was one of the first countries in the world to introduce iodised salt.
wichtigste: Iodised salt is table salt with a small addition of iodine.
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make important hormones.
In the past, goitre was common in Switzerland because of iodine deficiency.
In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries with iodised salt.
Swiss soils have little iodine because glaciers and rain have washed it away.
Sea fish naturally contains a lot of iodine.
Heated iodine forms violet vapour.

abschnitte.text: **Iodised salt** is normal table salt to which a tiny amount of an iodine compound is added. You cannot taste the addition. In Switzerland, iodised salt today contains about 25 milligrams of iodine per kilogram of salt. The salt comes from the **Swiss Saltworks**, which extract it from the ground at Rheinfelden, Riburg and Bex. Most bakeries also use iodised salt, so iodine gets into our diet through bread.

The **thyroid gland** is a small organ in the neck shaped like a butterfly. It makes **hormones** that control metabolism, growth and the development of the brain. It needs iodine for these hormones. If there is not enough iodine, the thyroid gland grows larger to capture more of it. This visible swelling in the neck is called a **goitre**.

During the Ice Age, glaciers removed the top layer of soil, and rain washed out the iodine over thousands of years. That is why Swiss soils and the plants growing on them contain little iodine. In the past, a great many people in some Alpine valleys had a goitre. With severe iodine deficiency, children were also born with developmental disorders. In 1922 the canton of **Appenzell Ausserrhoden** was the first to introduce iodised salt; other cantons soon followed, and goitre became rare.

There is a lot of iodine in **sea fish** such as cod or coley and in seaweed. Milk and eggs also contain some iodine. Anyone in Switzerland who hardly eats fish depends on iodised salt. Experts recommend choosing iodised salt when salting food at home, but not eating too much salt overall. By the way, sea salt does not automatically contain a lot of iodine.

Iodine is a chemical element from the group of **halogens**. Pure iodine forms shiny greyish black crystals. If you heat them, a beautiful **violet vapour** forms, which is where the name comes from: the Greek word for “violet-coloured”. Iodine was discovered in 1811 by the Frenchman Bernard Courtois in the ash of seaweed. In the past, wounds were disinfected with **tincture of iodine**, and if you drip iodine solution onto a potato, the starch in it turns bluish black.

begriffe.erklaerung: A butterfly-shaped organ in the neck that makes hormones.
An enlargement of the thyroid gland, often caused by iodine deficiency.
A chemical messenger that controls processes in the body.
A group of elements that includes iodine, chlorine and fluorine.
A nutrient in potatoes and grain that turns bluish black with iodine.

gewusst: Iodine is one of the few elements that can change directly from solid to gas when heated.
A person needs only about 150 micrograms of iodine a day, which is just 0.15 milligrams.
Switzerland is regarded worldwide as a pioneer in fighting iodine deficiency with salt.

teile.einleitung: Autoprotolysis is the name for a reaction in which molecules of the same kind exchange a proton among themselves. The best known example is water: even completely pure water contains tiny amounts of ions. This process is the basis of the pH scale, with which we measure how acidic or alkaline something is.
wichtigste: For the autoprotolysis of water: 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
The ionic product of water Kw is 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/L² at 25 °C.
At 25 °C: pH plus pOH equals 14.
In pure water at 25 °C there is one oxonium ion for about 555 million water molecules.
Ultrapure water conducts electricity only extremely weakly, because hardly any molecules are protolysed.
At higher temperatures Kw becomes larger, because autoprotolysis is endothermic.
Liquid ammonia also shows autoprotolysis, forming NH₄⁺ and NH₂⁻.

abschnitte.text: Water molecules are constantly colliding. Very occasionally, one molecule gives a **proton** to another. This produces an **oxonium ion** H₃O⁺ and a **hydroxide ion** OH⁻. Because the ions quickly react back to water, an equilibrium is set up, written 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.

If you multiply the concentrations of the two ions, at 25 °C you always get 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/L². This value is called the **ionic product of water** Kw. In pure water both ions are equally common, 10⁻⁷ mol/L each. That is why neutral water at 25 °C has a **pH of 7**.

Because the ionic product is fixed, the two ions are linked: if one concentration rises, the other falls. If a solution has pH 4, the hydroxide ion concentration is 10⁻¹⁰ mol/L. At 25 °C, **pH plus pOH always equals 14**. So a solution with pOH 3 has pH 11 and is alkaline.

Autoprotolysis is **endothermic**, which means it needs heat. At higher temperatures more ions are formed and Kw becomes larger. That is why pure water at 60 °C has a pH below 7, even though it is still **neutral**. Neutral simply means that there are equal numbers of oxonium and hydroxide ions.

Because there are so few ions, **ultrapure water** conducts electric current only extremely weakly. Tap water conducts much better, because it contains dissolved salts. Ultrapure water is used, for example, in laboratories and in making **computer chips**. Its conductivity can be used to check how pure water is.

Water is not the only substance that shows autoprotolysis. In liquid **ammonia**, ammonium ions NH₄⁺ and amide ions NH₂⁻ are formed in the same way. Pure acetic acid and sulphuric acid also exchange protons among themselves. For a substance to do this, it must be an **ampholyte**, that is, able to give off and take up protons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reaction in which a proton passes from one particle to another.
The ion H₃O⁺, formed when water takes up a proton.
The ion OH⁻, left behind when water gives off a proton.
A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
The name for a reaction that takes in heat.

gewusst: A glass of pure water still contains countless ions, because a glass holds a huge number of molecules.
A pH below 7 does not always mean acidic; with hot water the neutral point shifts.
In water, a proton jumps on from molecule to molecule extremely fast, much faster than other ions travel.

teile.einleitung: Baking powder is a white powder that makes cake mixture light and airy during baking. It consists mainly of bicarbonate of soda and an acid, which produce carbon dioxide gas in the moist, hot mixture. Unlike yeast, baking powder is not alive; it works purely chemically.
wichtigste: Baking powder makes cake mixture rise.
The most important ingredient of baking powder is bicarbonate of soda.
In the mixture, baking powder produces carbon dioxide gas.
Baking powder works most strongly in the hot oven.
The many small holes in a cake come from gas bubbles.
Without baking powder, a sponge cake turns out flat and dense.
Marble cake and other sponge cakes are usually baked with baking powder.

abschnitte.titel: What baking powder is made of
abschnitte.text: Baking powder is a **white powder** made of three parts. The most important is **bicarbonate of soda**, chemically sodium hydrogen carbonate. To this is added an **acidifier**, for example a phosphate or cream of tartar. As the third part, a little starch is mixed in, which keeps the powder dry so that it does not react too early.

As soon as baking powder gets wet, the bicarbonate of soda and the acid react with each other. This produces **carbon dioxide** gas. In the hot oven the reaction becomes particularly strong, and the gas bubbles expand further in the heat. The mixture sets, and the bubbles are left behind as many small **pores** in the cake.

Baking powder is used above all for **sponge cakes** such as marble cake, lemon cake or muffins. These mixtures are soft and runny, so yeast would be too slow here. Baking powder works fast, and you do not have to wait for the mixture to rise. If you forget it, the cake turns out **flat and dense**.

In the past, dough was made airy only with yeast, sourdough or stiffly beaten egg white. In the 19th century, chemists found out that bicarbonate of soda forms a gas with an acid. Soon baking powder came on sale as a ready mixture in **sachets**. Today it sits in the store cupboard of almost every Swiss kitchen.

It is best to mix baking powder with the **flour** first, so that it spreads evenly. The finished mixture should be put into the preheated oven quickly. During the first few minutes you should not open the **oven door**, otherwise the cake sinks. At the end you check with a wooden skewer whether the cake is baked through inside.

begriffe.erklaerung: A white salt, chemically sodium hydrogen carbonate, that forms gas with acid.
An acidic substance in baking powder that reacts with the bicarbonate of soda.
A gas that puffs up the mixture and makes holes in the cake.
A substance that makes a dough or mixture light and airy.

gewusst: If you put a little baking powder in vinegar, it fizzes up at once, which shows the same reaction as in the mixture.
Baking powder works twice: a little in the wet mixture already and even more strongly in the hot oven.
Baking powder can also be used for cleaning, because bicarbonate of soda removes grease and smells.

teile.einleitung: Esters are a large group of chemical compounds that often smell wonderful. They give bananas, apples and pineapples their smell, but they are also found in fats, waxes, medicines and plastics. They are formed when an acid reacts with an alcohol.
wichtigste: Esters are formed from an acid and an alcohol, with water being split off.
Their characteristic feature is the -COO- group between two carbon chains.
Many fruit flavours are esters; isoamyl acetate, for example, smells of banana.
Fats and oils are esters of glycerol and three fatty acids.
Natural waxes such as beeswax consist mainly of esters of long chain acids and alcohols.
Esters boil at lower temperatures than carboxylic acids of the same mass, because they do not form hydrogen bonds with each other.
Acetylsalicylic acid, known as aspirin, is an ester.

abschnitte.text: An ester is formed when a **carboxylic acid** reacts with an **alcohol**. The two molecules join together, and a water molecule is split off. This reaction is called **esterification** and is usually speeded up with a little sulphuric acid. Typical of esters is the group of atoms -COO-, which links two carbon chains. The reaction can also be reversed: with water, an ester is split back into acid and alcohol.

Many small esters are volatile and smell fruity. **Isoamyl acetate** smells of banana, ethyl butyrate of pineapple. Methyl salicylate, made from salicylic acid and methanol, smells of wintergreen and is found in some sports ointments. The food industry uses such esters as flavourings, for example in sweets or chewing gum. Perfumes often contain esters too.

Chemically speaking, butter, olive oil and rapeseed oil are esters: one molecule of **glycerol** is joined to three fatty acids. Waxes such as beeswax consist of esters of very long acids and alcohols and are therefore solid and water repellent. If you boil fat with caustic soda solution, the ester is split and soap is formed. This special kind of ester splitting is called **saponification**.

**Acetylsalicylic acid** is an ester of acetic acid and salicylic acid and became known in 1899 under the name aspirin. Ethyl acetate is a solvent in glues and nail varnish. Polyesters are huge chain molecules made of many ester bonds. The polyester PET is used to make drinks bottles and fleece jumpers.

Esters are usually colourless and dissolve poorly in water. They boil at lower temperatures than carboxylic acids of similar mass, because no **hydrogen bonds** form between ester molecules. That is why small esters evaporate easily and we can smell them. Ring shaped esters that form within a single molecule are called **lactones**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The reaction of an acid with an alcohol, which produces an ester and water.
An organic acid with the group -COOH, for example acetic acid.
Splitting an ester with an alkali; with fats this produces soap.
A plastic made of long chains linked by many ester bonds.
A ring shaped ester that forms within one molecule.

gewusst: Many strawberry and banana sweets smell of fruit only thanks to artificially made esters.
A fleece jumper and a PET bottle are made of the same substance, a polyester.
The name ester was coined in the 19th century by the German chemist Leopold Gmelin.

teile.einleitung: Glass is a transparent, hard material that is made mainly from sand. The raw materials are melted at over 1000 degrees and the melt is left to solidify. Windows, bottles, spectacles and even the fibres that carry internet data are made of glass.
wichtigste: Glass is made mainly from sand.
Melting it requires temperatures of over 1000 degrees.
Glass that is heated very strongly becomes soft and can be shaped.
A glassblower uses a pipe to shape hot glass into vases and vessels.
Glass is hard but brittle and easily breaks into sharp pieces.
Behind the glass of a mirror there is a thin layer of metal.
In Switzerland, waste glass is collected separately by colour and recycled.

abschnitte.text: The most important raw material is **quartz sand**, which consists mainly of silicon dioxide. Soda is added so that the sand melts at a lower temperature, and lime so that the glass becomes firm and durable. This mixture is melted at over 1000 degrees, in industry usually at around 1500 degrees. As it cools, the particles do not form an ordered lattice: glass is **amorphous**, a solidified melt.

Glass is transparent, hard and does not rust. It hardly reacts with food, which is why it is well suited for bottles and jars. At the same time it is **brittle**: if a drinking glass falls on a hard floor, it breaks into sharp pieces, which you should never pick up with your bare hands. If glass is heated strongly, it slowly becomes soft instead of suddenly turning liquid.

A **glassblower** uses a long tube, the blowpipe, to pick up a ball of glowing glass and blows it up. This is how vases, bowls and Christmas tree baubles are made. Window glass today is usually made as **float glass**, by letting liquid glass solidify completely flat and smooth on a bath of liquid tin. At the Glasi Hergiswil in the canton of Nidwalden you can watch glassblowers at work.

People made the first glass objects several thousand years ago in Mesopotamia and Egypt, first beads and small vessels. Around the time of the Romans, glassblowing with a pipe was invented, and glass thus became an everyday product. In the Middle Ages, colourful stained glass windows decorated churches. Today there are special glasses for screens, laboratory equipment and **optical fibres**, which carry light and data over long distances.

Window panes, spectacle lenses, marbles, drinking glasses and mirrors are made of glass. Behind the glass, a mirror has a thin layer of silver or aluminium that reflects the light. Waste glass can be melted down again and again without getting worse. In Switzerland it is collected separately by the colours clear, brown and green, and a very large part of it is recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine sand that consists mainly of silicon dioxide.
Without an ordered lattice; the particles lie in disorder as in a liquid.
Breaks suddenly instead of bending.
A very thin thread of glass that carries light and data.

gewusst: Glass also forms in nature, for example as obsidian from volcanic lava or when lightning strikes sand.
The fact that old church windows are thicker at the bottom is not because glass flows, but because of the way they were made at the time.
Waste glass can be melted down as often as you like and made into new bottles.

teile.einleitung: Precious metals are metals that hardly rust or tarnish in air and water. They include gold, silver and platinum. Because they are rare, beautiful and durable, they are used for jewellery, coins and in technology.
wichtigste: A precious metal hardly reacts with air and water.
The most important precious metals are gold, silver and the platinum metals such as platinum, palladium and rhodium.
Silver has the chemical symbol Ag, and gold the symbol Au.
18 carat gold contains 75 per cent pure gold.
A large part of the gold traded worldwide is refined in Switzerland.
Palladium and rhodium are used in the catalytic converters of cars.
Aqua regia, a mixture of two acids, can even dissolve gold.

abschnitte.text: Precious metals are metals that are very **unreactive**; they hardly react with oxygen and water. That is why they stay shiny for a long time and do not rust like iron. The precious metals include **gold**, silver and the six **platinum metals**: platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium and ruthenium. Copper is sometimes called a semi precious metal.

The chemical symbols come from Latin. Gold is called aurum in Latin and has the symbol Au, and silver is called argentum and has the symbol Ag. Platinum comes from the Spanish word platina, which means little silver. Platinum was studied more closely in Europe only in the 18th century.

The purity of gold is often given in **carats**; 24 carats means pure gold. So 18 carat gold contains 18 out of 24 parts gold, which is 75 per cent. On bars, the purity is given per thousand; 999.9 means 999.9 parts gold out of 1000. Pure gold is very soft, which is why it is mixed with other metals for jewellery.

Switzerland is a centre of the world gold trade. In large **refineries**, mainly in Ticino and the canton of Neuchâtel, a large part of the world's gold is purified and cast into bars. The Swiss National Bank keeps part of its reserves in gold. The Goldvreneli, a gold coin with the head of Helvetia, is also well known.

Precious metals are needed for jewellery, coins and watches, but also for technology. In mobile phones and computers, thin layers of gold conduct electricity reliably. Palladium, platinum and rhodium help in the **catalytic converter** to change poisonous exhaust gases. But precious metals cannot resist everything: silver tarnishes dark because of sulphur compounds in the air, and aqua regia, made of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid, even dissolves gold.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of the purity of gold; 24 carats is pure gold.
Here, a plant that purifies gold and silver and casts them into bars.
A very aggressive mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid.
A group of six rare precious metals that includes platinum.

gewusst: From a single gram of gold you can draw a wire several kilometres long.
Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal.
All the gold people have ever mined, melted together, would make a cube with sides only about 22 metres long.

teile.einleitung: A catalyst is a substance that makes a chemical reaction run faster without being used up itself. It works like a short-cut tunnel through a mountain: the destination stays the same, but the route becomes easier. Catalysts clean car exhaust, help with the production of fertiliser and work as enzymes in our body.
wichtigste: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.
It lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
A catalyst does not change the total energy released.
The catalytic converter in a car turns poisonous carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide.
In many catalytic converters, the precious metal platinum does the work.
Catalysts in living things are called enzymes.
In the Haber-Bosch process, ammonia is made with an iron catalyst.

abschnitte.text: For a reaction to start, it needs a push of energy, the **activation energy**. You can imagine it as a mountain that the substances must get over. A catalyst opens up a different route with a lower mountain, rather like a tunnel through the Alps. That is why the substances react faster, but in the end the same products form with the same energy balance.

The catalyst takes part in the reaction, but is released again at the end. That is why a small amount is often enough to convert a great deal of substance. A nice school experiment is **manganese dioxide** in hydrogen peroxide: it foams vigorously because oxygen is released. The manganese dioxide then lies unchanged in the glass.

In the exhaust of many cars there is a **catalytic converter** with a honeycomb structure coated with platinum, palladium or rhodium. It turns poisonous carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide. It also turns nitrogen oxides into harmless nitrogen and burns up remains of fuel. In Switzerland catalytic converters were introduced in the 1980s to make the air cleaner.

In living things too, chemical reactions are taking place all the time that would be far too slow without help. This is the job of **enzymes**, the catalysts of life. The **amylase** in saliva starts breaking starch down into sugar already in the mouth. That is why bread tastes sweetish if you chew it for a long time.

Most chemical products are made with catalysts today. In the **Haber-Bosch process**, ammonia is formed from nitrogen and hydrogen with an iron catalyst. From it, artificial fertiliser is made, which feeds a great many people worldwide. Plastics, fuels and margarine are also produced with the help of catalysts.

In 1835 the Swedish chemist Jöns Jakob Berzelius coined the term **catalysis**. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “loosening”. The German Wilhelm Ostwald researched how catalysts work and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1909. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch later also received Nobel Prizes for their work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
Energy needed for a reaction to start at all.
A protein that acts as a catalyst in the body.
Speeding up a chemical reaction with a catalyst.

gewusst: Without enzymes, digesting a meal would take many years.
About half of the nitrogen in our body comes from fertiliser made with the Haber-Bosch process.
A catalytic converter only works properly once it is a few hundred degrees hot.

teile.einleitung: A descaler is a cleaning product that dissolves limescale deposits in household appliances and bathrooms. It usually contains an acid that turns the hard limescale into soluble substances. Especially in regions with hard water, it is needed regularly for the coffee machine, kettle and shower.
wichtigste: Descalers contain an acid such as citric acid.
Limescale forms mainly where water is heated.
When water is heated, dissolved lime particles come out as a solid coating.
More limescale forms in regions with hard tap water.
In Switzerland, water hardness is given in French degrees of hardness (°fH).
After descaling, appliances are rinsed through several times with clean water.
Descaler must never be mixed with chlorine based cleaners, because poisonous chlorine gas can form.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the limescale come from?
abschnitte.text: Rainwater seeps through the ground and dissolves calcium and magnesium compounds from the rock as it does so. Water becomes **hard** above all from limestone, as found in the **Jura** and the limestone Alps. In the water, the lime is present as dissolved **calcium hydrogen carbonate**. When the water is heated, carbon dioxide escapes, and insoluble **calcium carbonate** settles as a white coating. That is why kettles, coffee machines and hot water tanks in particular get furred up.

In Switzerland, water hardness is given in **French degrees of hardness**, abbreviated °fH. One French degree corresponds to 10 milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre of water. In large parts of the Central Plateau and the Jura, the water tends to be hard. In areas with granite and gneiss, for example in parts of Ticino, the Grisons and Valais, it is often softer. You can find out the exact value for where you live from the local water supplier.

Limescale is a base and reacts with **acids**. Typical active ingredients in descalers are citric acid, lactic acid, acetic acid or sulphamic acid. The acid turns the insoluble limescale into soluble salts that can be rinsed away. Carbon dioxide is produced, which you often notice as little bubbles and a gentle fizzing. **Vinegar** from the kitchen also works as a home remedy, but it smells strongly and can attack some rubber seals.

A layer of limescale acts like an **insulating layer** between the heating element and the water. The appliance then needs more electricity and more time to heat the water. Limescale can also block thin pipes, so that the coffee machine only drips or breaks down. Many appliances therefore show when they need descaling. How often this is necessary depends on the water hardness and on how much the appliance is used.

After descaling, the appliance is rinsed through several times with clean water so that no residue ends up in the coffee or tea. Descaler must be kept away from small children and must not get into the eyes. It should **never be mixed with chlorine based cleaners**, because poisonous **chlorine gas** can be produced. On marble or natural stone, acid can attack the surface, because these stones are themselves made of lime.

begriffe.erklaerung: States how much calcium and magnesium is dissolved in the water.
The everyday word for calcium carbonate, a white, hard substance.
A substance that can dissolve limescale and often tastes sour, such as citric acid.
The chemical name for lime, the main component of limestone and marble.

gewusst: Stalactites and stalagmites in caves form in a similar way to limescale marks: water evaporates and lime is left behind.
Lime in drinking water is not unhealthy; calcium and magnesium are even important minerals.
An egg in vinegar loses its lime shell after a while and becomes soft and rubbery.

teile.einleitung: The equivalence point is the moment in a titration when exactly as much alkali has been added as there was acid, or the other way round. The two substances have then completely neutralised each other. With this point, chemists can determine very precisely how concentrated a solution is.
wichtigste: At the equivalence point, acid and base have reacted in exactly matching amounts.
When sodium hydroxide solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid, dissolved sodium chloride is present at the equivalence point.
The point at which the indicator changes colour is called the end point.
On a titration curve, the equivalence point is found as the point of inflection in the steepest part of the pH jump.
With weak bases such as ammonia, the equivalence point lies in the acidic range.
Polyprotic acids such as phosphoric acid have several equivalence points.

abschnitte.text: In a **titration**, a solution of known concentration is dripped from a measuring tube, the **burette**, into a sample. This goes on until the reaction is just complete. This moment is called the **equivalence point**. From the volume used, you can calculate how much substance was in the sample.

At the equivalence point, for a monoprotic acid: amount of acid equals amount of alkali. If, for example, 15 mL of hydrochloric acid at 0.1 mol/L is in the flask, you need **7.5 mL** of sodium hydroxide solution at 0.2 mol/L. If 20 mL of hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 25 mL of sodium hydroxide solution at 0.1 mol/L, the hydrochloric acid has 0.125 mol/L. With sulphuric acid, you have to remember that each molecule gives off **two protons**.

So that you can see the equivalence point, you add an **indicator**, a dye that changes colour at a particular pH. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution and turns pink in alkaline solution. The moment of the colour change is called the **end point**. A good indicator is chosen so that the end point and the equivalence point almost coincide.

If you keep measuring the pH during the titration, you get a **titration curve**. Near the equivalence point the pH suddenly changes a lot; this is the **pH jump**. The equivalence point lies at the point of inflection in the middle of this jump. Today electronic meters record such curves automatically.

Only when a strong acid reacts with a strong base is the equivalence point at **pH 7**. If you titrate the weak base ammonia with hydrochloric acid, ammonium chloride is formed, and the solution is **acidic** at the equivalence point. With acetic acid and sodium hydroxide solution it is the other way round, and the point lies in the alkaline range. Phosphoric acid H₃PO₄ even has three equivalence points; for 0.5 mol you need 1.5 mol of sodium hydroxide to reach the third.

begriffe.erklaerung: A method for finding the concentration of a solution by adding another solution drop by drop.
A long glass tube with a scale and a tap, from which you can measure out precisely.
A dye that has a different colour depending on the pH.
The reaction of an acid with a base, which produces water and a salt.

gewusst: With a good titration, concentrations can be determined to better than one per cent.
The acidity of wine, vinegar or fruit juice is also measured in laboratories by titration.
Red cabbage juice can serve as a home made indicator; it turns red in acid and green to blue in alkali.

teile.einleitung: Glucose, also known in everyday life as dextrose or grape sugar, is the most important sugar in nature. Plants make it with sunlight, and our body uses it as a fast source of energy for muscles and brain. Its name comes from the Greek word glykys, which means “sweet”.
wichtigste: Glucose has the molecular formula C6H12O6.
In everyday life glucose is called dextrose; it tastes a little less sweet than table sugar.
Glucose is a carbohydrate and a simple sugar.
Table sugar, sucrose, consists of glucose and fructose.
In Fehling’s test, glucose forms a brick-red precipitate.
Without oxygen, yeast ferments glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The hormone insulin lowers the amount of glucose in the blood.

abschnitte.text: Glucose is a **simple sugar**, that is a carbohydrate made of only one sugar unit. Its molecule consists of 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms; the formula is C6H12O6. It is found in grapes, other fruit and honey, hence the name **grape sugar**. You can buy it in any shop as a white powder or in tablets. It tastes a little less sweet than ordinary table sugar.

Plants produce glucose during **photosynthesis**. Using the energy of sunlight, they turn carbon dioxide from the air and water into glucose and oxygen. They link the glucose into long chains: into **starch** as a store, for example in potatoes and grain, and into cellulose, the building material of wood and plant fibres. Glucose is thus the basis of almost all food chains on Earth.

In the body, starch from bread, pasta or rice is broken down into glucose, which passes from the gut into the blood. The cells burn it with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water and gain energy in this way. The brain depends particularly on glucose. The body stores surplus glucose as **glycogen** in the liver and muscles. Because dextrose does not have to be digested first, it goes into the blood very quickly.

The amount of glucose in the blood is called **blood sugar** and is closely controlled by the body. If it rises after a meal, the pancreas releases the hormone **insulin**, which helps the cells take up glucose. If it falls too low, the hormone glucagon makes sure that glucose is released from the glycogen store. In the disease diabetes, this control does not work properly, and those affected have to measure their blood sugar regularly.

Glucose can be detected with **Fehling’s test**: you heat it with a blue copper solution, and a brick-red precipitate forms. Without oxygen, yeasts ferment glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This **fermentation** is used in baking bread, where the gas makes the dough rise. It also plays a part in making wine and beer.

Our table sugar is chemically called **sucrose** and is a double sugar made of glucose and fructose. In Switzerland it is obtained from sugar beet, in the sugar factories at Aarberg and Frauenfeld. Experts advise not eating too much added sugar, for example in sugary drinks. Too much sugar can cause tooth decay and increase the risk of being overweight.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sugar made of only one unit, for example glucose or fructose.
A group of nutrients that includes sugar, starch and cellulose.
The storage form of glucose in the liver and muscles.
A hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood sugar.
The breakdown of sugar by yeasts or bacteria without oxygen.

gewusst: A single starch grain from a potato consists of countless glucose units linked together.
If you chew a piece of bread for a long time, it tastes sweet, because saliva breaks starch down into sugar.
The paper of a book also consists mostly of glucose, namely of cellulose, which is built from long glucose chains.

teile.einleitung: Lime, in the everyday sense, means calcium carbonate, a white substance found in rock, shells and eggshells. Whole mountain ranges such as the Jura consist mostly of limestone. At home we know it as limescale, the annoying white layer in the kettle.
wichtigste: Chemically, it is calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3.
The Jura mountains consist mostly of limestone.
Mussel shells, snail shells and eggshells consist mainly of calcium carbonate.
In the sea, corals build huge reefs out of calcium carbonate.
Stalactites and stalagmites in caves are made of calcium carbonate.
Tap water with a lot of dissolved calcium carbonate is called hard water.
If you drip vinegar onto limestone, it fizzes because carbon dioxide is produced.

abschnitte.text: It is a compound of calcium, carbon and oxygen that chemists call **calcium carbonate**. It is white, rather soft and hardly dissolves in pure water. Depending on how it formed, it occurs as limestone, chalk or marble. Marble is limestone that has been transformed deep in the Earth by heat and pressure.

Many sea creatures build their shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, for example mussels, snails and **corals**. When they die, their remains sink to the sea floor. Over millions of years they are pressed together and become **limestone**. That is why fossilised shells and ammonites are often found in the limestone of the Jura and the Alps.

The whole **Jura** is built of limestone that formed in a sea about 150 million years ago. Many mountains in the Prealps, such as the Säntis or Pilatus, are also made of limestone. Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and forms caves, sinkholes and underground rivers. The Hölloch in the Muotathal in the canton of Schwyz is one of the longest caves in the world, with more than 200 kilometres of passages.

When water flows through limestone, it dissolves some calcium carbonate and carries it along. When this water drips from the ceiling in a cave, the calcium carbonate is deposited again very slowly, and this is how **stalactites and stalagmites** form. Our tap water also contains dissolved calcium carbonate; a lot of it makes the water **hard**. When it is heated, the calcium carbonate settles as a layer of limescale in the kettle or coffee machine.

Calcium carbonate reacts with acids; it foams and fizzes because the gas **carbon dioxide** is produced. That is why you can remove limescale stains with vinegar or citric acid. Geologists recognise limestone by putting a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid on it. Acid rain also attacks monuments made of limestone and marble.

If you heat limestone to about 900 °C, carbon dioxide escapes and **quicklime** is formed. With water it becomes slaked lime, which mixed with sand gives a mortar. In the air this takes up carbon dioxide again and becomes as hard as stone. Limestone is also the most important raw material for cement.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name of limestone, with the formula CaCO3.
Water with a lot of dissolved calcium carbonate and magnesium.
A column or icicle of calcium carbonate that grows in caves from dripping water.
A white powder produced by strongly heating limestone.

gewusst: The White Cliffs of Dover in England consist of chalk, that is the tiny calcium carbonate shells of sea creatures.
A stalactite often grows only about one centimetre in a hundred years.
A hen’s eggshell consists of about 95 per cent calcium carbonate.

teile.einleitung: Barbecue charcoal is charcoal that gives a hot, even glow when you have a barbecue. It is made when wood is strongly heated without much air. To make barbecuing fun, you need to know a few safety rules.
wichtigste: Barbecue charcoal is made from wood.
People who make charcoal are called charcoal burners.
Charcoal burners make charcoal in a large pile of wood, the charcoal kiln.
The charcoal is ready when it is covered with grey ash.
To light it you use firelighters and never methylated spirits or petrol.
A charcoal barbecue must never burn indoors, because a poisonous gas is produced.
Sausages are turned with barbecue tongs.

abschnitte.text: Barbecue charcoal is **charcoal**, that is wood that consists almost only of carbon. It is black, light and breaks easily. When it burns it gives off a lot of heat, but hardly any flames and little smoke. Besides pieces of charcoal there are **briquettes**, which are pressed blocks of charcoal powder. Briquettes burn longer and more evenly, but take more time to light.

abschnitte.titel: The charcoal burner and his kiln
abschnitte.text: Charcoal is made when wood is heated to several hundred degrees without much air getting in. The wood does not burn; instead water and other substances escape as gases. In the past, **charcoal burners** did this in a **charcoal kiln**, a large pile of wood covered with earth. A kiln glows for several days, and the charcoal burner has to watch it day and night. In Switzerland this old craft is still practised today in the Entlebuch, for example in Romoos. Today most barbecue charcoal is made in factories in large ovens.

To light it, you put **firelighters** between the charcoal or use a chimney starter. You must never use methylated spirits or petrol, especially not on charcoal that is already glowing, because a dangerous jet of flame can shoot up. It often takes about half an hour for the charcoal to be ready. You can tell because it is covered with a fine layer of **grey ash** and no longer has flames. Only then do you put sausages, vegetables or meat on the grill.

Burning charcoal produces **carbon monoxide**, a gas that you can neither see nor smell and that is very poisonous. That is why a charcoal barbecue must never be used in a flat, a tent or a garage, not even for heating. Children should always keep their distance from the hot barbecue. Sausages are turned with long **barbecue tongs** so that you do not burn yourself. The embers stay hot for many hours and should only go in the bin once they have cooled down completely.

A large part of the barbecue charcoal sold in Switzerland comes from abroad. Sometimes trees from tropical forests are cut down for it, which harms the forests. An **FSC label** on the packet shows that the wood comes from responsibly managed forests. Charcoal from Switzerland or neighbouring countries also has shorter transport routes. If you like, you can also light a fireplace with wood from the forest and wait until there is a nice bed of embers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Strongly heated wood that consists almost only of carbon.
A craftsman who makes charcoal from wood.
A large, covered pile of wood in which wood turns into charcoal.
An invisible, odourless and very poisonous gas.
A pressed block of charcoal powder.

gewusst: Charcoal is much lighter than the wood it was made from.
As early as the Stone Age, people painted animals on cave walls with charcoal.
In the past, a great deal of charcoal was needed to smelt iron from ore.

teile.einleitung: The ideal gas is a model that makes it easy to describe and calculate how gases behave. You imagine the gas particles as tiny points that fly about and do not attract one another. With the equation p · V = n · R · T, the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas can be calculated.
wichtigste: The ideal gas is a simplified model of gases.
In the model, the particles are points and do not attract one another.
The equation of state is p · V = n · R · T.
The universal gas constant R is about 8.314 J/(mol·K).
If you compress a gas to a third at the same temperature, the pressure triples.
Real gases behave almost ideally at high temperature and low pressure.
In 1873 Johannes Diderik van der Waals put forward an equation for real gases.

abschnitte.text: A gas consists of countless tiny particles that constantly fly about in all directions and bump against the walls of their container. In an **ideal gas** you imagine that these particles have no size of their own, so they are **points**. In addition, they do not attract each other and only collide like billiard balls. Such a gas does not exist in reality. But the model is so good that it can be used to calculate air, helium or nitrogen in everyday life quite accurately.

The **equation of state** is p · V = n · R · T. Here p is the pressure, V the volume, n the amount of substance in moles and T the temperature in kelvin. R is the **universal gas constant**, about 8.314 J/(mol·K). The temperature must always be given in **kelvin**; 0 kelvin corresponds to minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. At 0 °C and normal air pressure, one mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres.

If you compress a gas at the same temperature to a third of its volume, the pressure becomes three times as great. If you heat a gas at the same pressure from 27 °C to 327 °C, the temperature rises from 300 to 600 kelvin, and the volume doubles. One mole of gas in a 10-litre container at 300 kelvin exerts a pressure of about 249 kPa. That is about two and a half times normal air pressure. Calculations like these are needed all the time in chemistry, physics and engineering.

The equation combines several older **gas laws**. In the 17th century Robert Boyle and Edme Mariotte found that pressure and volume are inversely related at the same temperature. Around 1802 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac showed that gases expand evenly when heated. In 1811 Amedeo Avogadro realised that equal volumes of gas contain the same number of particles. In 1873 **Johannes Diderik van der Waals** put forward an improved equation for real gases that takes into account the size and attraction of the particles.

A hot-air balloon rises because the heated air expands and so becomes lighter than the cold air outside. Bicycle tyres have less pressure in cold winter than in summer. You must never heat a spray can, because the pressure inside rises sharply and it can burst. When you pump up a tyre, the air in the pump is compressed and gets warm. At very high pressure or low temperature the model no longer fits well, and then gases even turn liquid.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly the gas particles push against the walls of their container.
The space a gas takes up.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
A unit of amount for a very large number of particles, rather like a dozen for 12.
An actual gas whose particles have a size and attract one another.

gewusst: One litre of air contains about 27 thousand billion billion gas particles.
It cannot get colder than 0 kelvin, that is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.
Of all real gases, helium behaves particularly like an ideal gas.

teile.einleitung: Filtration is a method for separating solid substances from a liquid or a gas. The mixture is allowed to run through a filter, which holds back the larger particles. You come across it in the laboratory, in the kitchen when making coffee and at the waterworks.
wichtigste: When filtering, substances are separated by the size of their particles.
The clear liquid that runs through the filter is called the filtrate.
The solid that is left in the filter is called the residue.
A mixture of sand and water can easily be filtered.
Dissolved salt passes through the pores of the filter and so cannot be separated this way.
In the laboratory, the folded filter paper is placed in a funnel.
In many waterworks, the water flows through sand and gravel to remove suspended particles.

abschnitte.text: In **filtration**, a mixture is poured onto a filter with tiny holes, the pores. Small particles such as water molecules fit through, while larger grains get stuck. So it makes use of the **particle size** of the substances. You know the principle from the coffee machine, where the filter holds back the ground coffee.

In the laboratory, you fold a round filter paper and put it in a **funnel**, which stands over a beaker. Then you slowly pour in the mixture. The clear liquid that runs out at the bottom is called the **filtrate**, and the solid in the paper is called the **residue**. A fluted filter, folded many times, has a larger surface, so the liquid runs through faster.

abschnitte.titel: What works and what does not?
abschnitte.text: A mixture of liquid and undissolved grains floating in it is called a **suspension**, for example sand in water or chalk in water. Such mixtures can be filtered well. Salt water, on the other hand, is a solution: the salt has broken up into tiny particles and fits through the pores. To get the salt back, you have to let the water evaporate.

In many waterworks, water from lakes or rivers flows slowly through thick layers of sand and gravel. These **sand filters** hold back suspended particles and even many bacteria. Zurich, for example, gets a large part of its drinking water from Lake Zurich and cleans it with filters like these, among other methods. Filtering also plays an important part in sewage treatment works.

Filters are not only for liquids but also for air. The vacuum cleaner holds dust back in a filter, and face masks filter dust out of the air we breathe. The **kidneys** also work like a filter and clean our blood. The paper coffee filter was invented in 1908 by the housewife Melitta Bentz in Dresden.

begriffe.erklaerung: The liquid that runs through the filter.
The solid that is left behind in the filter.
A mixture of liquid and undissolved grains floating in it.
Tiny holes in a filter.

gewusst: Melitta Bentz made the first coffee filter from blotting paper from her son's school exercise book and a tin can with holes in it.
Mussels filter their food out of the water and can clean many litres of water every day as they do so.
With a pump that creates reduced pressure under the filter, filtering in the laboratory goes much faster.

teile.einleitung: Chromatography is a method for separating mixtures into their individual components. You can even try it at home with coffee filter paper, water and a felt tip pen. In laboratories it is used every day, for example to test food or doping samples.
wichtigste: Chromatography separates mixtures into their components.
The Greek word “chroma” means colour.
The substances travel different distances because they stick and dissolve to different degrees.
The moving solvent is called the mobile phase, and the paper the stationary phase.
Black felt tip ink often contains several colours.
At the beginning of the 20th century, the botanist Mikhail Tsvet was the first to separate leaf pigments.
The Rf value shows how far a substance travels compared with the solvent.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the Greek word **chroma**, which means colour, because the first experiments separated coloured substances. In chromatography, a mixture travels with a solvent through a material. The individual substances in the mixture travel at different speeds. This produces separate bands or spots of colour.

abschnitte.titel: An experiment with felt tip pens
abschnitte.text: You draw a dot with a **water soluble** felt tip pen on a strip of coffee filter paper. Then you stand the strip in a glass with a little water, so that the dot is just above the water. The water rises up the paper and carries the colours with it. You often discover that a black pen is really a mixture of blue, yellow, red or violet.

The solvent, which moves, is called the **mobile phase**. The paper, which stays where it is, is the **stationary phase**. Dyes that stick strongly to the paper stay lower down, while those that dissolve well in the solvent travel far up. The start line is drawn in pencil, because graphite does not dissolve in the solvent.

How far a substance travels is described by the **Rf value**. You divide the distance travelled by the dye by the distance travelled by the solvent front. If a dye travels 3 cm and the solvent front 6 cm, the Rf value is 0.5. Under the same conditions, each substance has a typical value, so substances can be identified.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the Russian botanist **Mikhail Tsvet** was the first to separate the pigments of green leaves. He let a leaf extract run through a glass tube filled with chalk powder and saw green and yellow bands. Tsvet had previously studied at the University of Geneva. The Britons Archer Martin and Richard Synge received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1952 for developing the method further.

In laboratories today, gas chromatography and liquid chromatography are used to separate tiny amounts of substances. In this way pollutants are found in drinking water, or food is checked for banned additives. At sports competitions, **doping** is detected with chromatography. The method is also essential in police work and in medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance made of several different substances.
The solvent that moves and carries the substances with it.
The material that stays where it is, for example paper.
A number that shows how far a substance travels compared with the solvent.

gewusst: The name Tsvet means “colour” in Russian, just as chroma does in Greek.
With modern chromatography, substances can be detected when only a billionth of a gram is present.

teile.einleitung: Carboxylic acids are organic acids that carry a special group of carbon, oxygen and hydrogen, the carboxyl group -COOH. They include well known substances such as acetic acid, formic acid and citric acid. Many of them occur in nature and give a sour taste or striking smells.
wichtigste: Carboxylic acids carry the carboxyl group -COOH.
Methanoic acid has the common name formic acid.
With a pKa of 3.75, methanoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid with a pKa of 4.76.
Butanoic acid is responsible for the smell of rancid butter.
Carboxylic acids have high boiling points, because pairs of molecules form dimers through hydrogen bonds.
The salts of acetic acid are called acetates.
Benzoic acid is used as the preservative E 210.
Oxalic acid is found in large amounts in rhubarb leaves.

abschnitte.text: Carboxylic acids consist of a carbon framework and the **carboxyl group** -COOH. Their names are formed from the name of the alkane with the ending “-oic acid”, for example methanoic acid, ethanoic acid or butanoic acid. Many also have old **common names**: methanoic acid is called formic acid, and ethanoic acid is called acetic acid. Acids with two carboxyl groups are called **dicarboxylic acids**; one example is oxalic acid.

The carboxyl group can give off a **proton**. This produces a negatively charged ion, the so called carboxylate ion. Carboxylic acids are mostly **weak acids**, which means they give off only part of their protons. Their strength is described with the pKa value: methanoic acid with 3.75 is stronger than acetic acid with 4.76.

Carboxylic acids boil at strikingly high temperatures. The reason: pairs of molecules hold together through two **hydrogen bonds** and form a **dimer**. Short carboxylic acids have a strong smell; acetic acid smells sharp and sour, and butanoic acid of rancid butter or sweat. Long chain carboxylic acids, the **fatty acids**, on the other hand, are almost odourless and are building blocks of fats and oils.

Ants squirt **formic acid** to defend themselves, and it is also found in the hairs of stinging nettles. Acetic acid is formed when bacteria turn the alcohol in wine or cider into it; vinegar contains about 5 per cent of it. Citric acid gives citrus fruits their sour taste. **Oxalic acid** is found in large amounts in rhubarb leaves, which is why only the stalks are eaten.

Many carboxylic acids and their salts are useful. As the preservative E 210, **benzoic acid** stops food going mouldy. The salts of acetic acid are called **acetates**; sodium acetate, for example, is found in hand warmers. When carboxylic acids react with alcohols, **esters** are formed, which often smell fruity and are used as flavourings.

abschnitte.titel: An acid with a special role
abschnitte.text: Methanoic acid is a special case among the carboxylic acids. Its molecule also contains a kind of **aldehyde group**. That is why, like an aldehyde, it can reduce other substances and gives a positive **Tollens' test**, in which a silver mirror forms. The other carboxylic acids do not show this reaction.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group -COOH that all carboxylic acids have in common.
An old, widely used name for a substance, such as acetic acid instead of ethanoic acid.
A carboxylic acid with a long carbon chain that is found in fats.
A substance formed from an acid and an alcohol, which often smells fruity.
A number for the strength of an acid; the smaller it is, the stronger the acid.

gewusst: The German name “Ameisensäure”, ant acid, comes from the fact that the acid used to be obtained from crushed ants.
The unpleasant smell of sweaty feet is partly due to short carboxylic acids.
The banana flavour in sweets often comes from an ester made from acetic acid.

teile.einleitung: The Gibbs free energy, also called free enthalpy, reveals whether a chemical reaction can take place by itself. It links two quantities: the heat that is released or taken in during a reaction, and the disorder, the entropy. It is named after the American physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs.
wichtigste: The Gibbs free energy of reaction is calculated with ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS.
At constant pressure and temperature, a reaction takes place spontaneously if ΔG is less than zero.
If ΔH is negative and ΔS positive, the reaction is spontaneous at any temperature.
Temperature can decide whether a reaction takes place spontaneously or not.
Through ΔG° = −R·T·ln K, the Gibbs free energy is linked to the equilibrium constant.
If ΔG° is exactly zero, the equilibrium constant K equals 1.
The Gibbs free energy is named after the American physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs.

abschnitte.text: **Josiah Willard Gibbs** lived from 1839 to 1903 and was a professor at Yale University in the USA. He is regarded as one of the founders of chemical **thermodynamics**, the study of energy and heat in the transformation of substances. In the 1870s he published papers on the equilibrium of substances. In them he introduced the quantity that bears his name today.

The change in Gibbs free energy is calculated with ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS. Here ΔH is the **enthalpy of reaction**, that is the heat given off or taken in. ΔS is the change in **entropy**, which can be described in simple terms as a measure of disorder. T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. If ΔG is negative, the reaction is called **exergonic** and can take place spontaneously; if ΔG is positive, it is called endergonic.

If ΔH is negative and ΔS positive, ΔG is always negative and the reaction takes place spontaneously at any temperature. If ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, the temperature decides. When lime is burnt, CaCO₃ breaks down into CaO and CO₂, with ΔH = +178 kJ/mol and ΔS = +161 J/(mol·K). The reaction only becomes spontaneous from about 1100 kelvin, that is at about 830 degrees Celsius. An everyday example: ice only melts by itself above 0 degrees Celsius.

In the ammonia synthesis N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, ΔH° = −92.2 kJ and ΔS° = −198.7 J/K. At 298 kelvin this gives ΔG° = −92.2 kJ − 298 K · (−0.1987 kJ/K), so about −33 kJ. The reaction is therefore spontaneous at room temperature. Because ΔS is negative, ΔG becomes less favourable at higher temperatures. Ammonia is an important starting material for fertiliser.

The Gibbs free energy is linked to the **equilibrium constant** K: ΔG° = −R·T·ln K. Here R is the gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K). If ΔG° equals zero, K is exactly 1. With ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol and 298 K, K comes out at about 10. The more negative ΔG°, the more products are present at equilibrium.

A negative ΔG only says that a reaction can take place, not how fast it does so. At room temperature, diamond should actually turn into graphite, but this takes an unimaginably long time. Wood does not burn by itself either, even though combustion is exergonic; it first needs a spark. How fast a reaction is depends on the **activation energy**, not on the Gibbs free energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The heat content of a system; ΔH is the heat given off or taken in during a reaction.
A quantity that, in simple terms, describes the disorder or spreading out of energy.
A reaction with a negative ΔG that can take place spontaneously.
Unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero; 0 degrees Celsius is 273.15 kelvin.
Energy needed for a reaction to start at all.

gewusst: Our cells couple reactions with a positive ΔG to the splitting of the energy carrier ATP, which has a strongly negative ΔG.
In 1863 Gibbs received the first doctorate in engineering ever awarded in the USA, at Yale University.
Diamonds are not quite stable thermodynamically, but they still stay diamonds practically for ever.

teile.einleitung: Chlorofluorocarbons, CFCs for short, are artificially made gases of carbon, fluorine and chlorine. They used to be found in fridges and spray cans, until researchers discovered that they destroy the protective ozone layer. Banning them worldwide is considered a great success for environmental protection.
wichtigste: CFCs are compounds of carbon, fluorine and chlorine.
Thomas Midgley developed them around 1930 as non toxic refrigerants.
In the stratosphere, ultraviolet radiation splits chlorine atoms off the CFCs.
A single chlorine atom can destroy about 100,000 ozone molecules.
The ozone hole over Antarctica was first described in 1985.
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 governs the phase out of CFCs.
Crutzen, Molina and Rowland received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 for their ozone research.

abschnitte.text: CFCs are small molecules in which one or two carbon atoms are bonded to **fluorine** and **chlorine**. A well known example is the refrigerant R-12, with the formula CCl₂F₂. They are non toxic, non flammable and very stable. That is why for decades they were used in fridges, air conditioning, spray cans and for foaming plastics.

The American chemist **Thomas Midgley** developed CFCs around 1930 as a safe refrigerant. Before that, fridges were cooled with poisonous or flammable gases such as ammonia. Midgley had earlier brought leaded petrol onto the market. Both inventions were at first seen as a blessing and later did great harm to the environment.

Because CFCs are so stable, they rise up into the **stratosphere**, 15 to 35 kilometres high. There, strong ultraviolet radiation splits off the chlorine atoms. A chlorine atom reacts with ozone: Cl + O₃ gives ClO + O₂; afterwards it is released again and destroys more ozone molecules. In this way a single chlorine atom can destroy about 100,000 ozone molecules, yet the **ozone layer** protects us from dangerous UV light.

As early as 1974, Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland warned of this danger. In 1985 British researchers first described the **ozone hole** over Antarctica, which opens there every spring. For their work, Paul Crutzen, Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995. In Arosa in the canton of Grisons, the ozone layer has been measured since 1926, one of the longest series of measurements in the world.

In the **Montreal Protocol** of 1987, countries agreed to ban CFCs step by step; today every country in the world takes part. The substitutes, the hydrofluorocarbons or HFCs, do not harm the ozone but are powerful **greenhouse gases**. That is why they too were restricted in 2016 by the Kigali Amendment. Experts expect the ozone layer over Antarctica to recover by around the 2060s.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas made of three oxygen atoms that absorbs UV radiation high up in the atmosphere.
A layer of the atmosphere at a height of about 15 to 50 kilometres.
A substance that takes in heat in fridges and carries it away.
A gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and so warms the climate.

gewusst: CFC molecules can last for over a hundred years in the atmosphere.
The Montreal Protocol was the first environmental treaty that all member states of the United Nations joined.
The ozone hole is not a real hole but an area in which the ozone layer has become very thin.
