teile.einleitung: Fire is produced when a substance burns with oxygen from the air and gives off light and heat as it does so. People have been using fire for hundreds of thousands of years for warmth, cooking and light. Fire is useful, but it can also be very dangerous.
wichtigste: Fire is burning in which light and heat are released.
A fire needs fuel such as wood, air with oxygen, and heat.
If you put a glass over a candle, it goes out, because there is no oxygen left.
When wood has burnt completely, ash is left over.
Wet wood makes a lot of smoke when it burns.
In case of fire in Switzerland, you call the fire brigade on 118.
Children may only light a fire together with adults.

abschnitte.text: A fire needs three things: a **fuel** such as wood, paper or wax, **oxygen** from the air and enough heat. This is called the fire triangle. If one of them is missing, the fire goes out. If you put a glass over a candle, the oxygen is soon used up, and the flame goes out.

Fire is a **chemical reaction**: the fuel combines with oxygen. This mainly produces carbon dioxide and water vapour, and light and heat are released. The parts that cannot burn are left over as **ash**. Wet wood burns badly and makes a lot of smoke, because the water has to evaporate first.

Early humans were already using fire several hundred thousand years ago. It gave warmth and light, kept wild animals away and made food easier to digest by cooking it. Later, fire was needed to melt metals and to fire pots. In Switzerland, bonfires burn on the hills on 1 August, and at the **Sechseläuten** in Zurich the Böögg, a snowman figure, is burnt.

In case of fire in Switzerland, you call the **fire brigade** at once on the number **118**. Most firefighters in Switzerland are volunteers who serve alongside their jobs. The important thing is: first get yourself to safety, then raise the alarm. Smoke is especially dangerous, because it is poisonous and you cannot see anything in it.

To put out a fire, you take away its heat, oxygen or fuel. Water cools, and a **fire blanket** smothers the flames. Burning fat in a pan must never be put out with water, because it sprays apart explosively; it is better to cover the pan. Smoke alarms in the home give early warning of a fire.

Matches, lighters and candles do not belong in children's hands without supervision. Children may only light a fire together with adults. When having a barbecue in the woods, you must use official fireplaces and obey fire bans in dry weather. Before you leave, you always put a fire out completely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical reaction of a substance with oxygen, which produces heat and light.
A substance that can burn, for example wood or gas.
The non burnable remains left over after a fire.
A fireproof blanket used to smother small fires.
A device that beeps loudly when there is smoke and so warns of fire.

gewusst: The flame of a candle is darker and cooler inside than at the edge.
The Böögg at the Sechseläuten is a snowman made of cotton wool that is filled with bangers.
Because there is no gravity on the space station, candle flames there are round like balls.

teile.einleitung: In an experiment, you try something out on purpose and watch closely what happens. This is how researchers find out how nature works. You can also do exciting experiments at home with simple things from the kitchen.
wichtigste: In an experiment, you try something out and observe.
Before the experiment, you write down a guess.
Afterwards you compare the result with the guess.
A good experiment can be repeated and gives the same result.
During an experiment you must never taste or eat anything without asking.
Many exciting experiments work with vinegar, salt, baking powder and water.
CERN near Geneva in Switzerland is one of the largest research laboratories in the world.

abschnitte.text: It starts with a **question**, for example: does an egg float in salt water? Then you write down a **guess**; experts call it a hypothesis. Now you carry out the test, watch closely and write everything down. At the end you compare the result with the guess.

In a good experiment, you only ever change one thing and keep everything else the same. If you want to know whether salt makes an egg float, you need a glass of salt water and a **comparison glass** of ordinary water. An experiment should be **repeated** several times to rule out chance. Other people should also get the same result with the same test.

If you pour vinegar onto baking powder, it **foams** strongly, because carbon dioxide is produced. A raw egg floats in very salty water, because salt water is denser than ordinary water. A gummy bear becomes much bigger overnight in water, because it soaks up water. A paper clip laid carefully on the surface of water can stay floating on top, thanks to **surface tension**.

abschnitte.titel: Red cabbage as a colour indicator
abschnitte.text: Red cabbage juice contains a dye that changes colour depending on the substance. If you mix it with vinegar, it turns **red**, because vinegar is an acid. With soapy water or bicarbonate of soda it turns blue to green. In this way you can test at home which liquids are acidic. Such a colour indicator is called an **indicator**.

You only do experiments with permission and preferably with an adult. You must never **taste or eat** anything without asking, even if it looks harmless. For tests with heat, fire or chemicals, you wear safety goggles. After the experiment you tidy up and wash your hands.

Famous researchers such as Galileo Galilei did experiments to test ideas, instead of relying only on old books. At **CERN** near Geneva, physicists make tiny particles collide in the LHC particle accelerator, which is almost 27 kilometres long. The Higgs particle was detected there in 2012. The World Wide Web was also invented at CERN.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned test to answer a question.
A guess that you check with an experiment.
Looking closely and writing down what happens.
A force that holds the surface of water together like a thin skin.

gewusst: Even an experiment in which the guess was wrong is a success, because you have learnt something.
Many discoveries were made by chance during experiments, for example penicillin.
The LHC at CERN lies about 100 metres deep underground, partly in France and partly in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Graphite is a soft, greyish black form of pure carbon. You use it almost every day, because the lead in a pencil is made of graphite. Although it is soft and greasy, it even conducts electricity.
wichtigste: Graphite consists of pure carbon, just like diamond.
Graphite is greyish black and feels smooth and greasy.
The lead in a pencil contains graphite and no actual lead.
The name comes from the Greek word for “to write”.
Graphite conducts electricity.
Graphite powder is good for lubricating sticking door locks.
A B on a pencil means that it writes soft and dark.

abschnitte.text: Graphite consists of many flat **layers**, in which the carbon atoms are arranged in hexagons like a honeycomb. Within a layer the atoms hold together very firmly. Between the layers, however, the forces are weak, so they slide easily over one another. That is why graphite is soft and feels greasy. Diamond also consists of carbon, but there the atoms are arranged quite differently, which is why it is extremely hard. Such different forms of the same element are called **allotropes**.

In the past, graphite was thought to be a kind of lead, which is why we still talk about pencil lead today. In reality the **lead** is made of graphite, which is mixed with clay and fired. A lot of clay makes the lead hard and light, shown by an **H**. A lot of graphite makes it soft and dark, shown by a **B**. When you write, fine flakes of graphite stay on the paper, which is why you can rub the line out. In Geneva the company Caran d'Ache has been making pencils and coloured pencils for many decades.

Electrons can move freely within the layers of graphite, so it conducts **electricity**. That is unusual for a non-metal. Graphite is therefore used for electrodes, for example in the batteries of mobile phones and electric cars. It also withstands very high temperatures without melting. That is why melting pots for metals are made from it.

Because the layers slide so easily, graphite powder is a good **lubricant**. It is sprayed, for example, into sticking door locks, where oil would attract dust. Graphite is also found in brake pads, seals and sports equipment such as tennis rackets. A single layer of graphite is called **graphene**. For research on graphene, two scientists received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.

Graphite occurs naturally in rocks and is mined, today mainly in China. It can also be made artificially from coal or petroleum coke. In the 16th century a particularly pure deposit of graphite was found at Borrowdale in England, and the first pencils were made with it. The mineral was given the name graphite in 1789 by the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner. He took it from the Greek word **graphein**, which means “to write”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical element of which graphite, diamond and coal are made.
One of several forms in which the same substance can occur.
The writing stick inside a pencil.
A part through which electricity flows into or out of a substance.
A single layer of graphite only one atom thick.

gewusst: Graphite and diamond consist of exactly the same element, but they are the softest and the hardest minerals known.
With a single pencil you can draw a line several kilometres long.
There has never been real lead in pencils.

teile.einleitung: Baker's yeast is a tiny fungus that makes dough for bread, plaited loaves and pizza light and airy. The yeast cells eat sugar and produce a gas that puffs up the dough. This process is called fermentation, and people have been using it for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Yeast is a tiny fungus made of single cells.
Yeast likes eating sugar best.
As it eats, it produces carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol; this is called fermentation.
The gas from the yeast makes the dough rise.
Yeast dough rises fastest in a warm place.
If yeast gets very hot, it dies.
The Swiss Sunday plaited loaf, the Zopf, is baked with yeast.
In the shops, fresh yeast is often sold as a cube.

abschnitte.text: Baker's yeast is a **yeast fungus** with the scientific name Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Each yeast cell is so small that you can see it only under a **microscope**. A gram of fresh yeast contains many billions of cells. Yeast reproduces when a small daughter cell grows out of a cell; this is called **budding**.

In the dough, enzymes break down some of the starch from the flour into sugar. The yeast eats this sugar and produces **carbon dioxide** and a little alcohol; this process is called **fermentation**. The gas forms many small bubbles that stay trapped in the stretchy dough. This is thanks to **gluten**, a sticky protein from wheat flour that works like an elastic net.

Yeast works best at a pleasant warmth, roughly between 25 and 35 °C. That is why yeast dough is left to rise in a **warm place**, often covered. In the fridge it rises more slowly but often gains more flavour. From about 50 °C the yeast dies, and during **baking** in the hot oven the alcohol evaporates too.

In the shops there is **fresh yeast**, usually as a small cube in the chiller cabinet. It is light brown, crumbly and keeps for only a few weeks. **Dried yeast** in a sachet keeps much longer, because the water has been removed from it. Both kinds make the dough airy, but you need a smaller amount of dried yeast.

Many Swiss families bake a **Zopf**, a plaited loaf of yeast dough with milk and butter, at the weekend. Bread, croissants, pizza and doughnuts are also made with yeast. Besides baking, yeast is used for beer and wine, because there too fermentation produces alcohol and fizz. Yeast also contains many **vitamins** of the B group.

As far back as ancient **Egypt**, several thousand years ago, people baked risen bread. But they did not know that tiny living things were responsible. Only in the 19th century did the French scientist **Louis Pasteur** show that yeast cells cause fermentation. After that, people began to grow and sell yeast on purpose.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which yeast turns sugar into gas and alcohol without oxygen.
A gas that puffs up the dough in bubbles.
A sticky protein in flour that makes the dough stretchy and holds in gas.
The way yeast cells reproduce, by a daughter cell growing out.

gewusst: The holes in bread are the traces of the gas bubbles made by the yeast.
Yeast was one of the first living things whose genetic material was completely decoded.
A single cube of yeast contains more yeast cells than there are people on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia. In them, one, two or three hydrogen atoms of ammonia are replaced by carbon groups. Many amines have a very noticeable smell, for example of fish, but they are also building blocks of dyes, medicines and substances in our body.
wichtigste: Amines contain a nitrogen atom to which carbon groups are attached.
Primary amines have the functional group -NH₂, the amino group.
Amines are divided into primary, secondary and tertiary amines by the number of carbon groups on the nitrogen.
Amines react as bases in water, because the lone pair on the nitrogen takes up a proton.
Trimethylamine causes the typical smell of fish.
Aniline is the simplest aromatic amine and was important for the dye industry.
With acids, amines form salts, for example methylammonium chloride from methylamine and hydrochloric acid.

abschnitte.text: Amines are derivatives of **ammonia** NH₃. If one hydrogen atom is replaced by a carbon group, a **primary amine** such as methylamine CH₃NH₂ is formed. With two groups it is called a secondary amine, and with three a tertiary amine. So what matters is how many carbon groups are attached directly to the nitrogen.

The nitrogen atom has a **lone pair** of electrons. With it, it can take up a proton, that is, a hydrogen ion. That is why amines react as bases in water, similarly to ammonia. With acids they form salts: methylamine and hydrochloric acid give **methylammonium chloride**. Such salts are usually odourless and dissolve well in water.

Small amines such as methylamine are gases at room temperature. Methylamine boils at about minus 6 °C, whereas methanol boils only at about 65 °C. The reason: between amine molecules, **hydrogen bonds** form through N-H, and these are weaker than the O-H bonds in the alcohol. Short amines dissolve well in water, but long carbon chains make them more soluble in fat.

Many amines smell very unpleasant. **Trimethylamine** is responsible for the smell of fish that is no longer quite fresh. When protein rots, **putrescine** and **cadaverine** are formed, which smell of decay. A tip from the kitchen: lemon juice on fish softens the smell, because the acid turns the amines into odourless salts.

**Aniline** is the simplest aromatic amine; an amino group is attached to a benzene ring. From the middle of the 19th century, brilliant **aniline dyes** were made from it. In Basel too, the chemical industry began with such coal tar dyes. Today aromatic amines are starting materials for plastics, dyes and medicines.

Amines are found everywhere in the body. Every **amino acid** carries an amino group, and proteins are built from amino acids. Messenger substances such as adrenaline, dopamine or histamine belong to the **biogenic amines**. They control, for example, the heartbeat, mood or defence reactions in allergies.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group -NH₂ attached to a carbon atom.
Two electrons on the nitrogen that form no bond and can capture a proton.
An amine with only one carbon group on the nitrogen.
A salt formed when an amine reacts with an acid.
An amine made in living things, for example a messenger substance.

gewusst: Methylamine is a gas at room temperature, even though it is almost as heavy as liquid methanol.
Lemon juice on fish works chemically: the acid binds the smelly amines as salts.
The name aniline comes from the indigo plant, which is called “anil” in Portuguese.

teile.einleitung: Gas chromatography, GC for short, is a method for separating and analysing mixtures of many substances. The substances are evaporated and travel with a carrier gas through a long, thin column, moving at different speeds. In this way even tiny amounts of a substance can be found in food, air or blood.
wichtigste: Gas chromatography is used to separate mixtures of substances and detect individual substances.
The substances must be able to evaporate without breaking down.
Helium is often used as the carrier gas.
A capillary column has a thin film of liquid on its inner wall as the stationary phase.
Under fixed conditions, the retention time is used to identify a substance.
A widely used detector is the flame ionisation detector.
Archer Martin and Richard Synge received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1952 for partition chromatography.

abschnitte.text: The word **chromatography** originally means colour writing, because the method was first developed with coloured plant substances. In gas chromatography, substances are separated that can be evaporated without breaking down. A gas, the **carrier gas**, pushes the evaporated mixture through a column. Helium is often used for this, sometimes also nitrogen or hydrogen.

The sample is injected, evaporates and enters a **capillary column**, a tube as fine as a hair and often 30 metres long. A thin film of liquid, the **stationary phase**, sticks to its inner wall. Each substance stays attached to it for a different length of time, rather like children who dawdle different amounts on the way to school. So the substances arrive at the end of the column one after another.

At the end of the column, a **detector** measures when and how much of a substance arrives. A widely used one is the flame ionisation detector, which detects organic substances as they burn in a hydrogen flame. The time from injection to arrival is called the **retention time** and is typical of each substance under fixed conditions. So that substances with high boiling points also arrive in a reasonable time, the oven temperature is often raised step by step.

The foundations were laid by the Britons Archer Martin and Richard Synge with partition chromatography, for which they received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1952. In the same year, Martin and Anthony James presented the first gas chromatography. **Ervin Kováts**, who later became a professor at EPFL, developed the retention index in 1958. It compares the retention time of a substance with that of simple hydrocarbons, the n-alkanes.

Gas chromatographs test food for residues of pesticides and examine air and water for pollutants. In doping tests in sport and in police work, they track down banned substances. Particularly powerful is the combination with a mass spectrometer, **GC-MS** for short, which separates substances and at the same time identifies them by their fragments. Fragrance companies in Switzerland also use GC to analyse the scents of flowers precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The gas that pushes the evaporated sample through the column.
The time a substance takes from injection to the detector.
A fixed layer in the column to which the substances stick for different lengths of time.
An instrument that recognises and reports arriving substances.

gewusst: A capillary column is as thin as a hair, but coiled up it fits into a small oven.
With gas chromatography, hundreds of different substances can be detected in a scent such as that of a rose.
Space probes have taken small gas chromatographs with them to examine the air and soil on other celestial bodies.

teile.einleitung: Decanting is a simple method for separating a mixture of a liquid and a solid. You wait until the solid has settled at the bottom and then carefully pour off the clear liquid. This works in the chemistry laboratory just as it does in the kitchen or with wine.
wichtigste: When decanting, you carefully pour off the liquid above the sediment.
First the solid must settle at the bottom; this is called sedimentation.
The method uses density: heavier particles sink to the bottom.
In the laboratory, the liquid is run down a glass rod so that nothing splashes.
Decanting separates less cleanly than filtering, because fine particles are easily carried along.
With old red wine, the wine is poured into a glass carafe, the decanter, to leave the deposit behind.
In sewage works, dirt settles in the primary settling tank, a principle like decanting.

abschnitte.text: Decanting is a **separation method** for mixtures of a liquid and an insoluble solid. Such a mixture is called a **suspension**, for example sand in water. First you let the container stand still. Then you pour off the clear liquid, and the sediment stays behind in the container.

Before you can decant, you need patience. The solid particles have a greater **density** than the liquid and therefore slowly sink to the bottom. This sinking is called **sedimentation**. Coarse grains of sand lie on the bottom after a few seconds, but fine clay can float in the water for hours. In laboratories, settling is often speeded up with a centrifuge, which spins the samples very fast.

abschnitte.titel: How it is done in the laboratory
abschnitte.text: You hold the beaker at a slant and pour off slowly and evenly. A **glass rod** at the rim of the glass guides the liquid cleanly into the next container without anything splashing. You stop before the sediment starts to run out. Because fine particles are often carried along, the liquid is sometimes filtered afterwards as well.

In older bottles of red wine, a sediment, the **deposit**, forms over the years. It consists of colour substances and tannins and tastes bitter. That is why the wine is poured slowly into a glass carafe, the **decanter**. The deposit stays behind in the bottle.

Decanting is done in the kitchen too, for example when you pour the water off boiled potatoes or lentils. In a **sewage works**, the waste water first flows slowly through the **primary settling tank**. There, undissolved dirt sinks to the bottom and is removed as sludge. When panning for gold in Swiss streams, the heavy gold is also separated from light sand because it sinks faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture in which solid particles float in a liquid, for example sand in water.
The sinking of solid particles in a liquid.
The solid substances that collect at the bottom of a container.
Tells you how heavy a substance is in relation to its volume.
Separating with a filter that holds back the solid particles.

gewusst: The word decanting comes from Latin and has to do with the spout or rim of a container.
When decanting wine, a candle is often kept burning under the neck of the bottle so that you can see when the deposit is coming.
Decanting is one of the oldest separation methods and was already used by the alchemists.

teile.einleitung: Caramel is melted and browned sugar with a sweet, slightly roasted taste. It forms when sugar is heated strongly, which changes the sugar chemically. Caramel is found in many sweets and desserts, from crème caramel to candied almonds.
wichtigste: Caramel is melted, brown sugar.
When sugar caramelises, it smells sweet and slightly roasted.
If you heat caramel for too long, it turns black and bitter.
Liquid caramel is hotter than boiling water and therefore dangerous.
Liquid caramel becomes hard as it cools.
For crème brûlée, sugar is sprinkled on the cream and browned with a flame.
Crème caramel, cream fudge and candied almonds are popular caramel treats.

abschnitte.text: Caramel forms when ordinary table sugar is heated strongly. The white sugar first melts into a clear liquid. With more heat it turns golden, then amber and finally brown. This process is called **caramelisation**.

From about 160 °C the sugar molecules start to break down and join together in new ways. Hundreds of new substances are formed, which provide **colour**, smell and flavour. At the same time water evaporates from the sugar. If it gets too hot, the sugar **chars**: it turns black, bitter and inedible.

For **crème caramel** (“Caramelköpfli” in Switzerland), liquid caramel is poured into little moulds and a custard is poured on top; when it is turned out, the sauce runs over the pudding. For crème brûlée, sugar on the cream is turned into a crunchy crust with a flame. **Cream fudge** (“Rahmtäfeli”) is cooked from sugar and cream until the mixture is light brown. Candied almonds from the fair have a coating of caramel.

Liquid caramel is much hotter than boiling water, which only reaches 100 °C. It also sticks to the skin and causes severe **burns**. Children should therefore only make caramel with adults. If you pour cold liquid into hot caramel, it can spit violently.

Strongly heated sugar is also used as a brown food colouring. This **caramel colour** colours cola, sauces and some breads dark, for example. On packaging it is listed with the number E 150. It hardly tastes sweet, because the sugar has been almost completely transformed.

What caramel is like after cooling depends on the temperature and the ingredients. Pure caramel sets glassy and hard like a boiled sweet. With cream and butter, a soft, chewy **toffee** or a sauce is made. As it cools, the mixture becomes firm because the molecules can no longer move freely.

begriffe.erklaerung: Browning sugar by heating it strongly.
A brown colouring made from strongly heated sugar, E 150.
The chemical name for ordinary table sugar.
A substance turning black because of too much heat.

gewusst: When it is being made, caramel can get hotter than 170 °C, almost twice as hot as boiling water.
Caramel contains hundreds of different flavour substances that were not in the sugar at all before.

teile.einleitung: In electroplating, an object is coated with a thin layer of metal with the help of electric current. This is how taps are chrome plated, jewellery is gold plated and screws are protected from rust. The process is named after the Italian researcher Luigi Galvani.
wichtigste: In electroplating, an object is coated with metal using current.
The object to be coated is connected to the negative terminal.
Ions of the coating metal are dissolved in the plating bath, so for silver, silver ions.
An anode made of the coating metal often slowly dissolves during the process.
The process is named after the Italian researcher Luigi Galvani.
Electroplating is used for decoration and often for protection against corrosion.
Before electroplating, the workpiece must be thoroughly cleaned and degreased.

abschnitte.text: The object is dipped into a bath of salt solution, the **electrolyte**, in which metal ions are dissolved. The object is connected to the negative terminal of a direct current source and so becomes the **cathode**. The positively charged metal ions move towards it, take in electrons and settle as a thin layer of metal. Often an **anode** made of the coating metal hangs at the positive terminal; it slowly dissolves and supplies new ions.

Depending on the metal, electroplating has its own name. In **chrome plating**, a hard, shiny layer of chromium is formed, for example on taps or bicycle handlebars. In zinc plating, a layer of zinc protects screws and sheet metal from rust, and in nickel plating a layer of nickel does. In gold and silver plating, jewellery, cutlery and watches get a precious coating.

Electroplating does not just make objects more attractive; it also protects them from **corrosion**, that is, from rust and other damage caused by air and water. Hard metal layers make surfaces more resistant to scratches. Cheap jewellery is often only gold plated, because a thin layer of gold is much cheaper than pure gold. In electronics, plug contacts get gold or silver layers so that the current flows well.

Before electroplating, the workpiece must be thoroughly cleaned and degreased. Even a fingerprint can stop the metal layer from sticking well at that spot. That is why a part often goes through several baths for cleaning, rinsing and pickling. The layers are usually only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick.

In the 18th century in Bologna, **Luigi Galvani** studied how frogs' legs twitch because of electricity. His fellow countryman Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800, which for the first time supplied a steady current. Soon afterwards it became possible to gold plate objects with this current. In Switzerland, electroplating is important, for example, in the watch industry, where cases and dials are coated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid with dissolved ions that can conduct electricity.
The negative terminal, where the metal is deposited during electroplating.
The slow destruction of a metal, for example by rust.
An electrically charged atom or molecule.

gewusst: Gold plating is often only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick, so much thinner than a hair.
Some people are allergic to nickel plated jewellery, which is why there are strict rules for nickel.
With a similar process, electroforming, you can make complete metal copies of objects.

teile.einleitung: A Brockenhaus is a shop that sells second hand things: furniture, crockery, clothes, books and toys. In Switzerland it is often simply called a “Brocki”. Anyone who shops there saves money and helps the environment, because things get a second life.
wichtigste: A Brockenhaus is a shop for second hand things.
In everyday Swiss speech it is called a “Brocki”.
The goods are mostly donations from private people.
Many Brockenhäuser are run by charitable organisations.
The profit often goes to social projects.
Reusing things saves raw materials, energy and waste.
The word comes from “Brocken”, meaning leftover pieces.

abschnitte.text: In a Brockenhaus you can find almost anything that people no longer need: **furniture**, lamps, plates, books, records, clothes and toys. The things are second hand but usually still in good condition. They are sold cheaply, often for just a few francs. Many people like going to the Brocki, because you can discover treasures and surprises there.

The German word **Brocken** means a piece or a leftover. The name goes back to a passage in the Bible saying that the leftover fragments should be gathered up so that nothing is lost. In the 19th century, church charities began to collect used items and pass them on. This led to the Brockenhäuser, which are known especially in **Switzerland**. In Germany people tend to say second hand shop instead.

Most Brockenhäuser receive their goods as **donations**. People drop things off or have them collected when a house is cleared, for example after a move. Staff check, clean and sort the things and give them a price. Many Brockis are run by charitable associations, churches or organisations such as the **Salvation Army**. In some, people work who are finding their way back into working life in this way.

Every object that goes on being used does not have to be made new. This saves **raw materials** such as wood, metal and crude oil, and a lot of energy too. In addition, less ends up in the rubbish and in the incinerator. This principle is called **reuse**; it is even better than recycling, because the object does not have to be taken apart at all.

In the Brocki you can see well what **materials** things were made of in the past and are made of today: porcelain, glass, brass, wood or plastic. Old pans made of copper or cast iron show that metals last a very long time. Plastics, on the other hand, often become brittle or discoloured over time. So a visit also becomes a little lesson in materials.

If you go to the Brocki, allow some time, because the goods on offer change all the time. With electrical appliances it is worth asking whether they have been tested. Things in good condition that you no longer need yourself can often be handed in there directly. This creates a **cycle** from which everyone benefits.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss short word for Brockenhaus.
Something you give away to help others.
Not aiming at profit for oneself but working for the good of everyone.
Using an object again instead of throwing it away.

gewusst: The word Brockenhaus is typical of Switzerland and hardly known in other countries.
Sometimes people discover valuable antiques in the Brocki for a small price.
Reusing things usually saves more energy than recycling.

teile.einleitung: Calcium is a chemical element with the symbol Ca. As a pure substance it is a silvery, fairly soft metal, but in nature it occurs only in compounds, for example in limestone. In our body, calcium is the building material for bones and teeth.
wichtigste: Calcium has the chemical symbol Ca.
Pure calcium is a silvery metal.
Our body needs calcium for bones and teeth.
Milk, cheese and green vegetables such as broccoli supply a lot of calcium.
Vitamin D helps the body to absorb calcium.
If you get too little calcium, your bones become brittle.
In nature, calcium is found in limestone, marble and gypsum.

abschnitte.text: Calcium has the **atomic number 20** and belongs to the **alkaline earth metals**. The pure metal has a silvery shine and is so soft that it can be cut with a knife. In air it quickly tarnishes, and with water it reacts, forming hydrogen. It was discovered and first made pure by the Englishman **Humphry Davy** in 1808.

Calcium is one of the most common elements in the Earth's crust. It is found above all in **limestone**, chalk and marble, which all consist of calcium carbonate. Gypsum also contains calcium. The **Jura** and many mountains of the Alps, for example in the Säntis area or on the Pilatus, consist largely of limestone, which formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures.

An adult has about one kilogram of calcium in their body. Almost all of it is in the **bones** and **teeth**, making them hard and strong. A small remainder is dissolved in the blood and is needed for muscles to work, for nerve signals and for blood clotting. If calcium is lacking over a long time, the bones become brittle; this is called **osteoporosis**.

Good sources of calcium are **milk**, yoghurt and above all **cheese**, of which a particularly large amount is eaten in Switzerland. Green vegetables such as broccoli and kale, nuts and some mineral waters also contain calcium. For the body to absorb it well, it needs **vitamin D**. The skin makes this vitamin itself when sunlight falls on it.

Calcium is also the reason why **limescale** builds up in the kettle or the shower. Water from limestone areas contains a lot of dissolved calcium and is called **hard water**. Limescale rings can be removed with vinegar or citric acid. In the building industry, quicklime is an important ingredient of mortar and cement.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of metals in the periodic table that includes calcium and magnesium.
The compound that limestone, chalk and eggshells are made of.
A disease in which the bones become thin and brittle.
Water with a lot of dissolved calcium and magnesium.

gewusst: Eggshells and seashells consist almost entirely of calcium carbonate.
The word calcium comes from the Latin “calx”, which means lime.
Calcium is the most common metal in the human body.

teile.einleitung: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist who set up one of the first periodic tables of the elements in 1869. He arranged the elements known at the time so cleverly that he could even predict elements that had not yet been discovered. Today his system hangs in almost every chemistry classroom in the world.
wichtigste: Dmitri Mendeleev came from Russia and was born in 1834.
In 1869 he presented his periodic table of the elements.
He arranged the elements mainly by their atomic mass.
If an element did not fit, he left gaps for elements not yet known.
The “eka-silicon” he predicted was later discovered as germanium.
At about the same time, the German chemist Lothar Meyer developed a similar system.
The element mendelevium was named in his honour.

abschnitte.text: Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev was born in 1834 in **Tobolsk** in Siberia. He was the youngest of many children in a large family. After his father's death, his mother took him to Saint Petersburg to study. Later he became **professor of chemistry** at the university there. He died in Saint Petersburg in 1907.

Mendeleev was writing a textbook and was looking for a way to order the roughly 60 elements known at the time. He sorted them by **atomic mass** and noticed that similar properties repeat at regular intervals. This repetition is called **periodicity**. He placed elements that behave similarly, such as lithium, sodium and potassium, one below the other. In March 1869 he presented his system to the Russian Chemical Society.

What was special about Mendeleev's system was the **gaps**. Where no known element fitted, he deliberately left a space. For these missing elements he even predicted properties such as atomic mass and density. He called them, for example, “eka-aluminium”, “eka-boron” and “eka-silicon”. Later they were discovered as **gallium** (1875), **scandium** (1879) and **germanium** (1886), and the values matched astonishingly well.

At the same time, the chemist **Lothar Meyer** in Germany was working on a similar arrangement. He stressed above all the regular change in properties such as atomic volume. The two scientists reached a very similar result independently of each other. In 1882 Mendeleev and Meyer jointly received the Davy Medal of the Royal Society in London.

Today the elements are no longer arranged by atomic mass but by **atomic number**, that is, the number of protons. But Mendeleev's basic idea has remained. Element 101, discovered in 1955, was named **mendelevium** in his honour. A crater on the Moon and a mineral also bear his name. In Russia he is still regarded as one of the country's greatest scientists.

begriffe.erklaerung: A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged according to their properties.
How heavy an atom of an element is.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus; it decides the place in the periodic table.
A pure substance made of only one kind of atom, for example gold or oxygen.

gewusst: A well known legend says that Mendeleev saw the order of the elements in a dream; whether this is true is uncertain.
Mendeleev sorted cards with the elements and their properties, rather like in a card game.
As well as chemistry, he worked on crude oil, balloon flights and precise weights and measures.

teile.einleitung: The Haber-Bosch process is a chemical process for making ammonia from the nitrogen in the air and hydrogen. Ammonia is used above all to make artificial fertiliser. Without this process, not nearly as many people in the world could be fed today.
wichtigste: In the Haber-Bosch process, ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen.
Fritz Haber discovered the reaction; the BASF engineer Carl Bosch made it usable on an industrial scale.
In 1913 the first large plant started operating in Oppau near Ludwigshafen.
The catalyst is mainly iron with promoters.
A reactor typically works at around 450 °C and very high pressure.
Today the hydrogen is usually obtained from natural gas by steam reforming.
The ammonia is separated off by cooling and liquefying it.
Gases that have not reacted are sent back into the reactor.

abschnitte.text: Plants need **nitrogen** to grow. Although the air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen, most plants cannot use it in this form. Around 1900 people feared that natural fertiliser would no longer be enough for the growing world population. With the Haber-Bosch process, nitrogen from the air can be turned into **ammonia**. From this, artificial fertiliser is made, with which a large part of the world’s food is grown today.

Around 1909 the German chemist **Fritz Haber** showed in the laboratory that ammonia can be made from nitrogen and hydrogen. The engineer **Carl Bosch** of the company BASF turned this into a process for huge factories. In 1913 the first large plant started up in Oppau near Ludwigshafen. Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the year 1918, Bosch in 1931. Haber is still controversial today, because he pushed for the use of poison gas in the First World War.

Nitrogen and hydrogen are strongly compressed, to about 150 to 300 bar. In the **reactor** they flow at around 450 °C over a **catalyst** made of iron with additives, the promoters. The reaction does give off heat, but at room temperature it would be far too slow. On each pass, only part of the gases turns into ammonia. The gas mixture is cooled so that the ammonia becomes liquid and runs off, and the remaining gases are sent back into the reactor in a **loop**.

The nitrogen is obtained from the air. Today the **hydrogen** is usually made from natural gas with a process called **steam reforming**. This produces a lot of carbon dioxide, which harms the climate. Worldwide, the Haber-Bosch process uses about one to two per cent of all energy. Researchers are working on obtaining the hydrogen from water in future, using electricity from sun and wind.

Experts estimate that without artificial fertiliser only about half as many people could be fed. Ammonia is also used to make plastics, medicines and, unfortunately, explosives too. However, too much fertiliser on the fields can pollute lakes and groundwater, for example with **nitrate**. In Switzerland, farmers therefore follow rules about how much fertiliser they may use. The process is regarded as one of the most important inventions of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sharp-smelling gas made of nitrogen and hydrogen, the basic material for fertiliser.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
The name for a reaction that gives off heat.
A process for making hydrogen from natural gas and steam.
Fertiliser made in factories, containing nutrients for plants.

gewusst: A considerable part of the nitrogen in your body has at some point passed through the Haber-Bosch process.
For the process, engineers had to develop new steel pipes that could withstand the high pressure and the hydrogen.
Ammonia is one of the chemicals produced in the largest quantities in the world.

teile.einleitung: Rubber is a stretchy material that springs back into its old shape after being pulled. Natural rubber comes from the milky sap of the rubber tree. Tyres, wellington boots, rubbers for erasing, balloons and shoe soles are made of rubber.
wichtigste: The special thing about rubber is that it is stretchy.
Natural rubber is obtained from the sap of a tree.
The milky sap of the rubber tree is called latex.
The rubber tree originally grows in the rainforest of South America.
Rubber does not let water through, which is why people like to wear wellington boots in the rain.
With a rubber you rub out pencil lines.
Balloons and the soles of trainers are usually made of rubber.

abschnitte.text: The **rubber tree** comes from the Amazon rainforest in South America. If you cut its bark at a slant, a white, milky sap flows out, called **latex**. From this the raw material **natural rubber** is obtained. Today most rubber plantations are in South East Asia, for example in Thailand and Indonesia. The workers collect the sap in small cups that hang on the trees.

Raw natural rubber is sticky when hot and hard and brittle when cold. In 1839 the American **Charles Goodyear** discovered that natural rubber becomes much better if it is heated with sulphur. This process is called **vulcanisation**. The long chains in the rubber link up with each other like a net. Only then does natural rubber become elastic, durable rubber.

Today a large part of rubber is made artificially from **crude oil**. This is called synthetic rubber. It was developed in the 20th century, when natural rubber was scarce or expensive. For many products, natural and synthetic rubber are mixed. Experts count rubber among the **elastomers**, that is plastics that can be stretched and spring back.

More than half of all rubber is used for the **tyres** of cars, lorries and bicycles. Wellington boots keep your feet dry because rubber does not let water through. Rubber soles on trainers cushion and do not slip. Seals, hoses, gloves, balls and balloons are also made of rubber. A **rubber** for erasing picks up the fine graphite particles of a pencil line and rubs them off the paper.

Old tyres can be made into rubber granules, for example for playground surfaces and artificial grass. Tyres wear down as you drive, and the fine **tyre wear particles** get into the environment as microplastics. A lot of rainforest in South East Asia has been cleared for new rubber plantations. Some people are allergic to natural latex, for example in gloves. For them there are products made of synthetic rubber.

begriffe.erklaerung: The raw material from which rubber is made.
The milky sap of the rubber tree.
Heating natural rubber with sulphur so that it becomes elastic and durable.
A material that can be stretched and springs back into its shape.

gewusst: In 1770 the English scientist Joseph Priestley noticed that you can rub out pencil lines with natural rubber.
Indigenous peoples of South America were playing with balls made of natural rubber centuries ago.
The English word “rubber” comes from “to rub”.

teile.einleitung: Freezing is the process in which a liquid becomes solid because it cools down. For water, this happens at 0 degrees Celsius, and liquid water turns into solid ice. That sounds simple, but water behaves in a very special way when it does so.
wichtigste: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and becomes solid.
When water freezes, the water particles arrange themselves into regular ice crystals.
Ice needs more room than liquid water, which is why it floats.
A full glass bottle can burst in the freezer, because the water expands.
Lakes freeze from the top downwards.
Hoar frost forms when water vapour settles as fine ice crystals on cold mornings.

abschnitte.text: In liquid water, the tiny water particles move freely about among each other. When the water gets colder, the particles slow down. At 0 degrees Celsius they hold on to each other and form a fixed lattice called an **ice crystal**. The opposite process, when ice becomes liquid again, is called **melting**.

Almost all substances get smaller when they become solid, but water does the opposite. Ice needs about a tenth more room than the same amount of liquid water. That is why a full glass bottle can **burst** in the freezer. Freezing water in cracks in rock can even split stones apart; this is called **frost weathering**.

Because ice is lighter than water, it floats on top. That is why a lake freezes over at the **surface** first. Under the ice, the water at the bottom stays about 4 degrees warm, so fish can survive the winter. A pond only freezes over when it has been very cold for a long time, and you may only go on the ice when it has been officially declared safe.

abschnitte.titel: Hoar frost, snow and frost flowers
abschnitte.text: On cold mornings there are often fine ice crystals on the grass and on car windows; this is **hoar frost**. It forms when water vapour from the air turns straight into ice. Snowflakes are frozen water vapour too and usually have six arms. Beautiful patterns sometimes form on cold windows, which are called **frost flowers**.

In the **freezer** it is about minus 18 degrees, so food stays fresh for a long time. If you pour squash into a mould with a stick, after a few hours you have an ice lolly. In winter, salt is spread on the roads, because salt water only freezes at lower temperatures. Cars need **antifreeze** in the cooling water so that the engine is not damaged.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid becomes solid. For water it is 0 degrees Celsius.
A tiny, regularly built piece of ice.
Fine ice crystals that settle on grass and objects on cold mornings.
When freezing water in cracks pushes stones apart.

gewusst: The Celsius scale was set so that water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees.
Very pure water can be carefully cooled below 0 degrees without freezing; this is called supercooled water.
Because of the salt, seawater only freezes at about minus 2 degrees.

teile.einleitung: An endothermic reaction is a chemical reaction that takes in energy from its surroundings, usually in the form of heat. That is why things often get cold during it, or energy has to be supplied all the time. The opposite is the exothermic reaction, which gives off energy, like a fire.
wichtigste: An endothermic reaction takes in energy.
The Greek prefix “endo” means inside or into.
The enthalpy of reaction of an endothermic reaction has a positive sign.
In the energy diagram, the products lie higher than the starting substances.
Photosynthesis is endothermic; plants use sunlight for it.
Lime burning is endothermic, which is why the kiln has to be heated strongly all the time.
If the energy supply stops, the endothermic reaction stops too.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek “endo” for inside and “thermos” for warm. In an **endothermic reaction**, heat is therefore taken into the system. Afterwards the products contain more energy than the starting substances. The **enthalpy of reaction** ΔH is therefore positive. With an **exothermic** reaction it is the other way round: it gives off energy and ΔH is negative.

In an **energy diagram**, you plot the energy of the substances over the course of the reaction. In an endothermic reaction, the products lie higher than the starting substances. In addition, every reaction needs a push at the start, the **activation energy**. With endothermic reactions, however, you do not just have to give a push but must supply energy continuously. If the energy supply stops, the reaction comes to a standstill.

The most important endothermic reaction on Earth is **photosynthesis**. Green plants build glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water. The energy needed comes from **sunlight**, which is captured by the green leaf pigment chlorophyll. The stored energy is later used by plants, animals and people as food.

In **lime burning**, limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated to about 900 °C. It breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide, and for this the kiln has to be heated strongly the whole time. Such reactions also take place at very high temperatures in Swiss cement works. In the **electrolysis** of water, electric current supplies the energy to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. If you switch off the current, the splitting stops at once.

**Instant cold packs** for sports injuries contain a salt and a small pouch of water. If you bend the pack, the pouch bursts and the salt dissolves in the water. This dissolving takes in heat, and the pack goes cold within seconds. Sherbet powder also feels slightly cool on the tongue, because it takes in a little heat as it fizzes. In baking, too, bicarbonate of soda breaks down in the heat in an endothermic reaction and makes the dough rise.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reaction that gives off energy, usually heat, to its surroundings.
The amount of heat taken in or given off in a reaction, abbreviated ΔH.
The energy needed for a reaction to start at all.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen.

gewusst: Melting ice also takes in heat, which is why ice cubes cool a drink so well.
Some cold packs can cool to well below room temperature within a few seconds, without a fridge.
Many substances in our food were originally built up with solar energy by endothermic photosynthesis.

teile.einleitung: The aluminium works at Chippis in Valais is one of the best known industrial plants in Switzerland. It was opened in 1908 and made the small village on the Rhone an important place for aluminium production. The history of the works shows how hydropower from the Alps brought industry into the mountain valleys.
wichtigste: Chippis is in the canton of Valais on the Rhone, right next to Sierre.
The aluminium works was opened in 1908.
It was built from 1905 by the Aluminium-Industrie AG, AIAG for short.
AIAG had begun producing aluminium in Neuhausen am Rheinfall in 1888.
The works was built in Valais because of the hydropower, which supplied a lot of electricity.
In 1917 about 1700 workers went on strike at the works.
From 1963 the company was called Alusuisse.

abschnitte.text: Chippis is a small municipality in the district of Sierre in central Valais. It lies on the left bank of the **Rhone**, where the Navizence flows out of the Val d'Anniviers into the Rhone valley. The area is part of the French speaking region of Valais. The large factory halls still shape the look of the place today.

Making aluminium by **electrolysis** needs an enormous amount of electric current. Around 1900, electricity could hardly be transported over long distances, so the works had to stand close to the power stations. Valais had steep valleys and lots of water from the glaciers, ideal for **hydroelectric power stations**. That is why AIAG built power stations on the Navizence and the Rhone, which supplied the works with electricity.

The **Aluminium-Industrie AG** (AIAG) had opened one of the first aluminium smelters in Europe in Neuhausen am Rheinfall in 1888. Because the electricity there was no longer enough, from 1905 it built the new works in Chippis, which was opened in 1908. The works grew quickly and gave work to thousands of people from Valais and from further afield. Many mountain farmers worked there as well as on their farms; they were called worker farmers.

The work at the hot electrolysis furnaces was hard, wages were low, and during the First World War prices rose sharply. In 1917 about 1700 workers downed tools and demanded better conditions. The **strike** was one of the great labour disputes in Switzerland at that time. It shows how much industrialisation changed life in Valais.

In the past, aluminium production gave off exhaust gases containing **fluorine**, which damaged forests, fruit trees, vines and animals in the surrounding area. Farmers in the Rhone valley complained about damage, which led to disputes and compensation payments for decades. Only with better filter systems did the pollution fall significantly. The example of Chippis shows that industry brings prosperity but also means responsibility for the environment.

From 1963 the company was called **Alusuisse** and was one of the largest Swiss industrial companies, with works all over the world. At the end of the 20th century, Alusuisse was merged with foreign companies and renamed several times. Electrolysis, that is, the production of new aluminium, has since been given up in Valais. But in Chippis and Sierre aluminium is still processed, for example into sheets and profiles for cars and aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: Breaking down a substance with electric current; this is how aluminium is obtained.
A plant that produces electricity from flowing water.
A collective stopping of work to achieve better conditions.
The name of the Swiss aluminium company from 1963.

gewusst: In its first decades, the works in Chippis was one of the largest employers in the whole of Valais.
Next to the works, houses for the workers' families were built in Chippis, which made the village grow a great deal.
Without the hydropower of the Alps, Switzerland would never have been one of Europe's early aluminium countries.

teile.einleitung: Green chemistry is a way of doing chemistry that produces as little waste, poison and energy use as possible. It does not only ask whether a reaction works, but also how clean and economical it is. In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner summed up their ideas in twelve principles.
wichtigste: Green chemistry aims to avoid waste instead of disposing of it later.
In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner formulated the twelve principles of green chemistry.
In 1991 Barry Trost introduced the idea of atom economy.
Addition reactions in principle have an atom economy of 100 per cent.
Roger Sheldon’s E factor shows how many kilograms of waste are produced per kilogram of product.
Catalysts are not used up and therefore save waste.
Supercritical carbon dioxide serves as an environmentally friendly solvent, for example when decaffeinating coffee.

abschnitte.text: The chemical industry makes medicines, plastics, paints and fertilisers. In the past this often produced large amounts of **waste** and poisonous by-products. Green chemistry wants to plan processes so that such problems do not arise in the first place. Important aims are fewer dangerous substances, less energy use and more **renewable raw materials**. The idea behind it is: prevention is better than clearing up.

In 1998 the US chemists **Paul Anastas** and **John Warner** published twelve principles of green chemistry. They include, for example: avoid waste, use substances that are as non-toxic as possible, and work at room temperature. Other rules call for safe solvents and for products that break down in nature after use. The principles are not laws but a kind of checklist for good chemistry. Today they are taught at many universities, including in Switzerland.

**Atom economy** was introduced by Barry Trost in 1991. It shows what percentage of the atoms from the starting substances ends up in the desired product. In the reaction of bromomethane with sodium hydroxide solution to give methanol and sodium bromide, it is only about 24 per cent; the rest becomes by-product. In **addition reactions**, in which two molecules simply join together, it is in principle 100 per cent. Roger Sheldon’s **E factor**, on the other hand, measures the amount of waste: if 50 kg of waste are produced for 2 kg of product, it is 25.

**Catalysts** speed up reactions without being used up themselves. That is why only small amounts of them are needed, which saves a lot of waste compared with substances that have to be added in large quantities. One example is **olefin metathesis**, for which Yves Chauvin, Robert Grubbs and Richard Schrock received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2005. The Nobel Committee called it a great step forward for green chemistry. Instead of poisonous solvents, water or **supercritical carbon dioxide** is often used today, which behaves like a liquid under high pressure.

When coffee is decaffeinated, supercritical carbon dioxide dissolves the caffeine out of the beans and then simply evaporates again. For the painkiller ibuprofen, an older process with six steps was replaced by a new one with only three steps, which produces much less waste. Washing powders contain enzymes that allow clothes to be washed clean even at low temperatures. Plastics made from plants and biodegradable packaging are also among the aims of green chemistry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The proportion of atoms from the starting substances that end up in the desired product.
Kilograms of waste per kilogram of product.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A liquid in which other substances dissolve.
A substance under high pressure and high temperature that is neither really a gas nor really a liquid.

gewusst: In the production of some medicines, 25 to over 100 kilograms of waste are produced per kilogram of active ingredient.
The carbon dioxide that decaffeinates coffee can be used again and again.
In the USA there has been a special award for particularly green chemical processes since 1996.

teile.einleitung: A battery is a small energy store that turns chemical energy into electrical energy. It is found in torches, remote controls and toys. Batteries that can be recharged are called rechargeable batteries.
wichtigste: In a battery, chemical energy is turned into electrical energy.
Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.
An ordinary AA alkaline battery has a voltage of 1.5 volts.
When the battery discharges, electrons flow from the negative terminal into the circuit.
Most mobile phones and electric cars contain lithium ion batteries.
Old batteries do not belong in the household rubbish, because they contain pollutants and valuable metals.
In Switzerland, shops must take back used batteries free of charge.

abschnitte.text: A battery consists of one or more **galvanic cells**. Each cell has two different materials as terminals and, between them, an **electrolyte** that conducts charged particles. If you connect the positive and negative terminals through a device, current flows. Meanwhile chemical reactions take place in the battery until the materials are used up.

At the **negative terminal**, electrons are released that travel through the wire to the positive terminal. This flow of electrons drives a lamp or a motor. The **voltage**, measured in volts, shows how strongly the battery pushes the electrons. An AA alkaline battery has 1.5 volts, and a 9 volt block battery consists of several small cells inside.

Around 1800 the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta built the **voltaic pile**. He stacked discs of zinc and copper on top of each other, separated by card soaked in salt water. This was the first battery to supply a steady current. The unit of voltage, the **volt**, is named after him.

A **rechargeable battery** is a battery that can be charged up again. During charging, the chemical reactions run backwards. Today mobile phones, laptops and electric cars mostly contain **lithium ion batteries**, which store a lot of energy in a small space. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their development was awarded in 2019.

Old batteries contain **pollutants** such as heavy metals, but also valuable metals such as zinc, nickel or lithium. That is why they never belong in the household rubbish. In Switzerland, all shops that sell batteries must take back used batteries free of charge. This is paid for through an **advance recycling fee**, which you pay when you buy them.

Batteries must not be opened, thrown into a fire or short circuited. Damaged lithium batteries can get very hot and even catch fire. Button batteries are dangerous for small children if they are swallowed. That is why they are kept safely, and it is best to tape over the terminals of old batteries before disposing of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a battery drives the current, measured in volts.
A substance in the battery that conducts charged particles.
A battery that can be charged up again.
One of the two connections of a battery, plus or minus.

gewusst: A potato or a lemon with two different metals stuck in it can be a tiny battery.
The word battery originally meant a group of cannons, that is, several identical things together.
In Switzerland, a large part of the batteries collected is turned back into metals.

teile.einleitung: The Erlenmeyer flask is a typical glass vessel from the chemistry laboratory. It has a flat bottom, a cone shaped body and a narrow neck. It is named after the German chemist Emil Erlenmeyer.
wichtigste: The Erlenmeyer flask is named after the chemist Emil Erlenmeyer.
It is cone shaped and has a flat bottom.
Thanks to the flat bottom, it stands on the table without a stand.
The narrow neck lets you swirl the contents without spilling.
In a titration, the burette drips a solution into the Erlenmeyer flask.
To measure liquids exactly, a measuring cylinder is used.
The filter flask is a thick walled Erlenmeyer flask with a side arm.

abschnitte.text: An Erlenmeyer flask has a wide, flat **bottom** and narrows like a cone towards the top. At the top it ends in a narrow **neck**, which can be closed with a stopper. Most flasks are made of heat resistant **borosilicate glass**. They come in many sizes, from a few millilitres to several litres.

Emil Erlenmeyer was a German chemist in the 19th century. He presented the flask named after him around 1860. Erlenmeyer worked mainly in **organic chemistry**, that is, with carbon compounds. His flask can still be found in almost every laboratory in the world today.

The narrow neck lets you **swirl** liquids vigorously without anything splashing out. The flat bottom makes sure the flask stands safely on the table or on a hotplate. A **round bottomed flask**, on the other hand, needs a stand or a cork ring. In addition, less liquid evaporates through the small opening.

In a **titration**, you find out how much of a substance is in a solution. The sample goes into the Erlenmeyer flask, often together with a dye, the **indicator**. From a **burette** you slowly drip in a second solution while swirling the flask. When the colour changes, you read off the burette how much you have used.

Many Erlenmeyer flasks have lines printed on them, but these show the volume only roughly. For exact amounts you use a **measuring cylinder** or a pipette. A special form is the **filter flask**, with thick walls and a side arm. It is used for filtering under reduced pressure, because it does not implode.

begriffe.erklaerung: A method for finding out the amount of a substance in a solution.
A long, thin glass tube with a tap and a scale for adding liquid drop by drop exactly.
A particularly heat resistant glass for the laboratory.
A dye that shows a change by changing colour.

gewusst: The Erlenmeyer flask is so typical that it is often used as a symbol for chemistry.
In biology, bacteria and yeasts are also grown in Erlenmeyer flasks.
Because the flask narrows at the top, it is easy to close with a ball of cotton wool or aluminium foil.

teile.einleitung: Concrete is an artificial stone made by mixing cement, gravel, sand and water. When fresh it is runny like porridge, and after a while it becomes rock hard. Houses, bridges, tunnels and dams are made largely of concrete.
wichtigste: Concrete is mixed from cement, gravel, sand and water.
Cement is a grey powder that acts as a binder.
Fresh concrete becomes hard after a while.
Liquid concrete is poured into a mould made of boards, the formwork.
Steel bars inside the concrete make it even stronger.
The concrete mixer lorry brings the concrete to the building site with a turning drum.
The Romans already knew a kind of concrete.

abschnitte.text: Concrete consists of **cement**, aggregate such as gravel and sand, and water. Cement is a grey powder made by burning limestone and clay at a very high temperature and then grinding them. Gravel and sand form the framework, and the cement glues everything together. Concrete is therefore a kind of artificial **stone**.

Concrete does not simply get hard by drying. The cement reacts chemically with the water; this is called **hydration**. Tiny crystals grow and lock into one another. After a few weeks the concrete has almost its full strength, and it even hardens under water.

The **concrete mixer lorry** brings fresh concrete to the building site. Its drum turns all the time so that the concrete does not get hard too early. On the site it is poured into **formwork**, a mould made of boards or metal panels. A vibrator is used to remove air bubbles so that the concrete becomes dense.

Concrete can withstand enormous pressure, but it breaks easily when it is pulled or bent. That is why **steel bars** are laid inside it to take up the pulling forces. This produces **reinforced concrete**, which is used for ceilings, bridges and tower blocks. In 1867 the French gardener Joseph Monier patented concrete plant tubs with iron inserts.

More than 2000 years ago, the **Romans** were already making a kind of concrete from lime, volcanic ash and stones. The dome of the Pantheon in Rome is made of it and still stands today. After the end of the Roman Empire, this technique was largely forgotten. Only in the 19th century, with modern cement, did people build a lot with concrete again.

In Switzerland, huge amounts of concrete are found in dams, tunnels and bridges. The **Grande Dixence** dam in Valais is one of the highest dams in the world. The Gotthard Base Tunnel is also lined with concrete. Because making cement releases a lot of CO₂, experts are researching more climate friendly kinds of concrete and recycled concrete.

begriffe.erklaerung: A grey powder that hardens with water and holds concrete together.
A mould made of boards into which liquid concrete is poured.
Concrete with steel bars inside it, which is particularly strong.
The chemical reaction of cement with water.

gewusst: After water, concrete is the material that humanity uses most.
The Pantheon dome in Rome is still the largest dome made of unreinforced concrete.
Concrete can even harden under water, which is why it is also used to build bridge piers in rivers.

teile.einleitung: With invisible ink you can write messages that cannot be seen on the paper. Only with a trick, such as heat or a colour, does the writing reappear. Behind it is exciting chemistry that you can try at home with lemon juice.
wichtigste: Invisible ink is a liquid whose writing is invisible once it has dried.
A simple invisible ink is lemon juice; milk works too.
It is best to write with a cotton bud.
Heat makes lemon writing visible and turns it brown.
Candle wax writing on white paper becomes visible when you paint over it with watercolour.
Writing in bicarbonate of soda water appears in colour when you brush red cabbage juice over it.
In the past, people used invisible ink for secret messages.

abschnitte.text: The best-known invisible ink is **lemon juice**. You dip a cotton bud into it and write with it on white paper. Once it has dried, almost nothing can be seen. If you warm the paper, for example with a hairdryer or an iron, the writing appears in brown. Milk, apple juice or onion juice also work in this way.

Lemon juice and milk contain sugar and other **organic substances**. When heated, these start to brown earlier than the paper, much like sugar when it caramelises. In addition, the acid in lemon juice makes the paper fibres more sensitive where you have written. So the writing turns brown while the rest of the paper stays light. Important: only heat it with the help of adults and never hold it over an open flame.

A completely different trick works with a white **candle**. You write firmly on white paper with the tip of the candle; the writing can hardly be seen. If you then paint over the sheet with watercolour, the paint runs off the wax in drops. Wax is **water-repellent**, so the writing stays white while the paper around it takes on colour.

Red cabbage juice contains dyes that change colour depending on whether a substance is acidic or alkaline. Such a substance is called an **indicator**. If you write with bicarbonate of soda water, which is alkaline, and then brush red cabbage juice over it, the writing appears greenish or blue. If you write with lemon juice or vinegar instead, the writing turns pink to red. This way you can even send coloured secret messages.

As early as ancient times, scholars described how you can write invisibly with plant juices. Over the centuries, merchants, diplomats and spies used invisible inks to hide messages. Especially in the two World Wars, secret messages were written between the harmless lines of a letter. Hiding messages is called **steganography**. Today digital encryption is usually used instead.

There are pens with ink that only glows under **UV light**; often a small lamp is built right in. Similar substances protect banknotes against forgery: on Swiss franc notes, certain patterns light up under UV light. Entry stamps at concerts or festivals are also often only visible under UV light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ink that is invisible after drying and only becomes visible through a trick.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether something is acidic or alkaline.
A surface on which water forms drops and runs off instead of soaking in.
The art of hiding messages so that nobody notices they exist.
Light that is invisible to humans and makes some substances glow.

gewusst: With red cabbage juice you can create different colours in a single message, depending on whether you wrote with something acidic or alkaline.
Sweat from your fingers also leaves invisible traces, which the police can make visible with special powders.
Many banknotes contain fibres that only glow in colour under UV light.

teile.einleitung: Basel is the most important centre of the chemical and pharmaceutical industry in Switzerland. Over 150 years, small dye factories on the Rhine grew into world famous companies such as Novartis, Roche and Syngenta. Their medicines and research laboratories still shape the city today.
wichtigste: The Basel chemical industry began in the 19th century with the making of dyes.
Geigy goes back to a trading house for drugs and dyes that existed from 1758.
Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche founded his company in Basel in 1896.
In 1996 Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz merged to form Novartis.
In 2000 the agrochemical company Syngenta was formed in Basel.
The Rhine was very important for the Basel chemical industry as a transport route and a source of water.
On 1 November 1986 a chemical warehouse burned at Schweizerhalle and poisoned the Rhine.
At 205 metres, the Roche Tower Building 2 is the tallest building in Switzerland (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: From about 1859, Basel firms made artificial **dyes** from coal tar, which were used to dye fabrics for the textile and silk ribbon industry. Basel was well placed on the **Rhine**, close to the borders with France and Germany. The river supplied water for the factories and served as a transport route for raw materials. The dye firms grew into the companies **Ciba**, Geigy and Sandoz.

**Geigy** goes back to a trading house for drugs and dyes that existed from 1758. **Sandoz** was founded in 1886, and in 1896 Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche founded the firm **Roche**. Over time the firms turned more and more to medicines. In 1970 Ciba and Geigy joined to form Ciba-Geigy.

In 1996 Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz merged to form **Novartis**, one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world. The agricultural division, which makes products for crop protection, was combined with a British partner in 2000 to form **Syngenta**. Other parts became separate firms, such as the speciality chemicals company Clariant. Today Novartis and Roche are two of the most valuable companies in Switzerland.

A lot of research is done in Basel. The Geigy chemist **Paul Hermann Müller** discovered that the substance DDT kills insects, and in 1948 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it. At the time DDT helped to fight diseases such as malaria, but it was later banned in many countries because of the damage it does to the environment. Today Basel researchers develop above all medicines against cancer, eye diseases or disorders of the nervous system.

In the night of **1 November 1986**, a warehouse belonging to the firm Sandoz burned at Schweizerhalle near Basel. With the water used to fight the fire, large amounts of poisonous chemicals got into the **Rhine**, which turned red. Fish and eels died along many kilometres. After this disaster, safety regulations were tightened, and the countries along the Rhine worked together more closely for a clean river.

The pharmaceutical industry is one of the most important employers in the Basel region. The Roche towers **Building 1** and **Building 2** shape the skyline; at 205 metres, Building 2 is the tallest building in Switzerland (as of 2025). On the **Novartis Campus** there are office buildings by famous architects. Medicines and chemicals are among the most important exports of the whole of Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of industry that researches and makes medicines.
The joining of two companies to form a new one.
An artificial dye originally made from coal tar.
Chemistry for farming, such as fertilisers and crop protection products.

gewusst: After the Schweizerhalle fire in 1986, the Rhine turned red from dyes that had leaked out.
Many Basel pharmaceutical firms began not with medicines but with colours for fabrics.
The discovery for which a Nobel Prize went to Basel in 1948 was made by the Basel chemist Paul Hermann Müller.

teile.einleitung: In an elimination reaction, a small molecule such as water or hydrogen bromide is split off from a molecule. A double or triple bond is formed as a result. Elimination is therefore the opposite of addition and an important method for making alkenes.
wichtigste: In an elimination, a small molecule is split off and a multiple bond is formed.
If ethanol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid to about 170 °C, ethene is formed.
According to Zaitsev's rule, the more highly substituted alkene is preferentially formed.
In E2 elimination, the splitting off happens in a single step.
With haloalkanes, elimination often competes with nucleophilic substitution.
High temperatures favour elimination.
With a very bulky base, the less substituted alkene is preferentially formed.

abschnitte.text: The word **elimination** comes from the Latin “eliminare” and means to remove. One atom or group of atoms is removed from each of two neighbouring carbon atoms. These two parts join to form a small molecule, for example water or HBr. In their place, a **double bond** forms between the two carbon atoms. The reverse reaction, in which something is added to a double bond, is called **addition**.

When water is split off, it is called **dehydration**. The classic example is ethanol heated with concentrated sulphuric acid to about 170 °C. This produces the gas **ethene**, the most important starting material for the plastic polyethylene. At lower temperatures, on the other hand, mainly diethyl ether is formed.

HBr can be split off from **haloalkanes** such as bromobutane. Usually a strong base is used, typically potassium hydroxide in ethanol. This is called **dehydrohalogenation**. In a similar way, industry makes vinyl chloride, the starting material for the plastic PVC.

Often the double bond can form in different places. **Zaitsev's rule**, after the Russian chemist Alexander Zaitsev, says that usually the more highly substituted, that is, more stable alkene is formed. That is why 2-bromobutane gives mainly but-2-ene. But if a very bulky base such as potassium tert-butoxide is used, the less substituted alkene is preferentially formed. This product is called the **Hofmann product**.

In **E2 elimination**, both parts are split off at the same time in a single step. In **E1 elimination**, one group breaks away first and a carbocation is formed; only afterwards is a proton given off. With haloalkanes, a **nucleophilic substitution** often takes place at the same time. High temperatures and strong, bulky bases favour elimination, while lower temperatures tend to favour substitution.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hydrocarbon with at least one C=C double bond.
The splitting off of water from a molecule.
A substance that can take up protons (H⁺).
A hydrocarbon in which a hydrogen atom is replaced by a halogen such as bromine.
The adding of a molecule to a multiple bond, the opposite of elimination.

gewusst: The German name “Saytzeff” is an old German spelling of the Russian name Zaitsev.
Ethene is also a natural plant hormone that makes fruit such as bananas ripen faster.
In E2 elimination, the two groups split off usually sit exactly opposite each other, like the two ends of a seesaw.

teile.einleitung: A mixture forms when you put two or more substances together without a new substance being created. Muesli, sand with stones or salad dressing are mixtures. The exciting part is that mixtures can be separated back into their parts.
