wichtigste: A mixture consists of at least two substances that do not combine chemically.
In some mixtures you can see the individual parts, for example in muesli.
In other mixtures you cannot see the parts, for example in salt water.
Oil and water do not mix; after a while the oil floats on top.
With a sieve you separate large parts from small ones.
With a magnet you can get iron out of a mixture.

abschnitte.text: If you pour sand and stones together, you get a **mixture**. Each substance keeps its properties: the stones stay hard and the sand stays grainy. Muesli is also a mixture of flakes, nuts and fruit. In contrast, a chemical reaction creates a completely **new substance**.

In a **heterogeneous mixture** you can recognise the different parts with the naked eye or with a magnifying glass. Examples are muesli, granite or sand with stones. In a **homogeneous mixture** everything looks the same, even though several substances are in it. Salt water, air and squash are such mixtures.

You can shake oil and water hard, but after a short time they separate again. The oil is lighter and floats on top. With the help of egg or mustard, however, you can combine the two into an **emulsion**; this is how mayonnaise is made, for example. Milk is also an emulsion of tiny droplets of fat in water.

You separate pasta from the cooking water with a **sieve**, and peas and rice can also be separated this way. You get iron nails out of sand with a **magnet**. You can pour dirty water through a coffee filter; this is called **filtering**. If you let salt water evaporate, the salt is left behind.

If you mix blue and yellow paint, it turns green, and yet both dyes are still in it. Concrete is a mixture of cement, sand, gravel and water. In Switzerland, salt is obtained from salty water in **salt works** such as those at Schweizerhalle or Bex. In sewage treatment plants, dirt is separated from waste water so that clean water can flow back into rivers and lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several substances together that have not combined into a new substance.
A mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix, such as oil and water.
Pouring a mixture through a fine filter so that solid parts are caught.
When water slowly turns into water vapour and disappears.

gewusst: The air we breathe is also a mixture of several gases.
Gold panners separate gold from sand because gold is much heavier and stays behind in the pan.
In Swiss streams such as the Grosse Fontanne in the Napf area, hobby gold prospectors also pan gold out of the sand.

teile.einleitung: Thermosetting plastics, or thermosets, are plastics that stay firm and hard after curing, even when strongly heated. Their molecules are linked together like a dense, three dimensional net. That is why they are found wherever it gets hot or great strength is needed.
wichtigste: Thermosets do not melt; when heated very strongly they decompose.
Their molecules are closely cross linked in three dimensions.
Bakelite is considered the world's first fully synthetic plastic.
Bakelite was invented by Leo Baekeland.
Pan handles and sockets are often made of thermoset, because it is heat resistant.
Glass fibre reinforced plastic with synthetic resin is used for boat hulls and rotor blades.
Elastomers are only loosely cross linked and are therefore rubbery.

abschnitte.text: Plastics are divided into three groups: **thermoplastics**, **elastomers** and **thermosets**. The German word “Duroplast” comes from the Latin “durus”, which means hard. Thermosets are shaped once and then cure. After that they can no longer be melted and reshaped. They are hard, strong and often brittle, which means they can break with a hard knock.

Plastics consist of very long chains of molecules, the **polymers**. In a thermoset these chains are firmly linked to one another at many points; they are **closely cross linked**. You can picture this like a dense climbing net. That is why heat cannot make the chains slide past each other. If it gets too hot, the bonds break and the material chars instead of melting.

In 1907 the Belgian American chemist **Leo Baekeland** made a hard plastic from phenol and formaldehyde. He named it after himself, **Bakelite**. Bakelite is considered the world's first fully synthetic plastic. Telephones, radio cases, light switches and jewellery used to be made from it. Today old Bakelite devices are popular collector's items.

Because thermosets are heat resistant, they are used to make pan handles, sockets and parts in electrical appliances. They do not conduct electricity and so protect against electric shocks. A well known thermoset is **melamine resin**, from which children's crockery and furniture surfaces are made. **Epoxy adhesive** also cures into a thermoset after its two components are mixed.

Synthetic resins are often reinforced with glass or carbon fibres. This produces, for example, **glass fibre reinforced plastic**, GRP for short. It is light and very strong and is used for boat hulls, the rotor blades of wind turbines and skis. With carbon fibres, particularly light parts are made for bicycle frames, racing cars and aircraft.

Thermoplastics such as PET can be melted down and reshaped. That is not possible with thermosets, because they do not melt. At most they can be ground up and used as a **filler**, or burned. That is why researchers are looking for new synthetic resins that can be recycled more easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: A giant molecule made of many identical building blocks linked together.
A plastic that softens when heated and can be reshaped.
A rubbery plastic that can be stretched and springs back.
When a liquid synthetic resin becomes solid through a chemical reaction.
A liquid or sticky starting material from which a thermoset is made by curing.

gewusst: Bakelite was so versatile that it used to be called “the material of a thousand uses”.
A rotor blade of a large wind turbine can be more than 80 metres long and is made mostly of fibre composite.
Thermosets burn rather than melt, which is why an overheated pan handle smells burnt.

teile.einleitung: Faraday's laws describe how much substance is deposited at an electrode during electrolysis. The English researcher Michael Faraday discovered them in the 1830s. With them you can calculate exactly how long a current has to flow to obtain, for example, one gram of copper or silver.
wichtigste: Faraday's first law states: the mass deposited is proportional to the charge that has flowed.
The charge is calculated as current times time, that is, Q = I · t.
The second law states: the same charge deposits amounts of substance in the ratio 1/z, where z is the charge number of the ion.
For 1 mol of electrons you need about 96,485 coulombs; this is the Faraday constant.
Michael Faraday published the laws in the 1830s.
The laws are important for making aluminium, chrome plating and gold plating.

abschnitte.text: **Michael Faraday** lived in England from 1791 to 1867 and was one of the most important natural scientists of his time. He came from a poor family, worked as a bookbinder's apprentice and taught himself a great deal. Later he did research on electricity, magnetism and chemistry at the Royal Institution in London. He introduced terms such as electrode, anode, cathode and ion together with the scholar William Whewell. In the 1830s he published his laws of electrolysis.

In **electrolysis**, current flows through a solution or a melt, and substances are deposited at the electrodes. Faraday found that the more electric **charge** flows through the solution, the more substance is deposited, in exact proportion. The charge Q is the current I times the time t. Twice as much current or twice as long a time therefore gives twice the amount of substance.

The second law takes into account how many electrons an ion needs. A silver ion Ag⁺ needs only one electron, a copper ion Cu²⁺ two and an aluminium ion Al³⁺ three. With the same charge, you therefore deposit only half as many moles of copper as of silver. This number is called the **charge number** z.

The **Faraday constant** F is about 96,485 coulombs per mole and is the charge of 1 mol of electrons. The mass deposited is calculated with m = M · I · t / (z · F). If 2 amperes flow through copper sulphate solution for one hour, this produces about 2.37 g of copper. For 1 mol of aluminium you need three times F, that is, about 289,500 coulombs. With a current of 5 amperes it takes about 5.4 hours for 1 mol of electrons to flow.

The laws are the basis of **electroplating**, in which objects are coated with a thin layer of metal, for example in chrome plating, nickel plating or gold plating. Aluminium is obtained by electrolysis of a melt and needs enormous amounts of electricity for it. In Switzerland, one of the first aluminium smelters in Europe was set up in 1888 at Neuhausen am Rheinfall; the hydropower of the Rhine supplied the energy. Pure copper for electric cables is also refined electrolytically.

begriffe.erklaerung: Breaking down a substance with electric current.
An amount of electricity, measured in coulombs; 1 coulomb flows when 1 ampere flows for one second.
The charge of 1 mol of electrons, about 96,485 coulombs.
States how many electrons an ion has to take in or give up.
A conductor through which current flows into or out of a solution or melt.

gewusst: Every year in London, Faraday gave Christmas lectures for children, a tradition that still exists today.
With a current of 1 ampere for 965 seconds, you deposit exactly one hundredth of a mole of silver, about 1.08 g.
The unit of electrical capacitance, the farad, is named after Michael Faraday.

teile.einleitung: The Avogadro constant tells you how many particles there are in one mole of a substance. There are unimaginably many, about 602 sextillion. With this number, chemists link the tiny world of atoms to amounts that can be weighed on a balance.
wichtigste: Since 2019 the Avogadro constant has been fixed at exactly 6.02214076·10²³ per mole.
Its unit is per mole, written mol⁻¹.
A mole is the amount of substance that contains exactly this many particles.
It is named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro.
In 1865 Josef Loschmidt was the first to estimate how many particles there are in a gas.
In 1909 Jean-Baptiste Perrin proposed the name “Avogadro's number”.
Other natural constants are linked to it, such as the Boltzmann constant and the Faraday constant.

abschnitte.text: Atoms and molecules are so small that they cannot be counted one by one. That is why chemists calculate in packets, just as you buy eggs by the dozen. Such a packet is called a **mole** and contains exactly 6.02214076·10²³ particles. This number is the **Avogadro constant**, and its unit is mol⁻¹.

One mole of water weighs about 18 grams, roughly one big gulp. So it contains about 6·10²³ water molecules. In 9 grams of water, that is half a mole, there are correspondingly about 3.0·10²³ molecules. In this way you can count particles with a balance and the **molar mass** without seeing them.

In 1811 the Italian physicist **Amedeo Avogadro** made a bold suggestion. Equal volumes of gas at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of particles, whatever the gas. At the time few people believed him, and only decades later did his idea catch on. Avogadro himself did not yet know the number.

In 1865 the Austrian scientist **Josef Loschmidt** estimated the size of molecules and so, for the first time, the number of particles in gases. The Frenchman **Jean-Baptiste Perrin** determined the number more precisely and in 1909 proposed the name “Avogadro's number”. Later it was determined particularly precisely by measuring an almost perfectly round sphere of silicon 28. Since the reform of the units of measurement in 2019, the value has been fixed exactly and is no longer measured.

If you divide the universal gas constant R by the Avogadro constant, you get the **Boltzmann constant**. It describes the energy of a single particle instead of a whole mole. If you multiply the Avogadro constant by the elementary charge of an electron, you get the **Faraday constant** of about 96,500 coulombs per mole. This is needed to calculate the amount of electricity required in electrolysis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit for amount of substance; one mole contains about 6·10²³ particles.
How many grams one mole of a substance weighs; for water about 18 grams.
A number in nature that never changes.
The smallest electric charge, carried by an electron or a proton.

gewusst: If you counted one water molecule from a mole of water every second, it would take more than a million times longer than the age of the universe.
The silicon sphere used for the measurement was so round that, enlarged to the size of the Earth, it would have hills only a few metres high.
In the USA, chemistry fans celebrate “Mole Day” on 23 October, because there the date is written as 10/23.

teile.einleitung: Calorimetry is the measurement of amounts of heat that are released or used up in chemical reactions, in melting or in burning. The measuring device is called a calorimeter. It is used, for example, to find out how much energy there is in food or fuels.
wichtigste: Calorimetry is the measurement of amounts of heat.
Liquid water has a specific heat capacity of about 4.18 J/(g·K).
200 g of water take in about 4.2 kJ of heat when warmed by 5 K.
The calorimeter constant shows how much heat the device itself takes in per kelvin.
A Dewar flask prevents heat losses.
A bomb calorimeter measures the change in internal energy at constant volume.
Unlike the net calorific value, the gross calorific value includes the heat of condensation of water.
Lavoisier and Laplace built an ice calorimeter in the 1780s.

abschnitte.text: The word **calorimetry** comes from the Latin calor for “heat” and the Greek metron for “measure”. In many reactions heat is released; they are called **exothermic**. In others heat is taken in; they are called endothermic. A **calorimeter** measures how large these amounts of heat are. Usually this is done by measuring how much a known amount of water warms up. Heat is given in joules or kilojoules.

To warm 1 gram of water by 1 kelvin, you need about 4.18 joules. This value is called the **specific heat capacity**. The heat is calculated as mass times heat capacity times temperature change. If 200 g of water warm up by 5 K, they have therefore taken in about 4.2 kJ. Because the container and the thermometer also absorb some heat, the **calorimeter constant** of the device is determined first.

If you mix 50 mL of hydrochloric acid and 50 mL of sodium hydroxide solution, each at 1 mol/L, the solution warms up by about 6.8 K. The 100 g of solution have taken in about 2.8 kJ of heat. Because 0.05 mol of acid were neutralised, this gives an **enthalpy of neutralisation** of about minus 57 kJ per mole. The minus sign shows that the reaction gives off heat. For such experiments a double-walled, evacuated **Dewar flask** is often used, similar to a vacuum flask.

In a **bomb calorimeter**, a sample burns in a tightly sealed steel container with pure oxygen. The container stands in a water bath, whose warming is measured precisely. Because the volume stays the same, the change in **internal energy** is measured directly. This is how the energy content of food, wood, heating oil or coal is determined. The **gross calorific value** also includes the heat released when the water vapour formed turns liquid again; the net calorific value does not.

In the 1780s the French scientists Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace built an **ice calorimeter**. They measured heat by how much ice melted, and even used it to study the heat given off by a live guinea pig. Heat used to be given in **calories**; 1 kilocalorie corresponds to about 4.18 kilojoules. On food packaging in Switzerland, both figures, kJ and kcal, are still given today. Modern condensing boilers use the heat of condensation of the water vapour and so save energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device for measuring amounts of heat.
The heat that 1 gram of a substance needs to warm up by 1 kelvin.
The name for a reaction that gives off heat.
A double-walled container with a vacuum in between, like a vacuum flask.
All the heat released when a substance burns, including the heat of condensation.

gewusst: Lavoisier and Laplace used a live guinea pig for their measurements.
The vacuum flask goes back to the Dewar flask, which James Dewar invented in 1892.
Water can store a particularly large amount of heat, which is why lakes and seas even out the climate.

teile.einleitung: Antoine de Lavoisier was a French scientist who fundamentally changed chemistry in the 18th century. With precise measurements on the balance, he showed what really happens when something burns and gave oxygen its name. That is why he is often called the father of modern chemistry.
wichtigste: Antoine de Lavoisier came from France and lived from 1743 to 1794.
He disproved the old phlogiston theory of combustion.
He named oxygen “oxygène” in French.
The balance was his most important measuring instrument.
He showed that water is a compound of two elements.
His wife Marie-Anne helped with the experiments and drew his apparatus.
In 1794, during the French Revolution, he was executed by guillotine.

abschnitte.text: Antoine Laurent de Lavoisier was born in **Paris** in 1743 and came from a wealthy family. He first studied law but was interested above all in the natural sciences. To earn money, he worked as a **tax farmer**, that is, a tax collector for the king. He put his free time and his fortune into a large laboratory of his own.

In his experiments, Lavoisier weighed all the substances very precisely before and after the reaction. He discovered that the **total mass** stays the same if all the gases are counted. This **law of conservation of mass** is still a foundation of chemistry today. It says that in a chemical reaction nothing is lost and nothing new is created.

People used to believe in the **phlogiston theory**: when something burned, an invisible substance called phlogiston escaped. But Lavoisier showed that metals become heavier when they burn, because they combine with a component of the air. He called this component **oxygène**, oxygen in English. This disproved the old theory.

Lavoisier proved that water is not an element but a compound of **hydrogen** and oxygen. He called hydrogen “hydrogène”, which means “water former”. In 1789 his famous textbook appeared, in which he set out a list of the elements known at the time. In the same year the **French Revolution** began.

His wife **Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier** was an important collaborator. She helped with the experiments, wrote down measurements and translated English scientific texts into French. Because she had learned to draw, she made precise pictures of his **apparatus**. After his death she made sure that his works were published.

During the French Revolution, the tax farmers came under suspicion of having enriched themselves. Lavoisier was arrested and executed by **guillotine** in Paris on 8 May 1794. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange is said to have remarked that it took only a moment to cut off that head, but a hundred years might not be enough to produce another like it. Today Lavoisier is regarded as the **father of modern chemistry**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary substance that people used to believe escaped during burning.
A basic substance that cannot be broken down further chemically.
In a chemical reaction, the total mass stays the same.
A device for executions that was used during the French Revolution.

gewusst: The name “oxygène” means “acid former”, because Lavoisier believed that all acids contained oxygen, which later turned out to be wrong.
Lavoisier's list of elements also included light and heat, which are no longer counted as elements today.
Lavoisier also helped to prepare the metric system with the metre and the kilogram.
